questions.s: A 2 kg block on a smooth plane inclined at 30° is tied by a light string, running parallel to the slope over a frictionless pulley at the top, to a 3 kg mass hanging freely. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the acceleration of the system?
questions.e: The hanging weight (30 N) pulls one way and the slope component of the block's weight, 2 × 10 × sin 30° = 10 N, the other way. a = (30 − 10)/(2 + 3) = 4 m/s². 6 m/s² ignores the slope component and 8 m/s² adds it.

questions.s: A 5 kg block on a rough plane inclined at 37° is tied by a string, running parallel to the slope over a frictionless pulley at the top, to a hanging mass m. The coefficient of static friction is 0.5. Take g = 10 m/s², sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8. For which range of m does the block stay at rest?
questions.e: The slope component of weight is 30 N and the maximum friction is 0.5 × 40 = 20 N. If the block tends to slide down, friction acts up: mg ≥ 30 − 20 = 10 N, so m ≥ 1 kg. If it tends to slide up, friction acts down: mg ≤ 30 + 20 = 50 N, so m ≤ 5 kg. 3 kg only balances the slope component with no friction.

questions.s: Which statement correctly describes the weight of an object?
o: the amount of matter in it, in kilograms
the gravitational force on it, in newtons
a quantity that is the same on every planet
the reading of a scale under it, in any lift
questions.e: Weight is the gravitational force on an object, W = mg, measured in newtons, and it changes with g. The amount of matter is mass, which is the same everywhere; a scale in an accelerating lift shows the apparent weight, not the true weight.

questions.s: Two forces, each of magnitude 10 N, act on a particle with an angle of 120° between them. What is the magnitude of their resultant?
questions.e: Two equal forces at 120° form, with their resultant, an equilateral triangle: R² = 10² + 10² + 2 × 10 × 10 × cos 120° = 100, so R = 10 N. 10√3 N is the resultant at 60°, and 20 N is for parallel forces.

questions.s: A light spring with spring constant 100 N/m is cut into two equal halves. The two halves are then used side by side (in parallel) to support a load. What is the spring constant of the combination?
questions.e: Each half stretches half as much under the same force, so each has k = 200 N/m. In parallel the constants add: 200 + 200 = 400 N/m. 200 N/m stops after cutting, and 100 N/m wrongly assumes cutting and recombining cancel out.

questions.s: A 1 kg book is held against a vertical wall by a horizontal push of 40 N. The coefficient of static friction between book and wall is 0.5. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the friction force on the book?
questions.e: The normal force equals the push, 40 N, so the maximum friction is 0.5 × 40 = 20 N. Only 10 N is needed to balance the weight, so static friction is 10 N upward. 20 N is the limit, not the actual value.

questions.s: A 2 kg box is pressed against a vertical wall by a horizontal force F. The coefficient of static friction between box and wall is 0.4. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the smallest F that stops the box sliding down?
questions.e: Friction must hold the weight: μF ≥ mg, so F ≥ 20/0.4 = 50 N. 8 N is μmg, which wrongly takes the normal force to be the weight, and 5 N forgets g.

questions.s: The resultant force on a body is doubled and, at the same time, its mass is halved. How does its acceleration change?
questions.e: a = F/m, so a′ = 2F/(m/2) = 4F/m: four times as large. Answering 'unchanged' treats the two changes as cancelling, but halving the mass increases the acceleration rather than reducing it.

questions.s: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s brakes with a constant braking force of 4000 N (ignore other resistance). What are its stopping time and stopping distance?
questions.e: a = 4000/1000 = 4 m/s², so t = v/a = 20/4 = 5 s and s = v²/(2a) = 400/8 = 50 m (or the average speed 10 m/s × 5 s). 100 m uses s = vt, forgetting the speed falls to zero.

questions.s: A 60 kg painter sits in a 20 kg chair hanging from a light rope that passes over a fixed frictionless pulley above him; he holds and pulls down on the free end of the rope. Take g = 10 m/s². What pull must he exert to rise with an acceleration of 1 m/s²?
questions.e: Treat painter plus chair (80 kg) as one body: two rope segments pull it up, each with tension T. 2T − 800 = 80 × 1, so T = 440 N, and his pull equals T. 880 N forgets that the rope he holds also pulls him up; 400 N is the value at constant speed.

questions.s: A 2 kg particle is in equilibrium under three forces. One of them, a force of 6 N towards the east, is suddenly removed. What is the particle's acceleration immediately afterwards?
questions.e: The other two forces had a resultant of 6 N west to balance the removed force, and they are unchanged, so the resultant is now 6 N west and a = 6/2 = 3 m/s² to the west. Answering 'east' gives the direction of the removed force, not of what remains.

questions.s: Spring A extends by 2 cm under a load of 4 N, and spring B extends by 4 cm under a load of 6 N (both within their elastic limits). Which statement is correct?
o: A is stiffer; its k is 200 N/m
B is stiffer; its k is 150 N/m
A is stiffer; its k is 2 N/m
questions.e: kA = 4/0.02 = 200 N/m and kB = 6/0.04 = 150 N/m, so A is stiffer. 2 N/m forgets to convert 2 cm to metres (it is 2 N/cm), and B only looks stiffer because it carries a larger load.

questions.s: In which direction does the normal force exerted by a surface on an object resting on it act?
questions.e: The normal force is the contact force at right angles to the surface ('normal' means perpendicular). It is vertical only when the surface is horizontal, and it need not equal the weight, for example on a slope or in an accelerating lift.

questions.s: A 3 kg block on a smooth horizontal table is joined by a light string over a frictionless pulley at the edge to a 2 kg mass hanging freely. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the tension in the string?
questions.e: a = 20/(3 + 2) = 4 m/s², and the tension alone accelerates the 3 kg block: T = 3 × 4 = 12 N. Check with the hanging mass: 20 − 12 = 2 × 4. 20 N would be the tension only if the system were held at rest.

questions.s: A ball is thrown vertically upward. Ignoring air resistance, what is the resultant force on the ball at the highest point of its flight?
o: zero, since it is momentarily at rest
the force of the throw, directed upward
questions.e: Once released, the only force on the ball is gravity, so the resultant is its weight, downward, at every point including the top. Being momentarily at rest does not mean zero force: the velocity is zero but the acceleration is still g downward.

questions.s: An 80 kg skydiver falls vertically at a constant (terminal) speed. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the air resistance on the skydiver?
questions.e: Constant speed means zero acceleration, so the air resistance balances the weight: 80 × 10 = 800 N, upward. Zero would mean free fall with acceleration g.

questions.s: An 80 kg skydiver is falling vertically, and at one instant the air resistance on her is 600 N. Take g = 10 m/s². What is her acceleration at that instant?
questions.e: The resultant force is 800 − 600 = 200 N downward, so a = 200/80 = 2.5 m/s² downward. 7.5 m/s² is 600/80, the air resistance alone, and 17.5 m/s² adds the forces.

questions.s: A 40 kg load hangs from a light, frictionless movable pulley. A light rope runs from a hook in the ceiling, down under the pulley and back up, so the pulley is held by two vertical rope segments; a worker holds the free end. Take g = 10 m/s². What force must the worker exert to hold the load at rest?
questions.e: The same tension T acts in both vertical segments supporting the pulley, so 2T = 400 N and T = 200 N, which is the worker's pull. 400 N ignores the second segment, and 100 N wrongly counts four supporting segments.

questions.s: A 40 kg load (including its light pulley) hangs from a movable pulley supported by two vertical segments of the same light rope; one end of the rope is fixed to the ceiling and a worker pulls the other end upward with a force of 250 N. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the acceleration of the load?
questions.e: The tension is 250 N in both segments, so the upward force on the load is 500 N. a = (500 − 400)/40 = 2.5 m/s² upward. 6.25 m/s² uses one segment and ignores the weight, and 12.5 m/s² ignores the weight.

questions.s: A horizontal force on a 4 kg block resting on a horizontal floor is slowly increased from zero. The friction force increases in proportion to the applied force up to 12 N, when the block starts to slide; after that the friction force stays at 10 N. Take g = 10 m/s². What are the coefficients of static and kinetic friction?
questions.e: The normal force is 40 N. The largest static friction, 12 N, gives μs = 12/40 = 0.3, and the sliding friction, 10 N, gives μk = 10/40 = 0.25. Swapping them would make kinetic friction larger than the maximum static friction, which is not the usual case; 3 and 2.5 divide by the mass instead of the weight.

questions.s: A 50 kg robot weighs 500 N on Earth. On Mars the gravitational field strength is 0.4 times Earth's. What is the robot's weight on Mars?
questions.e: Weight is proportional to g: W = 0.4 × 500 = 200 N, while the mass stays 50 kg. 20 N is 0.4 × 50, the mass multiplied instead of the weight, and 125 N divides by 0.4 instead of multiplying.

questions.s: A 2 kg block lies on top of a 3 kg block on a smooth horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction between the blocks is 0.4. A horizontal force of 10 N is applied to the top block. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the friction force between the blocks?
questions.e: If they move together, a = 10/5 = 2 m/s², and friction is the only horizontal force on the lower block, so it must be 3 × 2 = 6 N. This is below the maximum 0.4 × 20 = 8 N, so they do move together and friction is 6 N. 8 N assumes friction is always at its maximum; 4 N uses the top block's mass.

questions.s: A certain force gives a body of mass m₁ an acceleration of 6 m/s² and gives a body of mass m₂ an acceleration of 3 m/s². What acceleration does the same force give the two bodies when they are fastened together?
questions.e: F = 6m₁ = 3m₂, so m₂ = 2m₁ and the combined mass is 3m₁. Then a = F/(3m₁) = 6m₁/(3m₁) = 2 m/s². 4.5 m/s² averages the accelerations, and the combined body must accelerate less than either part alone.

questions.s: A puck sliding at 10 m/s on a horizontal surface comes to rest after travelling 20 m, slowed only by friction. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the coefficient of kinetic friction?
questions.e: From v² = 2as, a = 100/40 = 2.5 m/s², and since a = μg, μ = 2.5/10 = 0.25. 0.5 forgets the factor 2 in v² = 2as, and 2.5 is the deceleration itself, not divided by g.

questions.s: Two blocks on a smooth plane inclined at 30° are joined by a light string parallel to the slope: a 3 kg block above and a 2 kg block below. A force of 40 N parallel to the slope pulls the 3 kg block up the slope. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the tension in the string?
questions.e: For the system: 40 − 50 sin 30° = 5a, so a = 15/5 = 3 m/s². For the 2 kg block: T − 20 sin 30° = 2 × 3, so T = 16 N (the tension equals 40 × 2/5, independent of the angle). 24 N uses the 3 kg block's share, and 10 N only balances the lower block's slope component.

questions.s: Which statement is Newton's first law of motion?
o: A body accelerates in proportion to the resultant force acting on it
A body always slows down and stops unless a force keeps on pushing it
A body pushes back with an equal and opposite force on whatever pushes it
A body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless a resultant force acts
questions.e: The first law is the law of inertia: without a resultant force, a body keeps its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line. Proportional acceleration is the second law, the equal and opposite push is the third law, and the idea that motion needs a force is the old misconception the first law corrects.

questions.s: A light spring hangs vertically. With a 0.3 kg mass attached its length is 16 cm, and with a 0.5 kg mass attached its length is 20 cm. Take g = 10 m/s². What is its natural length?
questions.e: An extra 2 N gives an extra 4 cm, so k = 0.5 N/cm. The 3 N load stretches it by 6 cm, so the natural length is 16 − 6 = 10 cm. 6 cm is the extension, not the length, and 12 cm subtracts the 4 cm difference from 16 cm.

questions.s: A 60 kg passenger stands on a bathroom scale in a lift. While the lift is starting, the scale reads 660 N. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the lift's acceleration?
questions.e: N − mg = ma gives 660 − 600 = 60a, so a = 1 m/s², and it is upward because the reading exceeds the weight. 11 m/s² is 660/60, which forgets to subtract the weight.

questions.s: A 3 kg mass hangs from a spring balance in a lift, and the balance reads 24 N. Take g = 10 m/s². Which motion of the lift is consistent with this reading?
o: moving up and speeding up at 2 m/s²
moving down and slowing down at 2 m/s²
moving at a constant speed of 2 m/s
moving up and slowing down at 2 m/s²
questions.e: The reading is below the weight (30 N), so the acceleration is downward: 30 − 24 = 3a gives a = 2 m/s² downward. Moving up while slowing down has a downward acceleration. Moving down while slowing down has an upward acceleration and would give 36 N.

questions.s: A block slides down a rough plane inclined at 30° at constant speed. It is then projected up the same plane with a speed of 6 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s². How far up the plane does it travel before stopping?
questions.e: Sliding down at constant speed means friction equals mg sin 30°. Moving up, friction and the weight component both act down the slope, so a = 2g sin 30° = 10 m/s² and s = v²/(2a) = 36/20 = 1.8 m. 3.6 m ignores friction (a = 5 m/s²).

questions.s: An 8 kg block is held at rest on a smooth plane inclined at 30° by a rope parallel to the slope. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the normal force of the plane on the block?
questions.e: The rope is parallel to the slope, so only the weight component mg cos 30° = 80 × (√3/2) = 40√3 N acts into the plane, and the normal force balances it. 40 N is mg sin 30°, which equals the rope tension.

questions.s: A 1 kg ball and a 5 kg ball are released together from the same height in a vacuum. Which statement is correct?
o: it depends on the height of release
they land at the same time
questions.e: The heavier ball has five times the weight but also five times the mass, so a = mg/m = g for both, and they land together. A larger force does not mean a larger acceleration when the mass is larger in the same ratio.

questions.s: A locomotive pulls three identical carriages, each of mass 10 000 kg, along a level track with an acceleration of 0.2 m/s². The resistance on each carriage is 2000 N. What is the force in the coupling between the first and second carriages?
questions.e: That coupling pulls the last two carriages: T = 2 × (10 000 × 0.2 + 2000) = 2 × 4000 = 8000 N. 12 000 N is the force in the coupling behind the locomotive, which pulls all three carriages, and 4000 N ignores the resistance or counts only one carriage.

questions.s: A lift starts from rest and moves upward, reaching 4 m/s in 2 s with uniform acceleration. A 50 kg passenger stands on a scale in the lift. Take g = 10 m/s². What does the scale read during these 2 s?
questions.e: a = 4/2 = 2 m/s² upward, so N = m(g + a) = 50 × 12 = 600 N. 100 N is only ma, and 400 N would be the reading for a downward acceleration.

questions.s: Ahmed drags a box across a level floor at constant velocity with a horizontal rope whose tension is 30 N. What is the friction force on the box?
questions.e: Constant velocity means zero resultant force, so friction balances the pull: 30 N opposite to the motion. Friction larger than 30 N would make the box slow down.

questions.s: A 10 kg block rests on a plane inclined at 30°. Take g = 10 m/s². What are the components of its weight along the slope and perpendicular to the slope?
questions.e: Along the slope: mg sin 30° = 100 × ½ = 50 N; perpendicular: mg cos 30° = 50√3 N. Swapping them is the classic mistake; check with θ → 0, when the along-slope component must vanish, so it goes with sin θ.

questions.s: A small block sits on the smooth sloping face of a wedge inclined at 37° to the horizontal. The wedge is pushed horizontally with an acceleration that keeps the block at rest relative to the wedge. Take g = 10 m/s², sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8. What is this acceleration?
questions.e: Only gravity and the normal force act. Vertically N cos 37° = mg; horizontally N sin 37° = ma. Dividing gives a = g tan 37° = 10 × 0.75 = 7.5 m/s². 6 m/s² is g sin 37°, the block's acceleration down a stationary smooth slope.

questions.s: Two workers push a 20 kg crate across a floor in the same direction with 40 N and 60 N, and it moves at constant velocity. The worker pushing with 60 N suddenly stops pushing. What is the crate's deceleration while it is still sliding?
questions.e: At constant velocity, kinetic friction equals 40 + 60 = 100 N, and it stays 100 N while the crate slides. The resultant becomes 100 − 40 = 60 N against the motion, so the deceleration is 60/20 = 3 m/s². 2 m/s² uses only the 40 N push, and 5 m/s² ignores the remaining push.

questions.s: Ahmed (60 kg) and Carlos (40 kg) stand on smooth ice and push each other apart. During the push Ahmed's acceleration is 3 m/s². What is Carlos's acceleration?
questions.e: The force on Ahmed is 60 × 3 = 180 N, and by Newton's third law Carlos feels 180 N in the opposite direction, so a = 180/40 = 4.5 m/s². Equal forces do not give equal accelerations; the lighter person accelerates more. 2 m/s² uses the mass ratio the wrong way round.

questions.s: Two identical light spring balances are hooked end to end and hung from a ceiling, and a 2 kg mass is hung from the lower balance. Take g = 10 m/s². What do the balances read?
questions.e: Each light balance transmits the full 20 N load: the lower one holds the mass, and the upper one holds the lower balance (negligible weight) plus the mass. The load is not shared as it would be for balances side by side, so 10 N each is wrong.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg block on a smooth horizontal surface is pushed against a light spring of spring constant 400 N/m, compressing it by 5 cm, and is then released. What is the block's acceleration just after release?
questions.e: The spring force is kx = 400 × 0.05 = 20 N, so a = 20/0.5 = 40 m/s². 4000 m/s² uses x = 5 cm without converting, and 10 m/s² multiplies the force by the mass instead of dividing.

questions.s: A 2 kg block on a rough horizontal floor is attached to a horizontal light spring (spring constant 200 N/m) whose other end is fixed to a wall. The coefficient of static friction is 0.5. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the largest extension of the spring at which the block can remain at rest?
questions.e: Static friction can hold at most μmg = 0.5 × 20 = 10 N, so kx ≤ 10 N and x ≤ 10/200 = 0.05 m = 5 cm. 10 cm uses the weight (20 N) as the friction limit, and 1 cm forgets g.

questions.s: A block is released from rest on a rough plane inclined at 37°. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. Take g = 10 m/s², sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8. How long does it take to slide 8 m down the plane?
questions.e: a = g(sin 37° − μ cos 37°) = 10(0.6 − 0.2) = 4 m/s². From s = ½at², t² = 2 × 8/4 = 4, so t = 2 s. √2 s forgets the ½ in s = ½at², and 4 s forgets to take the square root.

questions.s: A 3 kg block lies on a rough horizontal table (coefficient of kinetic friction 0.2). Light strings over frictionless pulleys at opposite edges of the table connect it to a 4 kg mass hanging on one side and a 1 kg mass hanging on the other. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the acceleration of the system?
questions.e: The 4 kg side wins, so the block moves towards it and friction (0.2 × 30 = 6 N) opposes that. Net force = 40 − 10 − 6 = 24 N on a total mass of 8 kg, so a = 3 m/s². 3.75 m/s² ignores friction, and 6 m/s² divides by the 4 kg mass only.

questions.s: In which direction does the weight of an object near the Earth's surface act?
o: towards the centre of the Earth
perpendicular to the surface it rests on
in the direction of its motion
away from the centre of the Earth
questions.e: Weight is the gravitational pull of the Earth, which points towards the Earth's centre (vertically downward) whatever the object is resting on or however it moves. It is the normal force, not the weight, that is perpendicular to a supporting surface.

questions.s: A 20 kg sledge is pulled at constant velocity across level snow by a rope at 37° above the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.75. Take g = 10 m/s², sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8. What is the tension in the rope?
questions.e: N = 200 − 0.6T and the horizontal balance gives 0.8T = 0.75(200 − 0.6T) = 150 − 0.45T, so 1.25T = 150 and T = 120 N. Check: N = 128 N, friction 96 N = 0.8 × 120. 150 N takes N = mg and forgets that the rope lifts the sledge slightly.

questions.s: A light string passes over two small frictionless pulleys at the same height, with a 3 kg mass hanging from each end. A mass M is hung from the midpoint of the string between the pulleys. In equilibrium, each half of the string between the pulleys makes 30° with the vertical. Take g = 10 m/s². What is M?
questions.e: The tension everywhere in the string is 30 N (it supports a 3 kg mass at each end). At the midpoint, 2T cos 30° = Mg, so 2 × 30 × (√3/2) = 10M and M = 3√3 kg. 3 kg is the answer when the angle with the vertical is 60°, and 6 kg assumes vertical strings.

questions.s: The Earth pulls the Moon with a gravitational force F. How large is the gravitational force of the Moon on the Earth?
questions.e: The two pulls form a Newton's third-law pair, so they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. The Earth's much larger mass means the same force gives it a much smaller acceleration, which is why it seems as if only the Moon is affected.

questions.s: A 1000 kg car tows a 500 kg trailer along a level road. The driving force on the car is 3000 N and resistance can be ignored. What is the tension in the tow bar?
questions.e: For car plus trailer, a = 3000/1500 = 2 m/s². The tow bar alone accelerates the trailer: T = 500 × 2 = 1000 N. 2000 N is the resultant force on the car, and 1500 N simply halves the driving force.

questions.s: A 10 kg box rests on the floor of a lift that is accelerating downward at 2 m/s². The coefficient of kinetic friction between box and floor is 0.5. Take g = 10 m/s². What horizontal force is needed to slide the box across the floor at constant velocity relative to the lift?
questions.e: Vertically, mg − N = ma, so N = 10 × (10 − 2) = 80 N, and friction is 0.5 × 80 = 40 N, which the push must balance. 50 N uses N = mg as in a stationary lift, and 60 N uses g + a, the value for an upward acceleration.

questions.s: A resultant force of 1 N acts on a mass of 1 kg. What is its acceleration?
questions.e: a = F/m = 1/1 = 1 m/s²; this is the definition of the newton. g (about 9.8 or 10 m/s²) is the acceleration of free fall, which has nothing to do with this force.

questions.s: Three horizontal forces act on a particle: 9 N towards the east, 3 N towards the west and 8 N towards the north. What is the magnitude of the resultant force?
questions.e: The east-west forces combine to 9 − 3 = 6 N east, which is perpendicular to 8 N north, so R = √(6² + 8²) = 10 N. 14 N adds 6 and 8 directly, and 20 N adds all three magnitudes.

questions.s: Blocks of 1 kg and 3 kg on a smooth horizontal floor are joined by a light spring of spring constant 100 N/m. A constant horizontal force of 8 N pulls the 3 kg block, and the blocks move with the same acceleration while the spring's extension stays constant. What is the extension of the spring?
questions.e: Both blocks have a = 8/4 = 2 m/s². The spring is the only horizontal force on the 1 kg block, so it pulls with 1 × 2 = 2 N, and x = 2/100 = 0.02 m = 2 cm. 6 cm uses the 3 kg block's mass, and 8 cm assumes the spring carries the full 8 N.

questions.s: Why is it usually harder to start a heavy box sliding across a floor than to keep it sliding?
o: the box loses its inertia once it moves
kinetic friction is greater than static friction
the normal force on the box drops once it is moving
maximum static friction exceeds kinetic friction
questions.e: Before sliding, the push must exceed the maximum static friction μsN; once the box moves, the friction is μkN, and usually μk < μs. The mass, and so the inertia, and the normal force on a level floor do not change.

questions.s: A 2 kg block is pulled up a smooth plane inclined at 30° by a force of 16 N parallel to the slope. Take g = 10 m/s². What is its acceleration?
questions.e: The weight component down the slope is 2 × 10 × sin 30° = 10 N, so a = (16 − 10)/2 = 3 m/s² up the slope. 8 m/s² ignores the weight component, and 13 m/s² adds it.

questions.s: A light frictionless pulley hangs from the ceiling of a lift, with masses of 3 kg and 1 kg on either end of a light string over it. The lift accelerates upward at 2 m/s². Take g = 10 m/s². What is the tension in the string?
questions.e: In the lift the effective gravity is g + a = 12 m/s², so the masses accelerate relative to the lift at (3 − 1) × 12/4 = 6 m/s². The 1 kg mass then accelerates upward at 2 + 6 = 8 m/s², so T − 10 = 8 and T = 18 N (check: 30 − 18 = 3 × 4). 15 N is the tension in a stationary lift.

questions.s: A passenger notices that a bathroom scale in a lift shows 80% of her true weight. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the acceleration of the lift?
questions.e: N = m(g − a) = 0.8mg, so a = 0.2g = 2 m/s², downward because the reading is less than the weight. 8 m/s² confuses the apparent gravity, 0.8g, with the lift's acceleration.

questions.s: A spring obeys Hooke's law. The load on it is tripled, staying within the limit of proportionality. What happens to the extension?
questions.e: Hooke's law says F = kx, so the extension is proportional to the load: three times the load gives three times the extension. Nothing is squared, so 9 times is wrong.

questions.s: A 2 kg box sits on top of a 3 kg box, which rests on a rough floor (coefficient of kinetic friction 0.2). A horizontal force on the lower box drags the stack along at constant velocity, and the top box does not slip. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the friction force on the top box?
questions.e: The top box moves at constant velocity, so the resultant force on it is zero; the only possible horizontal force on it is friction, which must therefore be 0 N. The floor friction on the stack is 0.2 × 50 = 10 N, but that acts on the lower box; 4 N wrongly applies μ to the top box.

questions.s: What resultant force is needed to give a 1500 kg car an acceleration of 2 m/s²?
questions.e: F = ma = 1500 × 2 = 3000 N. 750 N divides the mass by the acceleration instead of multiplying.

questions.s: What is the weight of a 7 kg bag of rice on Earth? Take g = 10 N/kg.
questions.e: W = mg = 7 × 10 = 70 N. 7 N confuses mass with weight, and 17 N adds g instead of multiplying.

questions.s: A light spring has a spring constant of 50 N/m. What is its extension when it supports a load of 2 N?
questions.e: x = F/k = 2/50 = 0.04 m = 4 cm. 25 cm comes from k/F, and 100 cm from kF; the extension is the force divided by the stiffness.

questions.s: A book slides to the right across a horizontal table and slows down. In which direction does the friction force on the book act?
questions.e: Kinetic friction opposes the sliding of the book relative to the table, so it acts to the left, against the motion. That is also why the book slows down: its acceleration is to the left.

questions.s: A hammer strikes a nail and exerts a force of 500 N on it. How large is the force of the nail on the hammer during the impact?
questions.e: By Newton's third law the nail pushes back on the hammer with an equal and opposite force, 500 N. This is why the hammer slows down sharply on impact.

questions.s: A force of 10 N acts at 30° above the horizontal. What is its vertical component?
questions.e: The vertical component is F sin 30° = 10 × ½ = 5 N. 5√3 N is F cos 30°, the horizontal component.

questions.s: A spacecraft far from all stars and planets moves at 2 km/s with its engines switched off. What happens to its motion?
o: it gradually slows down and then stops
it keeps its speed and direction
it starts to move in a circle
questions.e: With no resultant force, Newton's first law says the craft keeps a constant velocity: the same speed in the same straight line. No force is needed to keep it moving; slowing down would need a force against the motion.

questions.s: A 55 kg student stands on a bathroom scale in a lift moving upward at a constant speed of 3 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s². What does the scale read?
questions.e: At constant velocity the acceleration is zero, so N = mg = 550 N, the same as at rest. The scale reading depends on the acceleration, not on the speed.

questions.s: An 8 kg crate is pulled across a horizontal floor by a horizontal force of 30 N. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. Take g = 10 m/s². What is its acceleration?
questions.e: Friction = 0.25 × 80 = 20 N, so the resultant is 30 − 20 = 10 N and a = 10/8 = 1.25 m/s². 3.75 m/s² ignores friction, and 6.25 m/s² adds friction to the pull.

questions.s: A box slides down a smooth slope inclined at 53° to the horizontal. Take g = 10 m/s², sin 53° = 0.8, cos 53° = 0.6. What is its acceleration?
questions.e: Along a smooth slope a = g sin θ = 10 × 0.8 = 8 m/s². 6 m/s² uses cos 53°, the perpendicular component, and 10 m/s² is free fall.

questions.s: The coefficient of static friction between a block and a plank is 1/√3. The plank is slowly tilted from horizontal. At what angle to the horizontal does the block start to slide?
questions.e: Sliding starts when mg sin θ = μs mg cos θ, that is tan θ = μs = 1/√3, so θ = 30°. 60° comes from tan θ = √3, inverting the coefficient.

questions.s: Masses of 7 kg and 3 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley on a light string and are released. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the tension in the string?
questions.e: a = (7 − 3) × 10/(7 + 3) = 4 m/s². For the 3 kg mass moving up, T − 30 = 3 × 4, so T = 42 N. 50 N is merely the average of the two weights.

questions.s: A 6 kg trolley on a smooth horizontal bench is joined by a light string over a frictionless pulley at the end of the bench to a 2 kg mass hanging freely. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the tension in the string?
questions.e: a = 20/(6 + 2) = 2.5 m/s², and the string alone accelerates the trolley: T = 6 × 2.5 = 15 N. Check: 20 − 15 = 2 × 2.5. 10 N simply halves the hanging weight, and 5 N uses the 2 kg mass with a = 2.5 m/s².

questions.s: A 40 kg child stands on a scale in a lift that accelerates upward at 2.5 m/s². Take g = 10 m/s². What does the scale read?
questions.e: N − mg = ma gives N = 40 × (10 + 2.5) = 500 N. 300 N uses g − a, which is for a downward acceleration, and 100 N is ma alone.

questions.s: A 4 kg lantern hangs from the midpoint of a cable stretched between two poles. Each half of the cable makes 30° below the horizontal. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the tension in the cable?
questions.e: Vertically, 2T sin 30° = 40 N, so T × 1 = 40 N and T = 40 N. 40√3/3 N uses cos 30°, which would be right if the angle were measured from the vertical; 80 N uses only one half of the cable.

questions.s: Two light springs with spring constants 150 N/m and 50 N/m hang side by side (in parallel) and together support a 10 N load, both stretching by the same amount. What is the extension?
questions.e: In parallel the constants add: k = 150 + 50 = 200 N/m, so x = 10/200 = 0.05 m = 5 cm. 20 cm uses the weaker spring alone, and 10 cm uses the average constant 100 N/m.

questions.s: Blocks of 4 kg and 1 kg are in contact on a rough horizontal floor (coefficient of kinetic friction 0.2 for both). A horizontal force of 20 N pushes the 4 kg block, which pushes the 1 kg block ahead of it. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the contact force between the blocks?
questions.e: Total friction is 0.2 × 50 = 10 N, so a = (20 − 10)/5 = 2 m/s². For the 1 kg block, P − 0.2 × 10 = 1 × 2, so P = 4 N. 2 N forgets the friction on the front block, and 16 N gives the 4 kg block's share of the push.

questions.s: A 6 kg box on a horizontal floor is pulled by a rope with tension 25 N at 37° above the horizontal; the box does not leave the floor. Take g = 10 m/s², sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8. What is the normal force on the box?
questions.e: The rope's vertical component is 25 × 0.6 = 15 N upward, so N = 60 − 15 = 45 N. 40 N uses the cosine component (20 N), and 35 N subtracts the whole tension.

questions.s: A constant resultant force increases the speed of a 2 kg cart from 3 m/s to 7 m/s in 2 s, in a straight line. What is the force?
questions.e: a = (7 − 3)/2 = 2 m/s², so F = 2 × 2 = 4 N. 2 N forgets to multiply by the mass, and 7 N uses the final speed instead of the change in speed.

questions.s: A 5 kg box rests on a slope inclined at 37°. The coefficient of static friction is 0.8. Laila pushes it with a force of 10 N up the slope, parallel to it, and it stays at rest. Take g = 10 m/s², sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8. What is the friction force on the box?
questions.e: The weight component down the slope is 30 N, the push supplies 10 N up the slope, so static friction must supply the other 20 N up the slope. This is within the limit 0.8 × 40 = 32 N, so the box does stay at rest. 40 N would add the push to the weight component.

questions.s: An 800 kg lift car hangs from its cable and accelerates downward at 1 m/s². Take g = 10 m/s². What is the tension in the cable?
questions.e: mg − T = ma, so T = m(g − a) = 800 × 9 = 7200 N. 8800 N uses g + a, the value for an upward acceleration, and 8000 N is the weight.

questions.s: Two forces of 5 N and 12 N act at a point, at an angle that can be chosen freely. Which value cannot be the magnitude of their resultant?
questions.e: The resultant lies between 12 − 5 = 7 N (opposite) and 12 + 5 = 17 N (parallel); 13 N occurs when they are perpendicular. 6 N is below the minimum, so it is impossible.

questions.s: A block is projected up a rough slope inclined at 30° with a speed of 8 m/s. The coefficient of kinetic friction is √3/5. Take g = 10 m/s². The block stops and slides back down. What is its speed when it returns to its starting point?
questions.e: μg cos 30° = (√3/5)(10)(√3/2) = 3 m/s². Going up, a = 5 + 3 = 8 m/s², so it travels 64/16 = 4 m. Coming down, a = 5 − 3 = 2 m/s², so v² = 2 × 2 × 4 = 16 and v = 4 m/s. 8 m/s would only be true without friction.

questions.s: A 1 kg block rests on a 2 kg board lying on a smooth floor. The coefficient of friction between block and board is 0.3 (take static and kinetic values equal). A horizontal force of 15 N pulls the board. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the acceleration of the board?
questions.e: Friction can give the block at most 0.3 × 10 = 3 m/s², so moving together needs at most 3 × 3 = 9 N; 15 N is more, so the block slips. The board then feels 15 N forward and 3 N friction backward: a = 12/2 = 6 m/s². 5 m/s² wrongly assumes they move together.

questions.s: A 3 kg block hangs from a rope, and a 2 kg block hangs below it on a light string. The rope pulls the 3 kg block upward with 75 N. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the tension in the string between the blocks?
questions.e: For both blocks, a = (75 − 50)/5 = 5 m/s² upward. For the lower block, T − 20 = 2 × 5, so T = 30 N. 20 N is its weight, correct only without acceleration, and 45 N gives the 3 kg block's share of the pull.

questions.s: A 2 kg ball moves at 3 m/s. What is the magnitude of its momentum?
questions.e: p = mv = 2 × 3 = 6 kg·m/s. 9 is ½mv², the kinetic energy in joules, not the momentum; 1.5 comes from dividing the mass by the speed instead of multiplying.

questions.s: Which of the following is a correct SI unit of impulse?
questions.e: Impulse is force × time, so its unit is N·s, which equals kg·m/s, the unit of momentum. N·m is the unit of work, and kg·m/s² is simply the newton.

questions.s: A constant force of 20 N acts on a body for 0.5 s. What is the impulse of the force?
questions.e: I = FΔt = 20 × 0.5 = 10 N·s. 40 N·s comes from dividing the force by the time instead of multiplying, and 20 N·s ignores the time altogether.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg ball moving horizontally at 8 m/s hits a wall and rebounds along the same line at 6 m/s. What is the magnitude of the change in its momentum?
questions.e: Take the rebound direction as positive: Δp = 0.5 × (6 − (−8)) = 0.5 × 14 = 7 kg·m/s. Subtracting the speeds gives 1 kg·m/s, which ignores the reversal of direction.

questions.s: A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s and bounces straight back at 10 m/s. The contact lasts 0.02 s. What is the magnitude of the average force of the wall on the ball?
questions.e: Δp = 0.2 × (10 + 10) = 4 kg·m/s, so F = Δp/Δt = 4/0.02 = 200 N. 0 N wrongly assumes no momentum change because the speed is unchanged; 100 N treats the ball as simply stopping; 4 N forgets to divide by the time.

questions.s: Why does bending your knees when landing from a jump reduce the risk of injury?
o: It makes the change in momentum of the body smaller
It makes the impulse from the ground much smaller
It lengthens stopping time, so average force is smaller
It changes the body's momentum into gravitational potential energy
questions.e: The body's momentum must fall from the same value to zero either way, so the impulse is fixed. Bending the knees increases Δt, and since F = Δp/Δt the average force on the legs is smaller. The impulse and the momentum change are not reduced.

questions.s: A force acting on a 2 kg body, initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface, increases uniformly from 0 to 40 N in 0.2 s. What is the speed of the body at 0.2 s?
questions.e: The impulse is the area under the force–time graph: ½ × 40 × 0.2 = 4 N·s, so v = 4/2 = 2 m/s. Using 40 × 0.2 = 8 N·s forgets that the graph is a triangle and gives 4 m/s.

questions.s: A 60 kg skater standing at rest on smooth ice throws a 3 kg ball horizontally at 10 m/s. With what speed does the skater recoil?
questions.e: The total momentum stays zero: 60v = 3 × 10, so v = 30/60 = 0.5 m/s. 0.05 m/s ignores the ball's speed (3/60), and 200 m/s inverts the mass ratio.

questions.s: The total momentum of a system of bodies is conserved when
o: the net external force on the system is zero
all collisions inside the system are elastic
the bodies in the system have equal masses
the total kinetic energy remains constant
questions.e: Momentum is conserved whenever the resultant external force on the system is zero; the internal forces cancel in pairs by Newton's third law. Elasticity concerns kinetic energy only: inelastic collisions conserve momentum too.

questions.s: A 2000 kg truck moves at 10 m/s, and a 1000 kg car has the same momentum. Which statement is correct?
o: The car has half the kinetic energy of the truck
The car and truck have equal kinetic energy
The car has twice the kinetic energy of the truck
The car has four times the kinetic energy of the truck
questions.e: The car's speed is 20 000/1000 = 20 m/s. Since Ek = p²/2m, for equal momentum the kinetic energy is inversely proportional to mass: car 200 kJ, truck 100 kJ. 'Four times' wrongly squares the mass ratio.

questions.s: A body has momentum 6 kg·m/s and kinetic energy 9 J. What is its mass?
questions.e: Ek = p²/(2m), so m = p²/(2Ek) = 36/18 = 2 kg (its speed is 3 m/s). Forgetting the factor 2 gives 4 kg; 1.5 is Ek/p, which is half the speed, not a mass.

questions.s: A 0.1 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5 m onto a hard floor and rebounds to a height of 1.8 m. The contact lasts 0.04 s. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the average force of the floor on the ball?
questions.e: Impact speed √(2 × 10 × 5) = 10 m/s downwards; rebound speed √(2 × 10 × 1.8) = 6 m/s upwards. Δp = 0.1 × 16 = 1.6 kg·m/s, so the net force is 1.6/0.04 = 40 N upwards. The floor must also balance the 1 N weight: N = 41 N. 40 N forgets the weight.

questions.s: An egg is dropped from the same height onto a pillow and onto concrete, and comes to rest each time. Which statement is correct?
o: The impulse is the same but the force is smaller on the pillow
The impulse on the egg is smaller on the pillow
The change in momentum is smaller on the pillow
The impulse is larger but acts over a longer time on the pillow
questions.e: In both cases the egg goes from the same speed to rest, so Δp and the impulse are equal. On the pillow the stopping time is longer, so the average force Δp/Δt is smaller. The impulse itself is not reduced; only the force is.

questions.s: Water leaves a hose at 2 kg per second with speed 5 m/s, hits a wall horizontally and then runs down the wall without bouncing back. What horizontal force does the water exert on the wall?
questions.e: Each second 2 kg of water loses 5 m/s of horizontal speed, so the momentum change per second is 2 × 5 = 10 kg·m/s and F = 10 N. 20 N would apply only if the water bounced straight back at 5 m/s.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg stone falls freely from rest for 3 s. Take g = 10 m/s² and ignore air resistance. What is the magnitude of its change in momentum?
questions.e: The impulse of gravity is mgt = 0.5 × 10 × 3 = 15 N·s, which equals Δp (check: v = 30 m/s, p = 0.5 × 30 = 15 kg·m/s). 30 is the speed without the mass, and 45 is the distance fallen, ½gt², in metres.

questions.s: A 2 kg body at rest on a smooth horizontal surface is acted on by a force of 10 N for 2 s and then by a force of 4 N in the opposite direction for 3 s. What is its final speed?
questions.e: Net impulse = 10 × 2 − 4 × 3 = 20 − 12 = 8 N·s, so v = 8/2 = 4 m/s, still in the direction of the first force. 16 m/s adds the impulses as if both forces pushed the same way; 8 m/s forgets to divide by the mass.

questions.s: Which pair contains two vector quantities?
questions.e: Impulse and momentum both have direction; impulse points along the force. Kinetic energy, work and power are scalars, so every other pair contains a scalar.

questions.s: A 1500 kg car brakes uniformly from 20 m/s to rest in 5 s. What is the magnitude of the average braking force?
questions.e: F = Δp/Δt = 1500 × 20/5 = 6000 N. 30 000 is the initial momentum in kg·m/s, not a force; 3000 N uses the average speed 10 m/s instead of the change in speed.

questions.s: A machine gun fires 10 bullets per second. Each bullet has mass 20 g and leaves at 500 m/s. What is the average recoil force on the gun?
questions.e: Each second the gun gives the bullets momentum 10 × 0.020 × 500 = 100 kg·m/s, so by Newton's third law the average recoil force is 100 N. 10 N is the momentum of a single bullet; 1000 N uses 0.2 kg instead of 0.020 kg.

questions.s: The velocity of a 2 kg object changes from 3 m/s due east to 4 m/s due north. What is the magnitude of the impulse on it?
questions.e: Δv is a vector difference: |Δv| = √(3² + 4²) = 5 m/s, so the impulse is 2 × 5 = 10 N·s. 2 N·s subtracts the speeds and 14 N·s adds them, ignoring direction; 5 N·s forgets the mass.

questions.s: A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley, and they stick together. What is their common speed?
questions.e: 2 × 3 = (2 + 1)v gives v = 2 m/s. 1.5 m/s is just half the initial speed and does not conserve momentum (3 kg × 1.5 m/s = 4.5 kg·m/s, not 6).

questions.s: A 4 kg rifle fires a 20 g bullet horizontally at 400 m/s. What is the recoil speed of the rifle?
questions.e: 0 = 0.020 × 400 − 4v gives v = 8/4 = 2 m/s. 8 is the bullet's momentum in kg·m/s, and 20 m/s comes from taking 20 g as 0.2 kg.

questions.s: A 50 kg boy running at 4 m/s jumps onto a stationary 150 kg cart that can roll freely. What is the speed of the boy and cart together?
questions.e: 50 × 4 = (50 + 150)v, so v = 200/200 = 1 m/s. Dividing by the cart's mass alone (200/150) gives 1.33 m/s, but the boy moves with the cart, so the total mass is 200 kg.

questions.s: An object at rest explodes into two pieces of mass 2 kg and 3 kg. The 2 kg piece moves off at 6 m/s. What total kinetic energy is released?
questions.e: Momentum: 2 × 6 = 3v, so the 3 kg piece moves at 4 m/s. Kinetic energy = ½ × 2 × 36 + ½ × 3 × 16 = 36 + 24 = 60 J. 36 J counts only the 2 kg piece.

questions.s: A 3 kg shell moving horizontally at 10 m/s explodes into a 2 kg piece and a 1 kg piece. The 2 kg piece continues forwards at 20 m/s. What is the velocity of the 1 kg piece?
questions.e: 3 × 10 = 2 × 20 + 1 × v gives 30 = 40 + v, so v = −10 m/s, that is 10 m/s backwards. 70 m/s comes from a sign error (30 + 40).

questions.s: A 3 kg block moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg block on a smooth surface, and they stick together. How much kinetic energy is lost?
questions.e: Common speed = 12/4 = 3 m/s. Kinetic energy before = ½ × 3 × 16 = 24 J; after = ½ × 4 × 9 = 18 J; loss = 6 J. 18 J is the kinetic energy that remains, not the loss; momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not.

questions.s: Which statement describes a perfectly inelastic collision between two bodies on a smooth surface?
o: Momentum is conserved; the bodies move off together
Momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved
Kinetic energy is conserved but momentum is not
Neither the momentum nor the kinetic energy is conserved
questions.e: With no external horizontal force, momentum is conserved in every collision. 'Perfectly inelastic' means the bodies stick and share a common velocity, which gives the greatest possible loss of kinetic energy. Conservation of both quantities describes an elastic collision.

questions.s: Ball A moving at 5 m/s collides head-on and elastically with an identical ball B at rest. What are their velocities just after the collision?
questions.e: In an elastic collision of equal masses with one at rest, the velocities are exchanged: A stops and B moves on at 5 m/s, conserving both momentum (5m) and kinetic energy (12.5m). Moving off together at 2.5 m/s conserves momentum but loses half the kinetic energy, so that collision would be inelastic.

questions.s: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on and elastically with a stationary 1 kg ball. What are the speeds of the 2 kg and the 1 kg ball afterwards, respectively?
questions.e: v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u/(m₁ + m₂) = 6/3 = 2 m/s and v₂ = 2m₁u/(m₁ + m₂) = 24/3 = 8 m/s. Check: momentum 4 + 8 = 12 kg·m/s and kinetic energy 4 + 32 = 36 J, both unchanged. The other pairs conserve momentum but not kinetic energy; for example 4 and 4 m/s gives only 24 J.

questions.s: A table-tennis ball moving at 4 m/s collides head-on and elastically with a stationary bowling ball, which is far more massive. What is the approximate velocity of the table-tennis ball just afterwards?
questions.e: With m₁ much smaller than m₂, v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u/(m₁ + m₂) ≈ −u, so the light ball bounces back at about 4 m/s while the heavy ball barely moves. Stopping dead happens only for equal masses, and 2u (8 m/s) is the result when a heavy ball hits a light one.

questions.s: A 1 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on and elastically with a stationary 2 kg ball. What is the velocity of the 1 kg ball afterwards?
questions.e: v₁ = (1 − 2) × 6/(1 + 2) = −2 m/s, so 2 m/s backwards, while the 2 kg ball gets 2 × 1 × 6/3 = 4 m/s forwards. Check: 1 × (−2) + 2 × 4 = 6 kg·m/s and 2 J + 16 J = 18 J, as before. 4 m/s forwards is the 2 kg ball's velocity.

questions.s: Two carts of mass 1 kg and 3 kg are held at rest on a smooth track with a compressed spring between them. When released, they fly apart. What is the ratio of the kinetic energy of the 1 kg cart to that of the 3 kg cart?
questions.e: The momenta are equal and opposite, and Ek = p²/2m, so the kinetic energies are inversely proportional to the masses: 3 : 1 (e.g. speeds 3 m/s and 1 m/s give 4.5 J and 1.5 J). 9 : 1 squares the speed ratio but forgets the mass ratio.

questions.s: A 50 kg person walks from one end to the other of a 4 m long boat of mass 150 kg. The boat is initially at rest on still water, and water resistance is negligible. How far does the boat move relative to the water?
questions.e: Total momentum stays zero, so the centre of mass does not move: 50x₁ = 150x₂, where x₁ + x₂ = 4 m is the person's displacement relative to the boat. So x₁ = 3 m and x₂ = 1 m. 3 m is how far the person moves relative to the water.

questions.s: Two skaters of mass 40 kg and 60 kg stand at rest on smooth ice and push each other apart. The 60 kg skater moves off at 2 m/s. What is the speed of the 40 kg skater?
questions.e: The total momentum stays zero: 40v = 60 × 2, so v = 3 m/s in the opposite direction. 1.33 m/s inverts the mass ratio; the lighter skater must move faster. Zero confuses zero total momentum with zero individual momenta.

questions.s: Why can a rocket accelerate in empty space far from any planet?
o: The exhaust gases push against the surrounding air
The vacuum of space pulls the rocket forwards
Its total momentum increases with no external force
It pushes gases backwards, which push it forwards
questions.e: The rocket exerts a backward force on the exhaust gases, and by Newton's third law the gases exert an equal forward force on the rocket. The total momentum of rocket plus gas stays constant; there is no air in space to push against.

questions.s: A 10 g bullet moving horizontally at 300 m/s embeds itself in a 0.99 kg wooden block hanging at rest on a light string. Take g = 10 m/s². To what height does the block rise?
questions.e: Collision (momentum): 0.01 × 300 = 1.00 × v, so v = 3 m/s. Swing (energy): h = v²/(2g) = 9/20 = 0.45 m. Energy cannot be conserved through the collision itself, because kinetic energy is lost as the bullet embeds; 0.90 m forgets the factor 2.

questions.s: A 2 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s to the right collides with a 3 kg trolley moving at 2 m/s to the left. They stick together. What is their velocity afterwards?
questions.e: Take right as positive: 2 × 4 + 3 × (−2) = 8 − 6 = 2 kg·m/s, so v = 2/5 = 0.4 m/s to the right. 2.8 m/s adds the momenta (14/5), ignoring the opposite directions.

questions.s: A small block of mass m slides at speed v₀ onto a long cart of mass 3m resting on a smooth floor. Friction acts between the block and the cart until they move together. What fraction of the initial kinetic energy is converted into heat?
questions.e: Momentum gives the common speed: mv₀ = 4mv, v = v₀/4. Final kinetic energy = ½(4m)(v₀/4)² = mv₀²/8, which is 1/4 of ½mv₀². So 3/4 of the kinetic energy becomes heat; 1/4 is the fraction that remains.

questions.s: A 0.2 kg ball moving at 5 m/s hits a wall and rebounds along the same line at 5 m/s. Which statement is correct?
o: Its momentum and its kinetic energy are both unchanged
Its momentum is unchanged; its kinetic energy changes
Its momentum changes by 2 kg·m/s; its kinetic energy is unchanged
Its momentum changes by 1 kg·m/s; its kinetic energy is unchanged
questions.e: Momentum is a vector: Δp = 0.2 × (5 − (−5)) = 2 kg·m/s. Kinetic energy depends only on speed, so it stays ½ × 0.2 × 25 = 2.5 J. 1 kg·m/s is the size of the momentum, not its change.

questions.s: A 0.4 kg ball is thrown vertically upwards at 10 m/s and caught at the same height when it comes back down at 10 m/s. Ignore air resistance and take g = 10 m/s². What is the impulse of gravity on the ball during the flight?
questions.e: The flight lasts 2 s, so the impulse is mgt = 4 × 2 = 8 N·s downwards. Check: Δp = 0.4 × (−10 − 10) = −8 kg·m/s. Zero wrongly uses the equal speeds, but the velocity has reversed.

questions.s: A 1000 kg cannon on smooth horizontal ground fires a 10 kg shell. The shell leaves with a velocity of 100 m/s relative to the ground at 60° above the horizontal. What is the recoil speed of the cannon?
questions.e: Only horizontal momentum is conserved, because the ground supplies vertical forces: 10 × 100 × cos 60° = 500 = 1000v, so v = 0.5 m/s. 1 m/s uses the full 100 m/s, and √3/2 m/s uses sin 60° instead of cos 60°.

questions.s: A firework at rest explodes into three fragments of equal mass. Two fragments fly off at 6 m/s at right angles to each other. What is the speed of the third fragment?
questions.e: The total momentum stays zero, so the third fragment's momentum cancels the vector sum of the other two: mv = m√(6² + 6²), so v = 6√2 m/s. 12 m/s adds the speeds as if the two fragments moved in the same direction.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg firework shell reaches the top of its vertical flight, 45 m above flat ground, where it is momentarily at rest. It explodes into pieces of 0.2 kg and 0.3 kg that fly off horizontally; the 0.3 kg piece moves at 20 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s² and ignore air resistance. How far apart are the pieces when they land?
questions.e: Momentum: 0.3 × 20 = 0.2v, so the other piece moves at 30 m/s in the opposite direction. Both fall for t = √(2 × 45/10) = 3 s, landing 60 m and 90 m from the launch point on opposite sides: 150 m apart. 30 m wrongly puts them on the same side.

questions.s: Two bodies have equal momentum but different masses. Which statement is correct?
o: The heavier body has the greater kinetic energy
Both bodies have the same kinetic energy
Both bodies have the same speed
The lighter body has the greater kinetic energy
questions.e: Ek = p²/2m, so for equal p the smaller mass has the larger kinetic energy (it also moves faster). Equal momentum means equal speed only if the masses are equal.

questions.s: A 2000 kg car moving east at 15 m/s collides with a 2000 kg van moving north at 20 m/s. They lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?
questions.e: Momentum east = 30 000 kg·m/s and north = 40 000 kg·m/s, so the total is √(30 000² + 40 000²) = 50 000 kg·m/s. Dividing by 4000 kg gives 12.5 m/s. 25 m/s divides by only one vehicle's mass; 17.5 m/s just averages the speeds.

questions.s: What is the momentum of a 1500 kg car travelling at 72 km/h?
questions.e: 72 km/h = 72/3.6 = 20 m/s, so p = 1500 × 20 = 3.0 × 10⁴ kg·m/s. 1.08 × 10⁵ uses 72 without converting km/h to m/s.

questions.s: The momentum of a body increases from 4 kg·m/s to 10 kg·m/s, in the same direction, in 3 s. What is the average net force on it?
questions.e: F = Δp/Δt = (10 − 4)/3 = 2 N. 6 N is the change of momentum itself, not divided by the time; 4.7 N comes from adding the momenta instead of subtracting.

questions.s: The kinetic energy of a moving body increases by 44% while its mass stays the same. By what percentage does its momentum increase?
questions.e: Ek = p²/2m, so p ∝ √Ek: √1.44 = 1.2, a 20% increase. 22% simply halves 44%, and 44% assumes momentum is proportional to kinetic energy.

questions.s: Block A (1 kg) moves at 4 m/s on a smooth surface towards block B (3 kg), which is at rest and has a light spring fixed to the side facing A. What is the maximum elastic potential energy stored in the spring during the collision?
questions.e: The spring is most compressed when A and B share a common velocity: 1 × 4 = 4v, v = 1 m/s. Their kinetic energy is then ½ × 4 × 1 = 2 J, so the spring stores 8 − 2 = 6 J. 8 J assumes all the kinetic energy is stored, which would violate conservation of momentum.

questions.s: A 50 kg man jumps horizontally off the back of a 200 kg boat that is at rest on still water. He leaves with a horizontal speed of 4 m/s relative to the water. Ignoring water resistance, what is the speed of the boat just afterwards?
questions.e: 0 = 50 × 4 − 200v, so v = 200/200 = 1 m/s in the opposite direction. 0.8 m/s divides by the total mass 250 kg, but the man is no longer on the boat; 16 m/s inverts the mass ratio.

questions.s: Which statement about impulse is correct?
o: Impulse equals the change in kinetic energy it produces
Impulse is a scalar quantity measured in joules
Impulse is the force divided by the time it acts
Impulse equals the change in momentum it produces
questions.e: The impulse–momentum theorem states FΔt = Δp, a vector equation with units N·s. The change in kinetic energy equals the work done, not the impulse.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from rest and falls 20 m. Take g = 10 m/s² and ignore air resistance. What is its momentum just before it lands?
questions.e: v = √(2gh) = √400 = 20 m/s, so p = 0.5 × 20 = 10 kg·m/s. 100 is the energy mgh in joules, and 20 is the speed without the mass.

questions.s: A 20 g bullet moving at 500 m/s passes through a 2 kg block resting on smooth ice and emerges at 300 m/s. What is the speed of the block afterwards?
questions.e: Momentum lost by the bullet = 0.020 × (500 − 300) = 4 kg·m/s, so the block moves at 4/2 = 2 m/s. 5 m/s and 3 m/s use the bullet's full initial or final momentum, and 8 m/s adds them.

questions.s: A 10 g bullet moving at 400 m/s passes horizontally through a 1 kg block at rest on a smooth surface and leaves at 100 m/s. How much kinetic energy is converted into heat and other forms?
questions.e: Block speed: 0.01 × (400 − 100) = 1 × v, so v = 3 m/s. The bullet's kinetic energy falls from ½ × 0.01 × 400² = 800 J to ½ × 0.01 × 100² = 50 J, and the block gains ½ × 1 × 9 = 4.5 J. Energy converted = 800 − 50 − 4.5 = 745.5 J. 750 J forgets the block's kinetic energy.

questions.s: A 0.06 kg tennis ball arrives at 30 m/s and is hit straight back at 20 m/s. The racket is in contact with the ball for 0.01 s. What is the magnitude of the average force on the ball?
questions.e: Δp = 0.06 × (20 + 30) = 3 kg·m/s, so F = 3/0.01 = 300 N. 60 N uses the difference of the speeds (10 m/s), ignoring the reversal; 120 N uses only the final momentum.

questions.s: A man standing at rest on frictionless ice throws a ball forwards. Which statement is correct?
o: He stays still because the ice exerts no force
He moves backwards and the total momentum stays zero
He moves backwards because the total momentum increases
He moves forwards with the ball because they were together
questions.e: Before the throw the total momentum is zero, and with no horizontal external force it stays zero, so the man gains backward momentum equal in size to the ball's forward momentum. The total momentum does not increase: the forces between man and ball are internal.

questions.s: Two identical 2 kg trolleys move towards each other, each at 3 m/s, collide and stick together. How much kinetic energy is lost?
questions.e: The total momentum is 2 × 3 − 2 × 3 = 0, so the joined trolleys stop. All the kinetic energy, 2 × ½ × 2 × 9 = 18 J, is lost. 9 J counts only one trolley; 36 J forgets the ½.

questions.s: A 2 kg block moving at 6 m/s strikes a stationary block of mass M on a smooth surface, and they stick together. Two-thirds of the initial kinetic energy is lost. What is M?
questions.e: Common speed = 12/(2 + M). The fraction of kinetic energy kept is m/(m + M) = 2/(2 + M), which must equal 1/3, so M = 4 kg. With M = 2 kg only half the energy would be lost.

questions.s: On a graph of the momentum of a body against time, what does the gradient represent?
o: The net force on the body
The kinetic energy of the body
questions.e: Gradient = Δp/Δt, which by Newton's second law is the resultant force. The impulse is a change in p (a vertical difference on this graph), not the gradient; acceleration is the gradient of a velocity–time graph.

questions.s: A horizontal water jet of cross-sectional area 2 cm² leaves a nozzle at 10 m/s and hits a vertical wall, after which the water runs down the wall. The density of water is 1000 kg/m³. What force does the jet exert on the wall?
questions.e: Mass per second = ρAv = 1000 × 2 × 10⁻⁴ × 10 = 2 kg/s. Each kilogram loses 10 m/s of horizontal speed, so F = 2 × 10 = 20 N (that is, ρAv²). 2 N is only the mass flow rate; 200 N takes 2 cm² as 2 × 10⁻³ m².

questions.s: A 0.15 kg cricket ball moves at 20 m/s. What is its momentum?
questions.e: p = mv = 0.15 × 20 = 3 kg·m/s. 30 is the kinetic energy ½mv² in joules, and 1.5 and 6 are slips by a factor of 2.

questions.s: A force of 50 N acts for 0.1 s on a 0.5 kg ball that is initially at rest. What speed does the ball reach?
questions.e: Impulse = 50 × 0.1 = 5 N·s = Δp, so v = 5/0.5 = 10 m/s. 5 m/s is the value of the impulse, not the speed; 2.5 m/s multiplies by the mass instead of dividing.

questions.s: A 30 000 kg railway wagon rolling at 2 m/s couples onto a stationary 10 000 kg wagon. What is the speed of the two wagons together?
questions.e: 30 000 × 2 = 40 000v, so v = 1.5 m/s. 1 m/s just averages 2 and 0, ignoring the masses; 6 m/s divides by the second wagon's mass only.

questions.s: In which situation is the momentum of the named system most nearly conserved?
o: A car braking on a rough road (the car)
Two pucks colliding on smooth ice (both pucks)
A box pushed across a floor (the box)
questions.e: On smooth ice the external horizontal forces on the pucks are negligible, so their total momentum is conserved. Road friction on the car, gravity on the ball and the push on the box are external forces that change each system's momentum.

questions.s: A 0.4 kg football at rest is kicked and leaves the foot at 25 m/s. The foot is in contact with the ball for 0.02 s. What is the average force on the ball?
questions.e: Δp = 0.4 × 25 = 10 kg·m/s, so F = 10/0.02 = 500 N. 10 N forgets to divide by the time; 250 N uses the average speed 12.5 m/s instead of the change in speed.

questions.s: An astronaut of total mass 100 kg floats at rest in space and throws a 2 kg tool at 5 m/s. With what speed does the astronaut move off?
questions.e: The total momentum stays zero: 100v = 2 × 5, so v = 0.1 m/s in the opposite direction. 10 is the tool's momentum in kg·m/s, and 2.5 m/s divides the speed by the tool's mass.

questions.s: A stationary 6 kg toy rocket breaks into two parts of 4 kg and 2 kg. The 4 kg part moves off at 3 m/s. What is the speed of the 2 kg part?
questions.e: The total momentum stays zero: 2v = 4 × 3, so v = 6 m/s in the opposite direction. 1.5 m/s inverts the mass ratio; 3 m/s wrongly assumes equal speeds.

questions.s: In a collision between two bodies with no external forces, which quantity is always conserved?
questions.e: With no external force the total momentum of the system is always conserved. Total kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions, and the individual bodies' momenta change because each exerts a force on the other.

questions.s: A force of 8 N acts on a body for 2 s and then decreases uniformly to zero over the next 2 s. What is the total impulse of the force?
questions.e: Impulse = area under the force–time graph = 8 × 2 + ½ × 8 × 2 = 16 + 8 = 24 N·s. 32 N·s treats the second part as a constant 8 N; 16 N·s counts only the first part.

questions.s: A 2 kg brick falls onto sand, hitting it at 5 m/s, and is brought to rest in 0.1 s. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the average force of the sand on the brick?
questions.e: Net upward force = Δp/Δt = 2 × 5/0.1 = 100 N. The sand's force minus the weight equals this: F − 20 = 100, so F = 120 N. 100 N forgets that the sand must also support the weight; 80 N subtracts it.

questions.s: A 1200 kg car moving at 10 m/s runs into the back of a stationary 800 kg car, and the two lock together. How much kinetic energy is lost?
questions.e: Common speed = 12 000/2000 = 6 m/s. Kinetic energy before = ½ × 1200 × 100 = 60 kJ; after = ½ × 2000 × 36 = 36 kJ; lost = 24 kJ. 36 kJ is what remains, not what is lost.

questions.s: A lump of clay of mass m moving at speed v hits a wall at right angles and sticks to it. What is the magnitude of the impulse exerted by the wall on the clay?
questions.e: The clay goes from momentum mv to zero, so the impulse has magnitude mv. 2mv would apply if it bounced back at the same speed; ½mv² is the kinetic energy, not an impulse.

questions.s: Two identical balls move towards each other along a straight line: A at 3 m/s to the right and B at 2 m/s to the left. They collide elastically. What are their velocities afterwards?
o: A: 3 m/s left; B: 2 m/s right
A: 2 m/s left; B: 3 m/s right
A: 0.5 m/s right; B: 0.5 m/s right
questions.e: In an elastic collision of equal masses the velocities are exchanged. Check: momentum m(3 − 2) = m(−2 + 3) = m, and kinetic energy ½m(9 + 4) is unchanged. Both moving at 0.5 m/s conserves momentum but loses kinetic energy; 'A 3 m/s left, B 2 m/s right' reverses the total momentum.

questions.s: A 40 kg girl running at 3 m/s jumps onto an 80 kg cart that is already moving at 1.5 m/s in the same direction. What is their common speed?
questions.e: 40 × 3 + 80 × 1.5 = 120 + 120 = 240 kg·m/s, so v = 240/120 = 2 m/s. 2.25 m/s simply averages the two speeds, ignoring the different masses.

questions.s: A 0.4 kg puck moving north at 5 m/s is struck by a stick and then moves east at 5 m/s. What is the magnitude of the impulse from the stick?
questions.e: |Δv| = √(5² + 5²) = 5√2 m/s, so the impulse is 0.4 × 5√2 = 2√2 N·s. Zero wrongly uses the unchanged speed; 4 N·s would need a complete reversal of direction.

questions.s: Which change doubles the momentum of a moving body?
o: Halving its mass and doubling its speed
Doubling both its mass and its speed
questions.e: p = mv, so doubling v at constant mass doubles p. Doubling the kinetic energy multiplies p by only √2; halving m and doubling v leaves p unchanged; doubling both quadruples p.

questions.s: A rocket expels 2 kg of gas every second at 500 m/s relative to the rocket. What is the thrust on the rocket?
questions.e: Thrust = (mass expelled per second) × (exhaust speed) = 2 × 500 = 1000 N, the rate of change of the gas's momentum. 250 N divides instead of multiplying, and 500 N forgets the mass rate.

questions.s: A 0.3 kg ball is dropped from a height of 0.8 m onto the floor and rebounds to a height of 0.2 m. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the magnitude of the change in its momentum during the bounce?
questions.e: Impact speed √(2 × 10 × 0.8) = 4 m/s downwards; rebound speed √(2 × 10 × 0.2) = 2 m/s upwards. Δp = 0.3 × (4 + 2) = 1.8 kg·m/s. 0.6 subtracts the speeds, ignoring the change of direction.

questions.s: A 1 kg block sliding at 6 m/s on a smooth floor hits and sticks to a stationary 2 kg block. The pair then slides onto a rough patch where the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.2. Take g = 10 m/s². How far do they slide on the rough patch before stopping?
questions.e: Common speed = 6/3 = 2 m/s. Friction gives a deceleration μg = 2 m/s², so s = v²/(2a) = 4/4 = 1 m. 9 m uses the 6 m/s speed from before the collision.

questions.s: Two children on skateboards, of total masses 30 kg and 45 kg, stand at rest and push each other apart. Ignoring friction, what is the ratio of the speed of the 30 kg child to that of the 45 kg child?
questions.e: The momenta are equal and opposite: 30v₁ = 45v₂, so v₁ : v₂ = 45 : 30 = 3 : 2. 2 : 3 is the mass ratio; the lighter child moves faster.

questions.s: A horizontal force of 20 N pushes a box 5 m across a floor in the direction of the force. How much work does the force do?
questions.e: W = Fs = 20 × 5 = 100 J. 4 J divides the force by the distance, and 200 J doubles the correct value.

questions.s: A sled is pulled 4 m along level snow by a rope whose tension is 50 N at 60° above the horizontal. How much work does the tension do?
questions.e: W = Fs cos θ = 50 × 4 × cos 60° = 100 J. 200 J ignores the angle, and 100√3 J uses sin 60° instead of cos 60°.

questions.s: Which unit is equivalent to the watt?
questions.e: Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t, so 1 W = 1 J/s. N·s is the unit of impulse, and J·s multiplies by time instead of dividing.

questions.s: What is the kinetic energy of a 4 kg ball moving at 5 m/s?
questions.e: Ek = ½mv² = ½ × 4 × 25 = 50 J. 100 J forgets the ½, 20 is the momentum mv, and 10 J is ½mv, which forgets to square the speed.

questions.s: A 2 kg book is lifted 3 m vertically. Take g = 10 m/s². By how much does its gravitational potential energy increase?
questions.e: ΔEp = mgh = 2 × 10 × 3 = 60 J. 6 J forgets g, and 20 (newtons) is the weight, not an energy.

questions.s: A box slides along a horizontal floor. How much work does the normal force from the floor do on the box?
o: Positive, as it holds the box up against gravity
Negative, as it opposes the weight of the box
Zero, as it is perpendicular to the motion
The same as the work done by friction
questions.e: W = Fs cos θ with θ = 90°, so cos θ = 0 and the normal force does no work. Friction acts along the surface and does negative work; the normal force does not.

questions.s: A 50 kg student climbs stairs, rising 6 m vertically in 10 s. Take g = 10 m/s². What average power does she use to raise her weight?
questions.e: Work = mgh = 50 × 10 × 6 = 3000 J, so P = 3000/10 = 300 W. 3000 W is the work, not divided by the time; 30 W forgets g.

questions.s: A car moves at a constant 20 m/s on a level road while its engine delivers 40 kW. What is the total resistive force on the car?
questions.e: At constant speed the driving force equals the resistance, and P = Fv, so F = 40 000/20 = 2000 N. 8 × 10⁵ N multiplies P by v instead of dividing; 200 N and 20 000 N are factor-of-10 slips.

questions.s: A 1500 kg car's engine has a constant output power of 60 kW, and the car moves on level ground against a constant resistance of 3000 N. What is its acceleration when its speed is 10 m/s?
questions.e: Driving force F = P/v = 60 000/10 = 6000 N, so a = (6000 − 3000)/1500 = 2 m/s². 4 m/s² ignores the resistance (6000/1500).

questions.s: The speed of a 2 kg block increases from 3 m/s to 7 m/s. What net work is done on the block?
questions.e: By the work–energy theorem, W = ½m(v₂² − v₁²) = ½ × 2 × (49 − 9) = 40 J. 16 J squares the change in speed, (7 − 3)², which is not the change in v²; 80 J forgets the ½.

questions.s: A block slides on a horizontal floor with an initial speed of 5 m/s. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. Take g = 10 m/s². How far does it slide before stopping?
questions.e: The work against friction equals the kinetic energy lost: μmgd = ½mv², so d = v²/(2μg) = 25/5 = 5 m. 10 m forgets the factor 2, and 1.25 m (v²/2g) leaves out μ.

questions.s: A car is braked to rest by the same constant braking force, once from speed v and once from speed 2v. How does the stopping distance from 2v compare with that from v?
questions.e: Fd = ½mv², so d ∝ v². Doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy and therefore the stopping distance. 'Twice as far' wrongly assumes d ∝ v.

questions.s: A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m. Take g = 10 m/s² and ignore air resistance. With what speed does it hit the ground?
questions.e: mgh = ½mv² gives v = √(2gh) = √400 = 20 m/s. 10√2 m/s comes from forgetting the 2, √(gh); 40 m/s is 2h, not a speed.

questions.s: A pendulum bob is released from rest 0.8 m above its lowest point. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², what is its speed at the lowest point?
questions.e: The tension is perpendicular to the motion and does no work, so mgh = ½mv² and v = √(2 × 10 × 0.8) = 4 m/s. 2√2 m/s forgets the 2, and 16 is v², not v.

questions.s: A stone is thrown from the top of a 15 m high cliff with a speed of 10 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², with what speed does it reach the sea below, whatever the direction of the throw?
questions.e: Energy: ½v² = ½ × 10² + 10 × 15, so v² = 100 + 300 = 400 and v = 20 m/s, independent of direction. 10√3 m/s ignores the initial speed; 25 m/s adds 10 and 15 without using energy.

questions.s: A spring of stiffness 200 N/m is compressed by 0.1 m. What elastic potential energy does it store?
questions.e: Ep = ½kx² = ½ × 200 × 0.1² = 1 J. 2 J forgets the ½, and 10 J forgets to square x.

questions.s: A spring of stiffness 800 N/m is compressed by 5 cm and then launches a 0.5 kg block along a smooth horizontal surface. What is the launch speed of the block?
questions.e: Ep = ½ × 800 × 0.05² = 1 J = ½ × 0.5 × v², so v² = 4 and v = 2 m/s. 2√2 m/s forgets the ½ in the spring energy, and 4 m/s is v², not v.

questions.s: A 2 kg block starts from rest and slides 5 m down a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The friction force on it is 5 N. Take g = 10 m/s². What is its speed at the bottom?
questions.e: Work by gravity = mg × 5 sin 30° = 20 × 2.5 = 50 J; work against friction = 5 × 5 = 25 J. So ½ × 2 × v² = 25 J and v = 5 m/s. 5√2 m/s ignores friction (v² = 50).

questions.s: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. While it is rising, which statement is correct?
o: Gravity does positive work and the potential energy increases
Gravity does negative work and the potential energy decreases
Gravity does negative work and the potential energy increases
Gravity does no work because it is a conservative force
questions.e: Gravity acts downwards while the ball moves up, so its work is negative, and W_gravity = −ΔEp means the potential energy increases. A conservative force still does work; it is only the work around a closed path that is zero.

questions.s: An electric motor uses 500 J of electrical energy to raise a 20 kg load through 2 m at constant speed. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the efficiency of the motor?
questions.e: Useful output = mgh = 20 × 10 × 2 = 400 J, so efficiency = 400/500 = 80%. 125% inverts the ratio; an efficiency can never exceed 100%.

questions.s: A pump raises 300 kg of water per minute through a height of 10 m. Its efficiency is 50%. Take g = 10 m/s². What is its input power?
questions.e: Useful power = 300 × 10 × 10/60 = 500 W. Input power = useful power/efficiency = 500/0.5 = 1000 W. 250 W multiplies by 0.5 instead of dividing, and 500 W is the output power.

questions.s: A force acting along the direction of motion increases uniformly from 0 to 30 N as a body moves 4 m. How much work does the force do?
questions.e: Work = area under the force–displacement graph = ½ × 30 × 4 = 60 J. 120 J treats the force as 30 N throughout, and 7.5 J divides the force by the distance.

questions.s: A box is pushed 3 m across a floor and then pushed back 3 m to its starting point. The friction force is 10 N throughout. What is the total work done by friction on the box?
questions.e: Friction always opposes the motion, so it does −10 × 3 = −30 J on each leg: −60 J in total. It is not zero, because friction reverses direction with the motion; it is not a conservative force.

questions.s: A roller-coaster car starts from rest at point A, 20 m above the ground, and runs along a frictionless track to point B, 15 m above the ground. Take g = 10 m/s². What is its speed at B?
questions.e: Only the 5 m drop matters: v = √(2 × 10 × 5) = 10 m/s. 10√3 m/s uses the 15 m height and 20 m/s the full 20 m; the shape of a frictionless track does not matter.

questions.s: A crane lifts a 1000 kg load vertically at a constant speed of 2 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s². What power does the crane deliver to the load?
questions.e: At constant speed the tension equals the weight, 10 000 N, so P = Fv = 10 000 × 2 = 20 kW. 2 kW uses the mass instead of the weight.

questions.s: Which statement about work is correct?
o: Work is a vector in the direction of the force
Work is a scalar and can be negative
Work is done whenever a force acts on a body
Work is zero whenever a body moves at constant speed
questions.e: W = Fs cos θ is a scalar; it is negative when the angle between force and displacement exceeds 90°, as for friction. A force on a stationary body does no work, and at constant speed individual forces still do work; only the net work is zero.

questions.s: A 60 kg cyclist rides up a slope at a constant 5 m/s, gaining height at a rate of 0.5 m/s. Ignoring friction and air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², what power must she supply?
questions.e: At constant speed all the power goes into potential energy: P = mg × (rate of gain of height) = 600 × 0.5 = 300 W. 3000 W uses the 5 m/s speed along the slope instead of the vertical rate.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg ball is thrown vertically upwards at 12 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², at what height above the launch point is its kinetic energy equal to its gravitational potential energy (zero at the launch point)?
questions.e: Total energy = ½ × 0.5 × 144 = 36 J. When Ek = Ep, each is 18 J, so 0.5 × 10 × h = 18 and h = 3.6 m. 7.2 m is the maximum height, where all the energy is potential.

questions.s: A small ball slides from rest down a smooth track from height h and then goes round a vertical circular loop of radius R at the bottom of the track. What is the minimum h for the ball to stay on the track at the top of the loop?
questions.e: At the top the minimum speed satisfies mg = mv²/R, so v² = gR. Energy: mg(h − 2R) = ½mgR, giving h = 2.5R. With h = 2R the ball would need zero speed at the top and would leave the track before reaching it.

questions.s: A 3 kg object moving at 4 m/s is acted on by a net force of 6 N in its direction of motion over a distance of 5 m. What is its final kinetic energy?
questions.e: Initial Ek = ½ × 3 × 16 = 24 J; net work = 6 × 5 = 30 J; final Ek = 24 + 30 = 54 J. 30 J is only the work done and forgets the initial kinetic energy.

questions.s: A 4 kg box is pulled at constant speed 3 m up a rough slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal by a force parallel to the slope. The friction force is 8 N. Take g = 10 m/s². How much work does the pulling force do?
questions.e: At constant speed the pull equals mg sin 30° + f = 20 + 8 = 28 N, so W = 28 × 3 = 84 J (60 J gain in potential energy plus 24 J of heat). 60 J ignores friction; 120 J uses the slope length 3 m as the height instead of 1.5 m.

questions.s: When the speed of a car is tripled, its kinetic energy is multiplied by
questions.e: Ek = ½mv², so tripling v multiplies Ek by 3² = 9. 3 assumes Ek is proportional to v; 27 cubes the factor.

questions.s: In which case does the named force do no work on the object?
o: Tension on a swinging pendulum bob
Friction on a box sliding across a floor
The weight of an apple falling from a tree
The push of a hand lifting a book upwards
questions.e: The tension acts along the string, perpendicular to the bob's velocity on its circular arc, so it does no work. In each other case the force has a component along the displacement.

questions.s: A 1000 kg car accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s on a level road. Ignoring resistance, what is the average power delivered to the car?
questions.e: Work = ΔEk = ½ × 1000 × 20² = 2 × 10⁵ J, so the average power = 2 × 10⁵/10 = 2 × 10⁴ W = 20 kW. 200 kW is the energy in kJ, not divided by the time; 40 kW forgets the ½.

questions.s: A 1000 kg car accelerates uniformly from rest at 2 m/s² on a level road with negligible resistance. What is the power of the driving force at the instant its speed is 15 m/s?
questions.e: F = ma = 2000 N, and the instantaneous power is P = Fv = 2000 × 15 = 30 000 W = 30 kW. 15 kW uses the average speed 7.5 m/s, which gives the average power over the run, not the power at 15 m/s.

questions.s: A 2000 kg truck with a maximum power of 80 kW climbs a straight slope for which sin θ = 0.1, against a resistance of 2000 N. Take g = 10 m/s². What is its maximum steady speed up the slope?
questions.e: At maximum steady speed the driving force equals mg sin θ + resistance = 2000 + 2000 = 4000 N, so v = P/F = 80 000/4000 = 20 m/s. 40 m/s ignores the component of the weight along the slope.

questions.s: A 0.2 kg ball is thrown horizontally at 5 m/s from a balcony 5 m above the ground. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², what is its kinetic energy just before it hits the ground?
questions.e: Initial Ek = ½ × 0.2 × 25 = 2.5 J; gravity then does mgh = 0.2 × 10 × 5 = 10 J of work; final Ek = 12.5 J. 10 J ignores the initial kinetic energy.

questions.s: A 2 kg block moving at 3 m/s on a smooth horizontal surface runs into a light spring of stiffness 800 N/m. What is the maximum compression of the spring?
