questions.e: All the kinetic energy is stored: ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J = ½ × 800 × x², so x² = 0.0225 and x = 0.15 m. 0.0225 m is x², not x, and 0.075 m and 0.3 m are slips by a factor of 2.

questions.s: A 1 kg block moving at 4 m/s crosses a 1 m rough strip (coefficient of kinetic friction 0.4) and then, on a smooth surface, compresses a light spring of stiffness 200 N/m. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the maximum compression of the spring?
questions.e: Kinetic energy 8 J minus the friction work μmgd = 0.4 × 10 × 1 = 4 J leaves 4 J = ½ × 200 × x², so x = 0.2 m. Ignoring friction gives 8 J and x = 0.2√2 m; 0.04 m is x², not x.

questions.s: Two balls of different masses are dropped together from the same height. Ignoring air resistance, which statement is correct as they reach the ground?
o: Same speed; the heavier has more kinetic energy
Same kinetic energy, but the lighter one is faster
The heavier one hits the ground faster
The lighter one has more kinetic energy
questions.e: v = √(2gh) does not depend on mass, so both arrive at the same speed, but Ek = ½mv² is larger for the heavier ball. Equal kinetic energy would need the lighter ball to move faster, which energy conservation does not allow.

questions.s: A 50 kg crate is pushed 10 m up a ramp onto a platform 2 m high, using a force of 125 N parallel to the ramp. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the efficiency of the ramp?
questions.e: Useful work = mgh = 50 × 10 × 2 = 1000 J; work input = 125 × 10 = 1250 J; efficiency = 1000/1250 = 80%. 20% is the fraction wasted against friction, and 125% inverts the ratio.

questions.s: A 2 kg block is released from rest at the top of a curved ramp 1.25 m high and reaches the bottom at 4 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s². How much work does friction do on the block?
questions.e: Work–energy theorem: W_gravity + W_friction = ΔEk, so 25 + W_friction = ½ × 2 × 16 = 16 J and W_friction = −9 J. Friction opposes the motion, so its work is negative; +9 J has the wrong sign.

questions.s: A 70 kg climber ascends 500 m. Her body turns food energy into useful work with an efficiency of 25%. Take g = 10 m/s². How much food energy does she use for the climb?
questions.e: Useful work = mgh = 70 × 10 × 500 = 3.5 × 10⁵ J. Energy input = 3.5 × 10⁵/0.25 = 1.4 × 10⁶ J. 8.75 × 10⁴ J multiplies by 0.25 instead of dividing.

questions.s: A 2 kg mass falls freely from rest. Ignoring air resistance, which quantity stays constant during the fall?
questions.e: Only gravity does work, so the kinetic energy increases exactly as the potential energy decreases and their sum stays constant. Momentum increases because a net force acts.

questions.s: A stone is dropped from rest from height H. Ignoring air resistance, at what height above the ground is its kinetic energy three times its gravitational potential energy (zero at the ground)?
questions.e: Total energy mgH = Ek + Ep = 3Ep + Ep = 4Ep, so mgh = mgH/4 and h = H/4. H/3 comes from splitting the energy into three parts instead of four; 3H/4 is the distance fallen, not the height.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from rest and falls for 2 s. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², what is the average power of gravity over the 2 s?
questions.e: Distance fallen = ½gt² = 20 m, so gravity does 0.5 × 10 × 20 = 100 J, and the average power is 100/2 = 50 W. 100 W is the instantaneous power mgv at the end of the 2 s, when v = 20 m/s.

questions.s: A rope pulls a box along level ground at a constant speed of 2 m/s. The tension in the rope is 40 N, acting at 60° above the horizontal. What is the power of the tension?
questions.e: P = Fv cos θ = 40 × 2 × cos 60° = 40 W. 80 W ignores the angle, and 40√3 W uses sin 60° instead of cos 60°.

questions.s: A 5 kg box starts from rest and is pulled 4 m across a horizontal floor by a horizontal force of 30 N. The friction force is 10 N. What is the final speed of the box?
questions.e: Net work = (30 − 10) × 4 = 80 J = ½ × 5 × v², so v² = 32 and v = 4√2 m/s. Ignoring friction gives 120 J and v = 4√3 m/s.

questions.s: Which quantity has the same unit as work?
questions.e: Work and every form of energy are measured in joules (1 J = 1 N·m), so kinetic energy shares the unit of work. Power is measured in J/s, momentum in kg·m/s and force in N.

questions.s: Block A (3 kg) rests on a smooth horizontal table and is joined by a light string over a smooth pulley at the edge to block B (2 kg), which hangs freely. The system is released from rest. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the speed of the blocks after B has fallen 0.5 m?
questions.e: Only B loses potential energy: 2 × 10 × 0.5 = 10 J. Both blocks move at the same speed, so 10 = ½ × (3 + 2) × v², v² = 4 and v = 2 m/s. √10 m/s forgets that A also gains kinetic energy.

questions.s: A 0.2 kg ball falls from rest through a height of 5 m and reaches the ground at 8 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the average air resistance force on the ball?
questions.e: Mechanical energy lost = mgh − ½mv² = 10 − 6.4 = 3.6 J, which equals the work against air resistance: F × 5 = 3.6, so F = 0.72 N. 3.6 N forgets to divide by the 5 m distance.

questions.s: The force needed to stretch a spring increases uniformly from 0 to 12 N as the spring is stretched by 6 cm. How much elastic potential energy is stored?
questions.e: Energy = area under the force–extension graph = ½ × 12 × 0.06 = 0.36 J. 0.72 J forgets the ½, and 36 J uses 6 cm as 6 m.

questions.s: If the extension of a spring is doubled, staying within its elastic limit, its elastic potential energy is multiplied by
questions.e: Ep = ½kx² ∝ x², so doubling x multiplies Ep by 4. The force only doubles, but the energy is the area of a triangle whose base and height both double.

questions.s: A 0.1 kg ball on a light string of length 0.5 m is whirled in a vertical circle. At the lowest point its speed is 5 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s². What is its speed at the highest point?
questions.e: The highest point is 2r = 1 m above the lowest, so v² = 25 − 2 × 10 × 1 = 5 and v = √5 m/s (just enough, since gr = 5 m²/s²). √15 m/s uses a height of 0.5 m, the radius, instead of the diameter.

questions.s: Object A has twice the mass and half the speed of object B. What is the ratio of the kinetic energy of A to that of B?
questions.e: Ek ∝ mv²: 2 × (½)² = ½, so the ratio is 1 : 2. 1 : 1 forgets to square the speed (it is the momentum ratio).

questions.s: A 2 kg box is placed gently on a horizontal conveyor belt moving at a constant 3 m/s. The box slips until it reaches the speed of the belt. How much heat is produced by friction?
questions.e: While slipping, the box's average speed is 1.5 m/s and the belt's is 3 m/s, so the belt travels twice as far as the box. Friction gives the box ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J of kinetic energy over distance d, and the sliding distance relative to the belt is also d, so the heat is f × d = 9 J. 18 J is the total work done by the belt (kinetic energy plus heat).

questions.s: A ball is projected at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², what maximum height does it reach?
questions.e: At the top only the horizontal component 20 cos 30° = 10√3 m/s remains, so the loss of kinetic energy per kilogram is ½(400 − 300) = 50 J = gh, giving h = 5 m. 20 m assumes the ball stops completely at the top, which is true only for a vertical launch.

questions.s: Which of the following mainly converts kinetic energy into gravitational potential energy?
o: A ball rolling down a hill
A compressed spring launching a toy car
A ball rising after being thrown upwards
A car braking to a stop on a level road
questions.e: A rising ball slows down as it gains height, so kinetic energy becomes gravitational potential energy. Rolling downhill does the reverse, the spring converts elastic energy into kinetic energy, and braking turns kinetic energy into heat.

questions.s: A 1 kg small block is released from rest at the rim of a smooth hemispherical bowl of radius 0.8 m. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the normal force of the bowl on the block at the bottom?
questions.e: Energy: v² = 2gR = 16 m²/s². At the bottom N − mg = mv²/R = 16/0.8 = 20 N, so N = 30 N, three times the weight whatever the radius. 20 N is only the centripetal part.

questions.s: A 50 kg girl on a swing passes through the lowest point at 4 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², how high above the lowest point does she rise?
questions.e: ½mv² = mgh gives h = v²/(2g) = 16/20 = 0.8 m, independent of her mass. 1.6 m forgets the ½ in the kinetic energy.

questions.s: A car's engine delivers 30 kW while the car moves at a constant 15 m/s. How much work does the engine do in 1 minute?
questions.e: W = Pt = 30 000 × 60 = 1.8 × 10⁶ J; the speed is not needed. 4.5 × 10⁵ multiplies the power by the speed, and 3.0 × 10⁴ uses 1 s instead of 60 s.

questions.s: A spring of stiffness 400 N/m is already stretched by 0.1 m. How much work is needed to stretch it further, to a total extension of 0.3 m?
questions.e: W = ½k(x₂² − x₁²) = ½ × 400 × (0.09 − 0.01) = 16 J. 8 J treats the extra 0.2 m as if starting from zero, and 18 J ignores the initial stretch (½ × 400 × 0.09).

questions.s: In which case is the mechanical energy of the object conserved?
o: A ball in free fall with no air resistance
A parachutist falling at constant speed
A box pulled up a smooth slope at constant speed
A car braking to a stop on a level road
questions.e: Mechanical energy is conserved when only gravity (or spring forces) does work, as in free fall. The parachutist loses potential energy without gaining kinetic energy, the pulled box gains energy from the pull, and braking turns kinetic energy into heat.

questions.s: A 2 kW motor with an efficiency of 80% raises a 400 kg load through 12 m at constant speed. Take g = 10 m/s². How long does it take?
questions.e: Useful power = 0.8 × 2000 = 1600 W; work needed = 400 × 10 × 12 = 48 000 J; t = 48 000/1600 = 30 s. 24 s assumes 100% efficiency, and 19.2 s applies the efficiency the wrong way (24 × 0.8).

questions.s: A body has kinetic energy 32 J and momentum 8 kg·m/s. What is its speed?
questions.e: Ek = ½mv² = ½pv, so v = 2Ek/p = 64/8 = 8 m/s (the mass is 1 kg). 4 m/s divides Ek by p and forgets the factor 2.

questions.s: A small block is released from rest at a height of 0.8 m on a smooth curved ramp that leads onto a rough horizontal floor with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.2. How far along the floor does the block travel before stopping?
questions.e: All the potential energy becomes heat on the rough floor: mgh = μmgd, so d = h/μ = 0.8/0.2 = 4 m, independent of the mass and of g. 0.16 m multiplies h by μ instead of dividing.

questions.s: A 2 kg block on a rough horizontal surface (coefficient of kinetic friction 0.25) is pushed against a spring of stiffness 500 N/m, compressing it by 0.2 m, and released from rest. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the block's speed when the spring reaches its natural length?
questions.e: Spring energy = ½ × 500 × 0.2² = 10 J. Friction does 0.25 × 2 × 10 × 0.2 = 1 J of negative work, leaving 9 J = ½ × 2 × v², so v = 3 m/s. √10 m/s ignores friction.

questions.s: A 3 kg object moves 5 m horizontally at constant height. Take g = 10 m/s². How much work does gravity do on it?
questions.e: Gravity is vertical and the displacement is horizontal, so θ = 90° and W = 0. 150 J wrongly multiplies the weight by a horizontal distance.

questions.s: A 60 kg sprinter accelerates from rest to 10 m/s in 4 s. Ignoring losses, what is her average power output?
questions.e: ΔEk = ½ × 60 × 10² = 3000 J, so P = 3000/4 = 750 W. 1500 W forgets the ½, and 3000 W is the energy, not divided by the time.

questions.s: A 1000 kg car with a rated power of 40 kW starts from rest with a constant acceleration of 1 m/s² against a constant resistance of 1000 N. For how long can the uniform acceleration last?
questions.e: During uniform acceleration F = ma + f = 1000 + 1000 = 2000 N. The power reaches 40 kW when v = 40 000/2000 = 20 m/s, after t = 20/1 = 20 s. 40 s uses the final maximum speed P/f = 40 m/s, which is reached later, with decreasing acceleration.

questions.s: A 2 kg ball falls from a table top 0.8 m high to the floor. Take g = 10 m/s² and take the table top as the zero of potential energy. What is the ball's potential energy on the floor, and what is the change in its potential energy?
questions.e: The floor is 0.8 m below the zero level, so Ep = −mgh = −2 × 10 × 0.8 = −16 J. The change is a decrease of 16 J whatever zero level is chosen; only the value of Ep depends on the choice.

questions.s: A 4 kg block is lowered vertically through 2 m at constant speed by a rope. Take g = 10 m/s². How much work does the rope do on the block?
questions.e: At constant speed the tension equals the weight, 40 N, acting upwards while the block moves 2 m down: W = −40 × 2 = −80 J. Gravity does +80 J, so the net work is zero, matching the unchanged kinetic energy.

questions.s: A lamp converts 100 J of electrical energy each second into 15 J of light. What is its efficiency?
questions.e: Efficiency = useful output/input = 15/100 = 15%. 85% is the fraction wasted as heat, and 115% adds instead of dividing; no efficiency can exceed 100%.

questions.s: A 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m/s brakes and stops in 40 m. What is the average braking force?
questions.e: Work–energy theorem: F × 40 = ½ × 1200 × 20² = 240 000 J, so F = 6000 N. 12 000 N forgets the ½ in the kinetic energy.

questions.s: A ball is dropped from a height of 2 m onto a hard floor. Each bounce keeps 80% of the ball's mechanical energy. Ignoring air resistance, how high does it rise after the second bounce?
questions.e: The rebound height is proportional to the energy kept: 2 × 0.8 × 0.8 = 1.28 m. 1.6 m is the height after the first bounce, and 1.2 m subtracts 20% of the original height twice.

questions.s: A small bob on a light string of length L is pulled aside until the string makes 60° with the vertical and is released from rest. What is the tension in the string when the bob passes through the lowest point? (m is the mass of the bob.)
questions.e: The bob falls L(1 − cos 60°) = L/2, so v² = gL. At the bottom T − mg = mv²/L = mg, giving T = 2mg. 3mg is the result for a release with the string horizontal.

questions.s: The work–energy theorem states that the net work done on a body equals
o: the change in its potential energy
the change in its kinetic energy
questions.e: W_net = ΔEk = ½mv₂² − ½mv₁². It equals the final kinetic energy only if the body starts from rest, and the change in momentum is the impulse, not the work.

questions.s: A bow string stores 20 J of elastic potential energy, and 80% of it is transferred to a 0.05 kg arrow shot vertically upwards. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², how high does the arrow rise?
questions.e: Kinetic energy given to the arrow = 0.8 × 20 = 16 J = mgh, so h = 16/(0.05 × 10) = 32 m. 40 m assumes all 20 J is transferred.

questions.s: A constant horizontal force of 10 N acts for 3 s on a 2 kg body that is initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface. How much work does the force do?
questions.e: a = 10/2 = 5 m/s², so s = ½ × 5 × 3² = 22.5 m and W = 10 × 22.5 = 225 J, which equals ½ × 2 × 15² since v = 15 m/s. 30 is force × time, the impulse in N·s, and 450 J forgets the ½.

questions.s: A block of mass m is attached to the lower end of a light vertical spring of stiffness k at its natural length and is lowered slowly by hand until it hangs at rest in equilibrium. What fraction of the gravitational potential energy lost by the block is stored in the spring?
questions.e: Equilibrium extension x = mg/k. The block loses mgx = kx² of potential energy, while the spring stores ½kx², so half is stored; the other half is work done on the hand. 1 would be true only if no other force did work, as when the block is released and oscillates.

questions.s: A worker pushes a trolley with a horizontal force of 40 N through 15 m in the direction of the force. How much work does he do?
questions.e: W = Fs = 40 × 15 = 600 J. 55 adds the force and the distance, and 1200 J doubles the correct value.

questions.s: What is the kinetic energy of a 0.1 kg ball moving at 20 m/s?
questions.e: Ek = ½mv² = ½ × 0.1 × 400 = 20 J. 40 J forgets the ½, 2 is the momentum mv, and 1 J forgets to square the speed.

questions.s: A 3 kg box sits on a shelf 2 m above the floor. Taking the floor as the zero level and g = 10 m/s², what is its gravitational potential energy?
questions.e: Ep = mgh = 3 × 10 × 2 = 60 J. 6 J forgets g, and 30 J is the weight, in newtons, not an energy.

questions.s: A motor does 6000 J of work in 2 minutes. What is its average power?
questions.e: P = W/t = 6000/120 = 50 W. 3000 W uses 2 s instead of 120 s, and 12 000 W multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.s: A child slides from rest down a smooth slide whose top is 3.2 m above its bottom. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the child's speed at the bottom?
questions.e: mgh = ½mv² gives v = √(2 × 10 × 3.2) = √64 = 8 m/s, independent of the child's mass and of the slide's shape. 64 is v², not v, and 6.4 m/s is 2h rather than √(2gh).

questions.s: A 2 kg block is pushed at constant speed for 5 m across a rough horizontal floor by a horizontal force. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.3. Take g = 10 m/s². How much work does the pushing force do?
questions.e: At constant speed the push equals the friction force μmg = 0.3 × 20 = 6 N, so W = 6 × 5 = 30 J. The net work is zero, but the pushing force itself does positive work.

questions.s: What is the kinetic energy of an 800 kg car moving at 15 m/s?
questions.e: Ek = ½mv² = ½ × 800 × 225 = 90 000 J = 9.0 × 10⁴ J. 1.8 × 10⁵ J forgets the ½, and 1.2 × 10⁴ is the momentum mv.

questions.s: A 2000 W electric kettle runs for 3 minutes. The water gains 2.88 × 10⁵ J of energy. What is the kettle's efficiency?
questions.e: Input energy = Pt = 2000 × 180 = 3.6 × 10⁵ J, so efficiency = 2.88 × 10⁵/3.6 × 10⁵ = 80%. 125% inverts the ratio, and 20% is the fraction wasted.

questions.s: The rubber of a catapult behaves like a spring of stiffness 800 N/m. It is stretched by 0.1 m and launches a 20 g stone. Assuming all the elastic energy goes to the stone, what is the launch speed?
questions.e: Elastic energy = ½ × 800 × 0.1² = 4 J = ½ × 0.02 × v², so v² = 400 and v = 20 m/s. 400 is v², and 10√2 m/s forgets the ½ in the kinetic energy.

questions.s: A 4 kg sled slides from rest down a hill 5 m high and reaches the bottom at 8 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s². How much energy is lost to friction?
questions.e: Potential energy lost = 4 × 10 × 5 = 200 J; kinetic energy gained = ½ × 4 × 64 = 128 J; energy lost to friction = 72 J. 128 J is the kinetic energy at the bottom, not the loss.

questions.s: A 1000 kg car with a constant output power of 50 kW has a maximum speed of 25 m/s on a level road. Assuming the resistance is constant, what is its acceleration when its speed is 10 m/s?
questions.e: At maximum speed the driving force equals the resistance: f = P/v_max = 50 000/25 = 2000 N. At 10 m/s the driving force is 5000 N, so a = (5000 − 2000)/1000 = 3 m/s². 5 m/s² ignores the resistance.

questions.s: In which case does the named force do positive work?
o: A hand lifting a bag upwards
Friction on a book sliding along a desk
Gravity on a ball moving upwards
Air resistance on a falling stone
questions.e: The hand's force and the displacement are both upwards, so W = Fs cos 0° > 0. Friction and air resistance oppose the motion, and gravity acts opposite to the rising ball's motion, so those forces do negative work.

questions.s: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 15 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², what maximum height does it reach?
questions.e: ½mv² = mgh gives h = v²/(2g) = 225/20 = 11.25 m. 22.5 m forgets the ½, and 7.5 m uses v/2 instead of v²/2g.

questions.s: A 3 kg block slides 2 m down a rough slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal at constant speed. Take g = 10 m/s². How much work does friction do on the block?
questions.e: At constant speed ΔEk = 0, so W_gravity + W_friction = 0. W_gravity = mg × 2 sin 30° = 30 × 1 = 30 J, giving W_friction = −30 J. −60 J uses the slope length as the height.

questions.s: If the speed of a moving body is halved, its kinetic energy becomes
o: the same as its original value
a quarter of its original value
questions.e: Ek = ½mv², so halving v multiplies Ek by (½)² = ¼. 'Half' would follow only if Ek were proportional to v, as momentum is.

questions.s: A cyclist moves at a steady 8 m/s while the driving force from the pedals is 50 N. What power does the cyclist supply?
questions.e: P = Fv = 50 × 8 = 400 W. 6.25 W divides the force by the speed, and 58 W adds them.

questions.s: A 0.2 kg ball on a light string of length 0.4 m moves in a vertical circle and only just completes the loop, the string becoming slack for an instant at the top. Take g = 10 m/s². What is its speed at the lowest point?
questions.e: At the top gravity alone provides the centripetal force: v_top² = gr = 4 m²/s². The lowest point is 2r = 0.8 m lower, so v² = 4 + 2 × 10 × 0.8 = 20 and v = 2√5 m/s. 4 m/s assumes zero speed at the top, and 2√3 m/s uses a drop of r instead of 2r.

questions.s: A 2 kg block slides 4 m down a smooth slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Take g = 10 m/s². How much work does gravity do on the block?
questions.e: The vertical drop is 4 sin 30° = 2 m, so W = mgh = 2 × 10 × 2 = 40 J; only the height matters. 80 J uses the slope length as the height, and 40√3 J uses cos 30° instead of sin 30°.

questions.s: Spring A, of stiffness k, is stretched by x. Spring B, of stiffness 2k, is stretched by x/2. What is the ratio of the elastic potential energy stored in A to that stored in B?
questions.e: E_A = ½kx², E_B = ½(2k)(x/2)² = ¼kx², so E_A : E_B = 2 : 1. 1 : 1 forgets to square the extension.

questions.s: A 50 kg girl slides from rest down a slide 4 m high and reaches the bottom at 6 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s². What percentage of her initial potential energy is lost to friction?
questions.e: Ep = 50 × 10 × 4 = 2000 J; Ek at the bottom = ½ × 50 × 36 = 900 J; energy lost = 1100 J, which is 55%. 45% is the fraction that becomes kinetic energy.

questions.s: A bicycle wheel turns steadily at 120 revolutions per minute. What is its angular velocity?
questions.e: 120 rev/min = 2 rev/s, so ω = 2πf = 2π × 2 = 4π rad/s. 240π rad/s comes from multiplying 2π by 120 without converting minutes to seconds.

questions.s: A small toy car moves round a circular track of radius 2 m at a constant speed of 4 m/s. What is the magnitude of its centripetal acceleration?
questions.e: a = v²/r = 4²/2 = 8 m/s². 32 m/s² comes from multiplying v² by r instead of dividing, and 2 m/s² from v/r, which is the angular velocity, not an acceleration.

questions.s: An object moves in uniform circular motion. Which of the following quantities stays constant?
questions.e: In uniform circular motion the speed is constant, but the direction of motion changes continuously. Velocity, acceleration and net force are vectors whose directions keep changing (the last two always point to the centre), so they are not constant.

questions.s: A car of mass 1000 kg rounds a flat, unbanked curve of radius 50 m at a constant speed of 10 m/s. What friction force from the road is needed to keep it on the curve? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: Friction provides the centripetal force: F = mv²/r = 1000 × 10²/50 = 2000 N. 10 000 N is the car's weight mg, which is balanced by the normal force and does not supply the sideways force; 200 N uses v instead of v².

questions.s: A car rounds a flat, unbanked curve of radius 20 m. The coefficient of static friction between tyres and road is 0.5. What is the greatest speed at which it can take the curve without skidding? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: Maximum friction μmg supplies the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r, so v² = μgr = 0.5 × 10 × 20 = 100 and v = 10 m/s. 10√2 m/s ignores μ (v² = gr = 200), and 100 m/s forgets to take the square root.

questions.s: A disc of radius 0.5 m rotates uniformly so that a point on its rim moves at 2 m/s. What is the period of rotation?
questions.e: ω = v/r = 2/0.5 = 4 rad/s, so T = 2π/ω = 2π/4 = π/2 s. π s comes from using the diameter 1 m instead of the radius, which halves ω.

questions.s: Two point masses attract each other with a gravitational force F. If the distance between them is doubled, what does the force become?
questions.e: Newton's law F = Gm₁m₂/r² is an inverse-square law, so doubling r divides F by 2² = 4, giving F/4. F/2 would be true only if the force were inversely proportional to r.

questions.s: The acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface is g. At a height of 2R above the surface (R is the Earth's radius), what is the acceleration due to gravity?
questions.e: g ∝ 1/r² with r measured from the Earth's centre. At height 2R, r = R + 2R = 3R, so g′ = g/3² = g/9. g/4 comes from taking r = 2R (forgetting to add the radius), and g/3 from an inverse rather than inverse-square law.

questions.s: A planet orbits the Sun in a circle whose radius is 4 times the radius of the Earth's orbit. What is its orbital period?
questions.e: Kepler's third law: T² ∝ r³, so T = (4)^(3/2) × 1 year = 8 years. 4 years assumes T ∝ r, and 16 years assumes T ∝ r².

questions.s: A satellite moves in a circular orbit around the Earth. It is moved to another circular orbit whose radius is 4 times larger. What is the ratio of its new orbital speed to its old orbital speed?
questions.e: GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), so v ∝ 1/√r. With r multiplied by 4, v is divided by √4 = 2, giving 1 : 2. 1 : 4 treats v as inversely proportional to r.

questions.s: A small ball on a light string of length 0.4 m is whirled in a vertical circle. What is the minimum speed it must have at the top of the circle for the string to stay taut? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: At the top with zero tension, gravity alone provides the centripetal force: mg = mv²/r, so v = √(gr) = √(10 × 0.4) = 2 m/s. 0 m/s would be correct only for a rigid rod, which can push; a string cannot. 2√5 m/s is the minimum speed at the bottom, not the top.

questions.s: A small ball on a light string of length 0.8 m moves in a vertical circle. What is the minimum speed it must have at the lowest point so that it just completes the circle? (g = 10 m/s², air resistance negligible)
questions.e: At the top the minimum speed satisfies v_top² = gr = 8. Energy conservation from bottom to top (rise 2r = 1.6 m): v_b² = v_top² + 4gr = 8 + 32 = 40, so v_b = 2√10 m/s. 4√2 m/s (v² = 4gr) assumes the ball can reach the top with zero speed, which is true for a rod but not a string.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg ball on a string of length 1 m swings in a vertical circle. At the lowest point its speed is 4 m/s. What is the tension in the string there? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: At the lowest point T − mg = mv²/r, so T = mg + mv²/r = 5 + 0.5 × 16/1 = 13 N. 3 N comes from subtracting the weight instead of adding it, and 8 N is only the centripetal force mv²/r.

questions.s: A car of mass 800 kg drives over the top of a hump-backed bridge whose curved surface has radius 40 m, at a speed of 10 m/s. What is the normal force from the road on the car at the top? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: At the top mg − N = mv²/r, so N = m(g − v²/r) = 800 × (10 − 100/40) = 800 × 7.5 = 6000 N. 10 000 N comes from adding mv²/r to mg, which applies at the bottom of a dip, not the top of a hump.

questions.s: A small ball on a light string moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.9 m (a conical pendulum), with the string making an angle of 45° with the vertical. What is the speed of the ball? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: The horizontal component of tension gives the centripetal force and the vertical component balances the weight, so tan θ = v²/(rg). With tan 45° = 1, v² = rg = 0.9 × 10 = 9 and v = 3 m/s. 9 m/s is v² without the square root.

questions.s: A road curve of radius 120 m is banked at an angle θ where tan θ = 0.75. At what speed can a car take the curve with no friction force needed? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: With no friction, the normal force provides both support and the centripetal force: tan θ = v²/(rg), so v² = 0.75 × 120 × 10 = 900 and v = 30 m/s. 40 m/s comes from using tan θ = 4/3 (inverting the ratio), and 900 m/s forgets the square root.

questions.s: A stone tied to a string moves in a horizontal circle at constant speed. In which direction does the net force on the stone act?
o: Away from the centre of the circle
Along the tangent, in the direction of motion
Along the tangent, against the motion
Towards the centre of the circle
questions.e: In uniform circular motion the net (centripetal) force always points towards the centre. There is no tangential force because the speed is constant; an 'outward' force is a common misconception from the feeling of being thrown outward in a turning car.

questions.s: Satellites A and B move in circular orbits around the same planet. The orbital radius of A is twice that of B. What is the ratio of the period of A to the period of B?
questions.e: By Kepler's third law T² ∝ r³, so T_A/T_B = (2)^(3/2) = 2√2. 8 is the ratio of r³ (forgetting to take the square root), and 2 assumes T ∝ r.

questions.s: The acceleration due to gravity at the surface of a planet of radius R is g, and G is the gravitational constant. Ignoring rotation, which expression gives the planet's mass?
questions.e: At the surface mg = GMm/R², so g = GM/R² and M = gR²/G. g/(GR²) inverts the relation, and gR/G forgets that the radius is squared.

questions.s: Which of the following statements about a geostationary satellite is correct?
o: It can hover over any city, including ones far from the equator
Its orbit lies in the Earth's equatorial plane
Its orbital speed is greater than 7.9 km/s
questions.e: To stay above the same point, the satellite must rotate with the Earth (period 24 h) and its orbit must be centred on the Earth's axis, so it lies in the equatorial plane. Its orbit is far above the surface, so its speed is less than 7.9 km/s (the speed of a satellite just above the surface); it cannot stay above a city away from the equator.

questions.s: What is the angular velocity of the minute hand of a clock?
questions.e: The minute hand turns through 2π rad in 3600 s, so ω = 2π/3600 = π/1800 rad/s. π/30 rad/s belongs to the second hand (period 60 s) and π/21600 rad/s to the hour hand (period 12 h).

questions.s: What is the ratio of the angular velocity of the hour hand of a clock to that of its minute hand?
questions.e: The hour hand has period 12 h and the minute hand 1 h. Since ω = 2π/T, the ratio is (1/12) : 1 = 1 : 12. 1 : 24 wrongly uses 24 h for the hour hand, which makes two turns per day.

questions.s: Two pulleys are joined by a belt that does not slip. The small pulley has radius 10 cm and turns at 6 revolutions per second. The large pulley has radius 30 cm. How fast does the large pulley turn?
questions.e: Points on the belt and both rims share the same linear speed: 2πf₁r₁ = 2πf₂r₂, so f₂ = 6 × 10/30 = 2 rev/s. 18 rev/s multiplies by the radius ratio instead of dividing; 6 rev/s assumes equal angular velocities, which is true only for wheels on the same axle.

questions.s: Points P and Q are on the same rotating disc, at distances r and 2r from the axis. What is the ratio of the centripetal acceleration of P to that of Q?
questions.e: Both points have the same angular velocity ω, so a = ω²r and a_P : a_Q = r : 2r = 1 : 2. 2 : 1 comes from using a = v²/r as if both points had the same speed, but Q moves twice as fast as P.

questions.s: A particle moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m with a constant angular velocity of 6 rad/s. What is its centripetal acceleration?
questions.e: a = ω²r = 6² × 0.5 = 18 m/s². 3 is ωr, which is the speed in m/s, and 72 m/s² comes from ω²/r.

questions.s: A body weighed with a spring balance reads slightly less at the equator than at the poles. Which of the following is one correct reason?
o: Part of gravity supplies the centripetal force of Earth's spin
The gravitational constant G has a smaller value near the equator
Greater air pressure at the equator pushes the body upward
Objects at the equator have a smaller mass than at the poles
questions.e: A body at the equator moves in a circle as the Earth rotates, so part of the gravitational pull is used as centripetal force and the balance reading is reduced. G is a universal constant and mass does not depend on location; air pressure is not the cause.

questions.s: A planet has twice the mass and twice the radius of the Earth. An astronaut weighs 600 N on the Earth's surface. What is her weight on the planet's surface?
questions.e: g = GM/R², so g′/g = 2/2² = 1/2 and her weight is 600 × 1/2 = 300 N. 600 N comes from cancelling 2 with 2, forgetting that the radius is squared.

questions.s: A satellite moves in a circular orbit just above the Earth's surface. Taking R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m for the Earth's radius and g = 10 m/s², what is its orbital speed?
questions.e: Gravity mg provides the centripetal force: mg = mv²/R, so v = √(gR) = √(6.4 × 10⁷) = 8 × 10³ m/s. 8000√2 m/s is √(2gR), which is the escape speed, not the orbital speed.

questions.s: A satellite moving just above the Earth's surface has orbital speed v₁. What is the orbital speed of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius 2R, where R is the Earth's radius?
questions.e: Orbital speed v = √(GM/r) is proportional to 1/√r. Doubling r from R to 2R divides the speed by √2, giving v₁/√2. v₁/2 treats v as inversely proportional to r.

questions.s: A satellite is moved from one circular orbit around the Earth to a higher circular orbit. Which of the following increases?
questions.e: For circular orbits v = √(GM/r), ω = √(GM/r³) and a = GM/r², all of which decrease as r grows, while T = 2π√(r³/GM) increases. A common mistake is thinking a higher satellite moves faster because it covers a longer path.

questions.s: The Moon orbits the Earth at a distance of about 60 Earth radii from the Earth's centre. In terms of g, the acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface, what is the centripetal acceleration of the Moon?
questions.e: The Moon's centripetal acceleration is the Earth's gravitational field at its distance, which falls as 1/r². At 60R it is g/60² = g/3600. g/60 uses an inverse rather than inverse-square law.

questions.s: Two uniform spheres, each of mass 1000 kg, have their centres 1 m apart. What is the gravitational force between them? (G = 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²)
questions.e: F = Gm₁m₂/r² = 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1000 × 1000/1² = 6.7 × 10⁻⁵ N. 6.7 × 10⁻⁸ N uses only one of the masses; 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ N leaves out both masses.

questions.s: Two point masses attract each other with force F. If one mass is doubled and the distance between them is tripled, what is the new force?
questions.e: F ∝ m₁m₂/r². Doubling one mass multiplies F by 2 and tripling r divides it by 9, so F′ = 2F/9. 2F/3 forgets to square the distance.

questions.s: At what height above the Earth's surface is the acceleration due to gravity one quarter of its value at the surface? (R is the Earth's radius)
questions.e: g ∝ 1/r², so g falls to one quarter when r = 2R, measured from the centre. The height above the surface is 2R − R = R. 2R is the distance from the centre, not the height.

questions.s: A moon moves in a circular orbit of radius r around a planet with period T. G is the gravitational constant. Which expression gives the mass of the planet?
questions.e: Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = m(2π/T)²r, so M = 4π²r³/(GT²). 4π²r²/(GT²) loses a factor of r by using ω²/r instead of ω²r; the other options rearrange incorrectly. The moon's own mass cancels.

questions.s: A satellite orbits very close to the surface of a uniform spherical planet with period T. G is the gravitational constant. Which expression gives the average density of the planet?
questions.e: With r ≈ R, M = 4π²R³/(GT²). Dividing by the volume (4/3)πR³ gives ρ = 3π/(GT²), independent of R. 4π/(3GT²) inverts the volume factor, and 3π/(GT) forgets to square T.

questions.s: A car goes round a flat circular track at constant speed. If its speed is doubled on the same track, by what factor does the required friction force change?
questions.e: The friction provides the centripetal force F = mv²/r, which is proportional to v². Doubling v multiplies F by 2² = 4. '2 times' forgets that the speed is squared.

questions.s: In a fairground rotor, riders stand against the inside wall of a vertical cylinder of radius 5 m. When it spins fast enough the floor drops away and friction from the wall holds them up. The coefficient of static friction is 0.5. What is the minimum angular velocity needed? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: The wall's normal force gives the centripetal force: N = mω²r. Friction must balance the weight: μN ≥ mg, so ω² ≥ g/(μr) = 10/(0.5 × 5) = 4 and ω = 2 rad/s. 4 rad/s is ω² without the square root.

questions.s: Which of the following quantities has the SI unit rad/s?
questions.e: Angular velocity is the angle turned per unit time, measured in rad/s. Period is measured in s, linear speed in m/s, and centripetal acceleration in m/s².

questions.s: A point on a rotating wheel moves in a circle of radius 0.2 m with a frequency of 5 Hz. What is its speed?
questions.e: v = ωr = 2πfr = 2π × 5 × 0.2 = 2π m/s. 10π m/s is ω (in rad/s) without multiplying by r, and 1 m/s multiplies f by r and forgets the 2π.

questions.s: A turntable makes 30 complete revolutions in 60 s at a steady rate. What is its period of rotation?
questions.e: The period is the time for one revolution: T = 60 s/30 = 2 s. 0.5 is the frequency in Hz (revolutions per second), not the period.

questions.s: The Moon moves in a nearly circular orbit around the Earth. Which force provides the centripetal force for this motion?
o: The Sun's gravitational pull on the Moon
An outward centrifugal force on the Moon
The Earth's magnetic force on the Moon
The Earth's gravitational pull on the Moon
questions.e: The centripetal force is not an extra force; it is supplied by a real force pointing to the centre of the orbit, here the Earth's gravitational attraction. A 'centrifugal force' would point outward and is not a real force on the Moon in an inertial frame.

questions.s: In Newton's law of gravitation F = Gm₁m₂/r², what is the SI unit of the gravitational constant G?
questions.e: Rearranging gives G = Fr²/(m₁m₂), so its unit is N·m²/kg². N·kg²/m² inverts the masses and the distance.

questions.s: A ball on a string moves in a horizontal circle on a smooth table. The string suddenly breaks. How does the ball move immediately afterwards?
o: Along the tangent at that point
In a spiral path away from centre
questions.e: Once the string breaks there is no horizontal force, so by Newton's first law the ball continues with the velocity it had, which is along the tangent. It does not fly radially outward, because there is no outward force.

questions.s: A point moves in a circle of radius 0.4 m with an angular velocity of 5 rad/s. What is its speed?
questions.e: v = ωr = 5 × 0.4 = 2 m/s. 12.5 m/s divides ω by r, and 10 m/s is ω²r, which is the centripetal acceleration in m/s².

questions.s: Astronauts in a spacecraft orbiting the Earth feel weightless. Why?
o: There is no gravity at that height
Gravity there is balanced by centrifugal force
The craft shields them from Earth's gravity
They and the craft fall freely together
questions.e: At typical orbital heights gravity is still about 90 % of its surface value. The astronauts and the craft are both in free fall with the same acceleration, so nothing presses on them and they feel weightless. Gravity is not switched off or balanced; it provides the centripetal force.

questions.s: A satellite moves in a circular orbit around the Earth. How much work does the Earth's gravitational force do on the satellite during one quarter of an orbit?
o: Work equal to its kinetic energy
questions.e: In a circular orbit the gravitational force points to the centre and is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed stays constant. Positive or negative work would change the kinetic energy.

questions.s: Two satellites of masses m and 2m move in circular orbits of the same radius around the Earth. What is the ratio of their periods?
questions.e: From GMm/r² = m(2π/T)²r, T = 2π√(r³/GM); the satellite's own mass cancels. Same radius gives the same period, 1 : 1. Thinking the heavier satellite is pulled harder misses that it also needs more centripetal force.

questions.s: A 2 kg mass moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.5 m with an angular velocity of 3 rad/s. What is the centripetal force on it?
questions.e: F = mω²r = 2 × 3² × 0.5 = 9 N. 3 N is mωr (forgetting to square ω), and 4.5 N comes from halving the result as if using ½mω²r.

questions.s: A child on a merry-go-round moves from 1 m to 2 m from the centre while the angular velocity stays the same. What happens to her speed?
questions.e: v = ωr, so with ω constant, doubling r doubles v. It does not stay the same, because points farther from the axis must travel a longer circle in the same time.

questions.s: Which expression gives the acceleration due to gravity at the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R? (G is the gravitational constant; ignore rotation)
questions.e: The force on a mass m is GMm/R² = mg, so g = GM/R². GMm/R² is the weight of the mass m, not the acceleration, and √(GM/R) is the orbital speed just above the surface.

questions.s: Which statement expresses Kepler's third law for planets in circular orbits around the Sun, where T is the period and r the orbital radius?
o: T/r is the same for all planets
T²/r³ is the same for all planets
T³/r² is the same for all planets
T·r² is the same for all planets
questions.e: Kepler's third law states that the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the orbital radius, so T²/r³ is the same for every planet of the same star. T³/r² swaps the powers.

questions.s: A planet moves round the Sun in an elliptical orbit. Where is its speed greatest?
o: At the point closest to the Sun
At the point farthest from the Sun
At the ends of the minor axis
questions.e: By Kepler's second law the line from the Sun to the planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, so the planet moves fastest when it is nearest the Sun. Its speed is not constant in an ellipse.

questions.s: A 1 kg ball is fixed to one end of a light rigid rod of length 0.4 m and moves in a vertical circle about the other end. At the top of the circle its speed is 1 m/s. What force does the rod exert on the ball there? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: The required centripetal force is mv²/r = 1 × 1²/0.4 = 2.5 N, less than the weight 10 N. Taking downward as positive, mg + F = 2.5 gives F = −7.5 N, so the rod pushes up with 7.5 N. 12.5 N comes from assuming the rod must pull down and adding the weight.

questions.s: A 0.2 kg ball on a light string of length 0.5 m moves in a vertical circle. At the top of the circle its speed is 3 m/s. What is the tension in the string at the top? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: At the top tension and weight both point down: T + mg = mv²/r, so T = 0.2 × 9/0.5 − 2 = 3.6 − 2 = 1.6 N. 3.6 N forgets the weight, 5.6 N adds it, and 13.6 N is the tension at the bottom.

questions.s: A binary star system consists of two stars of masses 2M and M orbiting their common centre of mass with the same period. What is the ratio of the speed of the 2M star to the speed of the M star?
questions.e: Both stars share the same angular velocity and the same mutual gravitational force, so 2Mω²r₁ = Mω²r₂, giving r₁ : r₂ = 1 : 2. Since v = ωr, the speeds are also 1 : 2. 2 : 1 wrongly assumes the heavier star moves faster.

questions.s: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at a height R above the Earth's surface, where R is the Earth's radius and g is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface. What is its period?
questions.e: With r = 2R and GM = gR², T = 2π√(r³/GM) = 2π√(8R³/(gR²)) = 2π√(8R/g) = 4π√(2R/g). 2π√(R/g) is the period of a satellite just above the surface, and 2π√(2R/g) forgets to cube the radius.

questions.s: Satellites A and B move in circular orbits around the Earth with radii r and 4r. What is the ratio of the centripetal acceleration of A to that of B?
questions.e: The centripetal acceleration of a satellite equals the gravitational field GM/r², so a_A : a_B = (1/r²) : (1/16r²) = 16 : 1. 4 : 1 uses an inverse rather than inverse-square law, and 1 : 16 inverts the ratio.

questions.s: A small ball is released from rest on a smooth track and slides down into a vertical loop of radius 0.4 m. What is the minimum release height, measured from the bottom of the loop, for the ball to just stay on the track at the top of the loop? (Treat the ball as a particle; g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: At the top the minimum speed satisfies v² = gR. Energy conservation: mgh = mg(2R) + ½mv² = mg(2R) + ½mgR, so h = 2.5R = 1.0 m. 0.8 m (2R) only gets the ball to the top height with zero speed, so it would leave the track before reaching the top.

questions.s: A 60 kg pilot flies a plane through the bottom of a vertical circle of radius 400 m at a speed of 100 m/s. What is the force of the seat on the pilot at the lowest point? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: At the bottom N − mg = mv²/r, so N = 60 × 10 + 60 × 100²/400 = 600 + 1500 = 2100 N. 1500 N is only the centripetal force and 900 N subtracts the weight instead of adding it.

questions.s: A car goes round a banked curve faster than the speed for which the curve was designed (the speed needing no friction). In which direction does the friction force on the tyres act along the road surface?
o: Up the slope of the bank
Zero, since the road is banked
Down the slope of the bank
questions.e: Above the design speed the horizontal component of the normal force is too small to supply mv²/r, so the car tends to slide up and outward. Friction opposes this tendency and acts down the slope, adding an inward component. Friction acts up the slope only when the car is slower than the design speed.

questions.s: A curve of radius 40 m is banked so that cars travelling at 20 m/s need no friction. What is the banking angle? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: With no friction, tan θ = v²/(rg) = 400/(40 × 10) = 1, so θ = 45°. Confusing tan θ with sin θ or cos θ would give a different angle.

questions.s: Two satellites orbit the same planet in circular orbits. The period of A is 8 times the period of B. What is the ratio of the orbital radius of A to that of B?
questions.e: Kepler's third law: r³ ∝ T², so r_A/r_B = (8²)^(1/3) = 64^(1/3) = 4. 8 : 1 assumes r ∝ T, and 64 : 1 is the ratio of r³, not r.

questions.s: An astronaut weighs 800 N on the Earth's surface. What is the gravitational force on her when she is at a height of 3R above the surface, where R is the Earth's radius?
questions.e: At height 3R the distance from the centre is 4R, so the force is 800/4² = 50 N. 200 N uses an inverse rather than inverse-square law. The force is not zero: gravity still acts and keeps her in orbit.

questions.s: Planet X has the same average density as the Earth but twice its radius. What is the ratio of the period of a satellite orbiting just above the surface of X to the period of one orbiting just above the Earth's surface?
questions.e: For a near-surface orbit GM/R² = 4π²R/T² with M = (4/3)πR³ρ, which gives T = √(3π/(Gρ)). The radius cancels, so equal densities give equal periods, 1 : 1. 2√2 : 1 applies Kepler's law as if the planet's mass were unchanged, but doubling R at the same density makes M eight times larger.

questions.s: A particle moves 3 m along the arc of a circle of radius 2 m. Through what angle does it turn about the centre?
questions.e: Angle in radians = arc length/radius = 3/2 = 1.5 rad. 0.67 rad divides the radius by the arc length, and 6 rad multiplies them.

questions.s: A body moves uniformly in a circle of radius 1 m with a period of π s. What is its centripetal acceleration?
questions.e: ω = 2π/T = 2π/π = 2 rad/s, so a = ω²r = 4 × 1 = 4 m/s². 2 m/s² is ωr, which is the speed in m/s, not the acceleration.

questions.s: A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius r around the Earth with speed v. G is the gravitational constant. Which expression gives the mass of the Earth?
questions.e: GMm/r² = mv²/r gives GM = v²r, so M = v²r/G. v²/(Gr) comes from equating GM/r² with v² instead of v²/r.

questions.s: A coin sits on a horizontal turntable 0.25 m from the axis. The coefficient of static friction between coin and turntable is 0.4. What is the greatest angular velocity at which the coin does not slide? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: Static friction supplies the centripetal force: μmg = mω²r, so ω² = μg/r = 0.4 × 10/0.25 = 16 and ω = 4 rad/s. 16 rad/s forgets the square root, and 1 rad/s multiplies by r instead of dividing.

questions.s: Two satellites move in circular orbits around the Earth. Compared with the satellite in the higher orbit, the satellite in the lower orbit has
questions.e: v = √(GM/r) increases as r decreases, and T = 2π√(r³/GM) decreases as r decreases. So the lower satellite is faster and has a shorter period; it does not have a longer period, because both its path is shorter and its speed is higher.

questions.s: An asteroid moves round the Sun in a circular orbit with a period of 27 years. What is its orbital radius in astronomical units (1 AU is the radius of the Earth's orbit)?
questions.e: Using Kepler's third law with the Earth (1 year, 1 AU): r³ = T² = 27² = 729, so r = 9 AU. 3 AU takes the cube root of T instead of T², and 27 AU assumes r ∝ T.

questions.s: A runner moves at constant speed round a circular track of radius 100 m and completes one lap in 20π s. What is the runner's centripetal acceleration?
questions.e: v = 2πr/T = 2π × 100/(20π) = 10 m/s, so a = v²/r = 100/100 = 1 m/s². 0.1 is ω = v/r in rad/s, and 10 is the speed in m/s.

questions.s: Two identical uniform spheres, each of mass m and radius r, are placed so that they just touch. G is the gravitational constant. What is the gravitational force between them?
questions.e: For uniform spheres the distance in Newton's law is measured between centres, which is 2r here, so F = Gm²/(2r)² = Gm²/(4r²). Gm²/r² wrongly uses the radius as the separation.

questions.s: Which quantity is the same for all geostationary satellites?
questions.e: All geostationary satellites have the same period (24 h), and since T² ∝ r³ they all have the same orbital radius (and speed). Their masses can differ, so their kinetic energies and the gravitational forces on them also differ.

questions.s: A planet has half the radius of the Earth and one-eighth of its mass. What is the acceleration due to gravity at its surface? (Take g = 10 m/s² at the Earth's surface.)
questions.e: g = GM/R², so g′/g = (1/8)/(1/2)² = (1/8)/(1/4) = 1/2, giving 5 m/s². 2.5 m/s² forgets to square the radius, and 1.25 m/s² ignores the change in radius.

questions.s: A 0.2 kg ball hangs on a light string. It is pulled aside until the string is horizontal and taut, then released from rest. What is the tension in the string as the ball passes through the lowest point? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: Energy conservation gives v² = 2gL at the bottom. Then T − mg = mv²/L = 2mg, so T = 3mg = 6 N, independent of the length. 4 N is only the centripetal force 2mg, and 2 N is the weight.

questions.s: A satellite in a circular orbit around the Earth is moved to a new circular orbit with 4 times the radius. What is the ratio of its new angular velocity to its old angular velocity?
questions.e: GM/r² = ω²r gives ω = √(GM/r³), so ω ∝ r^(−3/2). With r multiplied by 4, ω is divided by 4^(3/2) = 8, giving 1 : 8. 1 : 2 is the ratio of the speeds, not the angular velocities.

questions.s: A conical pendulum consists of a small bob on a string of length 0.8 m moving in a horizontal circle, with the string at 60° to the vertical. What is the period of its motion? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: T cos θ = mg and T sin θ = mω²L sin θ give ω² = g/(L cos θ), so the period is 2π√(L cos θ/g) = 2π√(0.4/10) = 2π × 0.2 = 0.4π s. 0.4√2π s is the simple-pendulum formula 2π√(L/g), which ignores the angle.

questions.s: A satellite orbits a planet of mass M in a circular orbit of radius r with period T. Another satellite orbits a planet of mass 4M in a circular orbit of radius 4r. What is its period?
questions.e: T = 2π√(r³/(GM)), so T′/T = √(4³/4) = √16 = 4, giving 4T. 8T applies Kepler's third law as if the central mass were the same.

questions.s: A bucket of water is swung in a vertical circle of radius 0.9 m. What is the minimum speed at the top for the water to stay in the bucket? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: At the minimum speed gravity alone provides the centripetal force at the top: v² = gr = 9, so v = 3 m/s. 9 m/s forgets the square root, and 3√5 m/s is the minimum speed at the bottom of the circle.

questions.s: A ceiling fan turns steadily at 300 revolutions per minute. What is its angular velocity?
questions.e: 300 rev/min = 5 rev/s, so ω = 2πf = 2π × 5 = 10π rad/s. 5π rad/s forgets the factor 2 in 2πf, and 600π rad/s uses 300 without converting minutes to seconds.

questions.s: A small wheel makes 4 complete revolutions every second. What is its period?
questions.e: The period is the reciprocal of the frequency: T = 1/f = 1/4 = 0.25 s. 4 s confuses the period with the frequency.

questions.s: A ball moves at a steady 6 m/s in a horizontal circle of radius 3 m. What is its centripetal acceleration?
questions.e: a = v²/r = 36/3 = 12 m/s². 2 m/s² is v/r (the angular velocity), and 108 m/s² multiplies v² by r.

questions.s: Two point masses attract each other with force F. Both masses are doubled and the distance between them is also doubled. What is the new force?
questions.e: F ∝ m₁m₂/r². Doubling both masses multiplies F by 4, and doubling r divides it by 4, so the force is unchanged. 4F forgets the effect of the larger distance.

questions.s: A particle moves in a circle of radius r with angular velocity ω. Which expression gives its centripetal acceleration?
questions.e: a = v²/r with v = ωr gives a = ω²r²/r = ω²r. ω²/r mixes up the formula with v²/r.

questions.s: A satellite moves in a circular orbit around the Earth. What is the angle between its velocity and the gravitational force on it?
questions.e: The velocity is along the tangent and gravity points to the centre of the circle, so they are perpendicular (90°). That is why gravity changes the direction but not the speed of the satellite.

questions.s: A 1500 kg car rounds a flat curve of radius 60 m. The maximum friction force the road can provide is 10 000 N. What is the greatest speed at which it can take the curve?
questions.e: F_max = mv²/r, so v² = F_max·r/m = 10 000 × 60/1500 = 400 and v = 20 m/s. 400 m/s forgets the square root.

questions.s: A car drives over the top of a hump whose curved surface has radius 22.5 m. What is the greatest speed at which it can pass over the top without losing contact with the road? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: Contact is just lost when the normal force is zero, so mg = mv²/r and v = √(gr) = √225 = 15 m/s. 225 m/s is v² without the square root, and 15√2 m/s uses √(2gr).

questions.s: A man weighs 720 N on the Earth's surface. What would be the gravitational force on him at a height above the surface equal to the Earth's radius?
questions.e: At height R the distance from the centre is 2R, so the force is 720/2² = 180 N. 360 N uses an inverse rather than inverse-square law, and 80 N uses 3R as the distance from the centre.

questions.s: A planet moves round the Sun in a circular orbit of radius 1/4 AU, where 1 AU is the radius of the Earth's orbit. What is its orbital period?
questions.e: Kepler's third law with the Earth as reference: T² = r³ = (1/4)³ = 1/64, so T = 1/8 year. 1/4 year assumes T ∝ r, and 1/16 year assumes T ∝ r².

questions.s: Satellites A and B move in circular orbits around the Earth with radii r and 4r. What is the ratio of the orbital speed of A to that of B?
questions.e: v = √(GM/r), so v_A : v_B = √(4r/r) = 2 : 1. 4 : 1 treats v as inversely proportional to r, and 1 : 2 wrongly assumes the outer satellite moves faster.

questions.s: A small stone on a light string of length 1.6 m is whirled in a vertical circle. What is the minimum speed it must have at the top for the string to stay taut? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: At the minimum speed the tension at the top is zero and mg = mv²/r, so v = √(gr) = √16 = 4 m/s. 0 m/s would apply to a rigid rod, not a string; 4√5 m/s is the minimum speed at the bottom.

questions.s: A 0.2 kg ball on a light string of length 0.5 m moves in a vertical circle. At the lowest point its speed is 5 m/s. What is the tension in the string there? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: At the bottom T − mg = mv²/r, so T = 2 + 0.2 × 25/0.5 = 2 + 10 = 12 N. 10 N is only the centripetal force, and 8 N subtracts the weight instead of adding it.

questions.s: A track of radius 160 m is banked at an angle θ with tan θ = 0.25. At what speed can a vehicle go round with no friction force needed? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: tan θ = v²/(rg), so v² = 0.25 × 160 × 10 = 400 and v = 20 m/s. 80 m/s comes from using tan θ = 4 (inverting the ratio).

questions.s: A satellite moves in a circular orbit around the Earth. If a second satellite with twice the mass moves in an orbit of the same radius, how does its orbital speed compare?
questions.e: From GMm/r² = mv²/r, v = √(GM/r); the satellite's mass cancels, so the speed is the same. A larger mass feels a larger gravitational force but also needs a proportionally larger centripetal force.

questions.s: Two lead spheres, each of mass 100 kg, have their centres 0.1 m apart. What is the gravitational force between them? (G = 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²)
questions.e: F = Gm₁m₂/r² = 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ × 100 × 100/(0.1)² = 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ × 10⁶ = 6.7 × 10⁻⁵ N. 6.7 × 10⁻⁶ N divides by r instead of r², and 6.7 × 10⁻⁷ N ignores the distance.

questions.s: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at a height of 3R above the Earth's surface, where R is the Earth's radius and g the acceleration due to gravity at the surface. What is its period?
questions.e: The orbital radius is 4R, not 3R. With GM = gR², T = 2π√(r³/(GM)) = 2π√(64R³/(gR²)) = 2π × 8√(R/g) = 16π√(R/g). 8π√(R/g) comes from using r² instead of r³, since 2π√(16R/g) = 8π√(R/g).

questions.s: A coin on a horizontal turntable starts to slide when the angular velocity reaches ω₀ if it is placed a distance r from the axis. At what angular velocity does it start to slide if placed at 4r?
questions.e: Sliding starts when μmg = mω²r, so ω ∝ 1/√r. At 4r the limit is ω₀/√4 = ω₀/2. ω₀/4 treats ω as inversely proportional to r.

questions.s: A 0.1 kg ball slides without friction down a track from rest at a height 3R above the bottom of a vertical loop of radius R. What is the normal force from the track on the ball at the top of the loop? (g = 10 m/s²; treat the ball as a particle)
questions.e: Energy: v² at the top = 2g(3R − 2R) = 2gR. At the top N + mg = mv²/R = 2mg, so N = mg = 0.1 × 10 = 1 N. 2 N is only the centripetal force; 0 N would be correct for a release height of 2.5R.

questions.s: Two stars of masses M and 3M, a distance L apart, orbit their common centre of mass with the same period. What is the orbital radius of the 3M star?
questions.e: Both stars have the same ω and feel equal gravitational forces, so M·r₁ = 3M·r₂ with r₁ + r₂ = L. Then r₂ = L/4 for the heavier star and r₁ = 3L/4 for the lighter one. 3L/4 is the radius of the lighter star.

questions.s: Which of the following changes would increase the period of a simple pendulum (small oscillations)?
o: Increasing the mass of the bob
Increasing the length of the string
Taking it to a place with larger g
questions.e: For small oscillations T = 2π√(L/g), so a longer string gives a longer period. The period does not depend on the mass or (for small swings) the amplitude, and a larger g shortens the period.

questions.s: A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 0.4 m. What is its speed?
questions.e: v = fλ = 50 × 0.4 = 20 m/s. 125 m/s comes from f/λ and 0.008 m/s from λ/f.

questions.s: Which statement correctly describes sound waves travelling through air?
questions.e: Sound in air consists of compressions and rarefactions: air particles vibrate back and forth along the direction of travel, so it is a longitudinal wave, and it needs a medium, so it is mechanical. Electromagnetic waves are transverse and need no medium.

questions.s: A 0.1 kg mass on a light spring of spring constant 40 N/m oscillates horizontally on a smooth surface. What is the period of oscillation?
questions.e: T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π√(0.1/40) = 2π√0.0025 = 2π × 0.05 = 0.1π s. 0.05π s forgets the factor 2, and 40π s uses √(k/m) instead of √(m/k).

questions.s: The displacement of a particle in simple harmonic motion is x = 0.05 sin(4πt), with x in metres and t in seconds. What are its amplitude and period?
questions.e: Comparing with x = A sin(ωt): A = 0.05 m and ω = 4π rad/s, so T = 2π/ω = 0.5 s. 2 s is the frequency in Hz taken as the period, and 0.1 m is the distance between the two extreme positions, not the amplitude.

questions.s: For a body in simple harmonic motion, where is the magnitude of its acceleration greatest?
questions.e: In SHM a = −ω²x, so the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and is greatest at the extremes, where |x| = A. At the equilibrium position the acceleration is zero and the speed is greatest.

questions.s: As water waves pass, a floating cork makes 30 complete up-and-down oscillations in 10 s. The distance between neighbouring crests is 2 m. What is the speed of the waves?
questions.e: The frequency is 30/10 = 3 Hz and the wavelength is 2 m, so v = fλ = 3 × 2 = 6 m/s. 60 m/s multiplies the number of oscillations by the wavelength without dividing by the time.

questions.s: A student claps her hands in front of a cliff and hears the echo 2 s later. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. How far away is the cliff?
questions.e: In 2 s the sound travels 340 × 2 = 680 m, which is to the cliff and back, so the cliff is 680/2 = 340 m away. 680 m forgets that the sound makes a round trip.

questions.s: Which of the following cannot travel through a vacuum?
questions.e: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs particles of a medium to pass on its vibrations, so it cannot cross a vacuum. Light, radio waves and X-rays are electromagnetic waves, which travel through empty space.

questions.s: In a standing wave of wavelength λ, what is the distance between two adjacent nodes?
questions.e: Adjacent nodes in a standing wave are half a wavelength apart, λ/2. λ/4 is the distance from a node to the nearest antinode.

questions.s: A car sounding its horn moves towards a stationary listener at constant speed. Compared with the frequency emitted by the horn, the listener hears
questions.e: By the Doppler effect, when a source moves towards a listener the wavefronts in front of it are squeezed together, so the listener receives a shorter wavelength and a higher frequency. At constant speed this higher frequency stays constant; it does not keep rising.

questions.s: A mass on a horizontal spring performs simple harmonic motion on a smooth surface. Which statement is correct?
o: At equilibrium the kinetic energy is greatest
At equilibrium the potential energy is greatest
At the extremes the speed is greatest
Total mechanical energy varies over a cycle
questions.e: At the equilibrium position the spring is unstretched, so the elastic potential energy is zero and all the energy is kinetic: the speed is greatest there. With no friction the total mechanical energy stays constant; at the extremes the speed is zero.

questions.s: The length of a simple pendulum is made 4 times longer. What happens to its period?
questions.e: T = 2π√(L/g), so T ∝ √L. Multiplying L by 4 multiplies T by √4 = 2. 'It quadruples' forgets the square root.

questions.s: Which property of a sound wave mainly determines the pitch that we hear?
questions.e: Pitch is determined by frequency: a higher frequency is heard as a higher note. Amplitude determines loudness, not pitch.

questions.s: In which of the following does sound travel fastest?
questions.e: Sound generally travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases (roughly 5000 m/s in steel, 1500 m/s in water and 340 m/s in air). It cannot travel through a vacuum at all.

questions.s: In a transverse wave, how do the particles of the medium move?
o: Parallel to the direction of travel
In circles around the direction of travel
Along with the wave at the wave speed
Perpendicular to the direction of travel
questions.e: In a transverse wave the particles oscillate at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels, as on a stretched rope. Oscillation parallel to the direction of travel describes a longitudinal wave; the particles do not travel along with the wave.

questions.s: Two pulses travel towards each other on a rope. One has a displacement of +3 cm and the other −2 cm. What is the displacement at the instant their peaks overlap exactly?
questions.e: By the principle of superposition the displacements add: (+3) + (−2) = +1 cm. 5 cm adds the sizes and ignores that the second pulse is on the opposite side.

questions.s: A mass on a spring oscillates in simple harmonic motion. If the amplitude is doubled, what happens to the period?
questions.e: The period of a mass–spring system is T = 2π√(m/k), which does not depend on the amplitude. A larger amplitude means a longer path but also a higher maximum speed, so the time per cycle is unchanged.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg mass on a spring oscillates with a period of 1.2 s. It is replaced by a 2 kg mass on the same spring. What is the new period?
questions.e: T = 2π√(m/k), so T ∝ √m. The mass is multiplied by 4, so the period is multiplied by 2: 2.4 s. 4.8 s assumes the period is proportional to the mass.

questions.s: A simple pendulum has a period of 2 s at a place where g = π² m/s². What is its length?
questions.e: T = 2π√(L/g) gives L = gT²/(4π²) = π² × 4/(4π²) = 1 m. 0.25 m comes from using T = 1 s, the time for one swing from side to side rather than a full oscillation.

questions.s: A simple pendulum has period T on the Earth. What would its period be on a planet where the acceleration due to gravity is one quarter of that on the Earth?
questions.e: T = 2π√(L/g), so T ∝ 1/√g. Dividing g by 4 multiplies T by √4 = 2, giving 2T. T/2 gets the direction wrong: weaker gravity gives a slower swing.

questions.s: A body performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude 0.1 m and period 0.2π s. What is its maximum speed?
questions.e: ω = 2π/T = 2π/(0.2π) = 10 rad/s, so v_max = Aω = 0.1 × 10 = 1 m/s. 10 m/s is Aω², which is the maximum acceleration in m/s².

questions.s: A particle performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude 0.02 m and frequency 5 Hz. What is the magnitude of its maximum acceleration?
questions.e: ω = 2πf = 10π rad/s, so a_max = Aω² = 0.02 × 100π² = 2π² m/s². 0.2π m/s² is Aω, the maximum speed in m/s, and 0.5π² m/s² uses ω = πf, forgetting the factor 2.

questions.s: The amplitude of a mass–spring oscillator is doubled. By what factor does its total mechanical energy change?
questions.e: The total energy equals the maximum elastic potential energy ½kA², which is proportional to A². Doubling A multiplies the energy by 4. '2 times' forgets that the amplitude is squared.

questions.s: A 0.5 kg block on a smooth horizontal surface is attached to a spring of spring constant 200 N/m. It oscillates with an amplitude of 0.1 m. What is its maximum speed?
questions.e: Total energy ½kA² = ½ × 200 × 0.01 = 1 J becomes kinetic energy at equilibrium: ½mv² = 1, so v² = 2/0.5 = 4 and v = 2 m/s. 4 m/s forgets the square root, and √2 m/s forgets the factor ½ in the kinetic energy.

questions.s: A body moves in simple harmonic motion with total energy E. What fraction of E is kinetic energy when its displacement is half the amplitude?
questions.e: Potential energy is ½kx² = ½k(A/2)² = ¼ of ½kA², so PE = E/4 and KE = E − E/4 = 3E/4. 1/2 assumes energy is shared in proportion to displacement rather than its square; 1/4 is the potential-energy fraction.

questions.s: A wave travels along a stretched string. If the frequency of the source is doubled while the wave speed stays the same, what happens to the wavelength?
questions.e: The speed is set by the string (its tension and mass per length), so v = fλ is constant. Doubling f therefore halves λ. 'It doubles' assumes λ grows with f, which would double the speed.

questions.s: At t = 0 the shape of a transverse wave on a rope is y = 5 sin(πx/2) cm, with x in metres, and the wave travels in the +x direction. In which direction is the rope particle at x = 2 m moving at that instant?
questions.e: At x = 2 m the displacement is 5 sin π = 0, with a crest at x = 1 m just behind it. As the wave moves in +x, that crest approaches x = 2 m, so the particle there is moving upward. Rope particles move only perpendicular to the rope, never along +x; a particle at y = 0 has its maximum speed, so it is not at rest.

questions.s: At t = 0 the shape of a wave on a rope is y = 0.1 sin(πx) m, with x in metres. The wave travels at 4 m/s. What is its frequency?
questions.e: One wavelength corresponds to πx = 2π, so λ = 2 m. Then f = v/λ = 4/2 = 2 Hz. 8 Hz multiplies v by λ instead of dividing.

questions.s: Two points lie 0.3 m apart along the direction of travel of a wave of wavelength 1.2 m. What is the phase difference between their oscillations?
questions.e: Phase difference = 2π × (distance/λ) = 2π × 0.3/1.2 = π/2. π/4 forgets the factor 2 in 2π.

questions.s: A string 1.2 m long is fixed at both ends and vibrates as a standing wave with 3 loops (antinodes). The wave speed on the string is 40 m/s. What is the frequency of vibration?
questions.e: Each loop is half a wavelength: 3 × λ/2 = 1.2 m, so λ = 0.8 m and f = v/λ = 40/0.8 = 50 Hz. 100 Hz takes one loop (0.4 m) as a full wavelength.

questions.s: A string of length 0.5 m is fixed at both ends. The speed of transverse waves on it is 200 m/s. What is its fundamental frequency?
questions.e: In the fundamental mode the string is half a wavelength long: λ = 2L = 1 m, so f = v/λ = 200 Hz. 400 Hz uses λ = L, and 100 Hz uses λ = 4L, which applies to a pipe closed at one end.

questions.s: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its third harmonic. How many nodes are there, including the two fixed ends?
questions.e: The third harmonic has 3 loops along the string. Three loops are separated by 2 nodes in between, plus the 2 fixed ends, giving 4 nodes. 3 is the number of antinodes.

questions.s: A pipe of length 0.25 m is closed at one end and open at the other. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. What is the fundamental frequency of the pipe?
questions.e: In the fundamental, a closed pipe holds a quarter wavelength: λ = 4L = 1 m, so f = 340/1 = 340 Hz. 680 Hz uses λ = 2L, which applies to a pipe open at both ends.

questions.s: A pipe of length 0.85 m is open at both ends. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. What is its fundamental frequency?
questions.e: An open pipe has antinodes at both ends, so the fundamental has λ = 2L = 1.7 m and f = 340/1.7 = 200 Hz. 100 Hz uses λ = 4L, which is for a pipe closed at one end, and 400 Hz uses λ = L.

questions.s: A sound wave passes from air into water, where sound travels faster. Which statement is correct?
o: Frequency stays the same; wavelength increases
Frequency increases; wavelength stays the same
questions.e: The frequency is set by the source and does not change when a wave enters a new medium. Since v = fλ and v increases, the wavelength increases. Thinking the frequency changes confuses frequency with speed.

questions.s: Two loudspeakers vibrate in phase and emit sound of wavelength 2 m. At point P the path difference from the two speakers is 3 m. What kind of interference occurs at P?
questions.e: The path difference 3 m equals 1.5λ, a half-integer number of wavelengths, so the waves arrive in antiphase and interfere destructively. Constructive interference would need a whole number of wavelengths, such as 2 m or 4 m.

questions.s: A pulse on a rope reaches an end that is tied firmly to a wall. How is the pulse reflected?
questions.e: At a fixed end the rope cannot move, so the wall pulls back opposite to the pulse and the reflection is inverted (a phase change of π). The pulse stays on the same rope, so its speed is unchanged. An upright reflection occurs at a free end.

questions.s: A tuning fork is struck harder so that it sounds louder. Which property of the sound wave has changed?
questions.e: Loudness depends on amplitude. The frequency is fixed by the fork, and the speed is fixed by the air, so the wavelength v/f does not change either.

questions.s: A body moves in simple harmonic motion x = A cos(2πt/T). What is the shortest time it takes to move from x = A to x = A/2?
questions.e: Set cos(2πt/T) = 1/2: the smallest positive solution is 2πt/T = π/3, so t = T/6. T/8 assumes the body moves at constant speed over the quarter cycle from A to 0, but it moves slowly near the extremes, so the first half of that distance takes longer than half of T/4.

questions.s: The periods of two simple pendulums at the same place are in the ratio 2 : 3. What is the ratio of their lengths?
questions.e: T = 2π√(L/g), so L ∝ T². The lengths are in the ratio 2² : 3² = 4 : 9. 2 : 3 assumes T ∝ L, and √2 : √3 inverts the square-root relation.

questions.s: A body moves in simple harmonic motion. Which statement is true at the instant its displacement is at its maximum positive value?
o: Velocity zero; acceleration maximum and negative
Velocity maximum; acceleration maximum and positive
questions.e: At an extreme the body momentarily stops, so v = 0. Since a = −ω²x, the acceleration there has its greatest size and points opposite to the displacement, i.e. negative. Velocity is maximum and acceleration zero only at the equilibrium position.

questions.s: In a sound wave in air the distance between a compression and the next rarefaction is 0.5 m. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. What is the frequency of the sound?
questions.e: A compression and the neighbouring rarefaction are half a wavelength apart, so λ = 1 m and f = v/λ = 340 Hz. 680 Hz takes 0.5 m as the full wavelength.

questions.s: A train moving away from a stationary observer sounds its whistle. Compared with the sound emitted, the observer receives sound with
questions.e: As the source moves away, the wavefronts behind it are spread out, so the wavelength reaching the observer is longer. The speed of sound in still air is unchanged, so f = v/λ is lower. The frequency cannot stay the same if the wavelength changes at the same speed.

questions.s: A listener moves towards a stationary source of sound in still air. Which statement is correct?
o: Higher frequency; shorter wavelength in air
Lower frequency; same wavelength in air
Same frequency; shorter wavelength in air
Higher frequency; same wavelength in air
questions.e: The source is at rest, so the wavefronts in the air are evenly spaced and the wavelength in the air is unchanged. Moving towards the source, the listener meets wavefronts more often, so the frequency heard is higher. A shorter wavelength in air happens only when the source itself moves towards the listener.

questions.s: A child on a swing has a natural period of 2.5 s. At what frequency should she be pushed to build up the largest amplitude?
questions.e: Resonance gives the largest amplitude when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency: f = 1/T = 1/2.5 = 0.4 Hz. 2.5 Hz confuses the period with the frequency.

questions.s: A mass on a light spring oscillates with period T. The same mass is then hung from two such springs side by side (in parallel). What is the new period?
questions.e: Two identical springs in parallel act as one spring of constant 2k. Since T = 2π√(m/k), doubling k divides T by √2, giving T/√2. √2 T would be correct for springs joined end to end (in series), which halves k.

questions.s: For a transverse wave, a displacement–time graph of one particle is a sine curve that repeats every 0.4 s, and a displacement–position graph of the wave at one instant is a sine curve that repeats every 2 m. What is the wave speed?
questions.e: The first graph gives the period T = 0.4 s and the second gives the wavelength λ = 2 m, so v = λ/T = 2/0.4 = 5 m/s. 0.8 m/s multiplies λ by T instead of dividing, and 0.2 m/s divides T by λ.

questions.s: A block hangs at rest from a vertical spring, which is stretched by 0.1 m. The block is then pulled down a little and released. What is the period of its oscillation? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: At equilibrium kx₀ = mg, so m/k = x₀/g = 0.1/10 = 0.01. Then T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π × 0.1 = 0.2π s. 20π s uses √(g/x₀) instead of √(x₀/g), and 0.1π s forgets the factor 2.

questions.s: A particle moves in simple harmonic motion with amplitude 5 cm and angular frequency 10 rad/s. What is its speed when its displacement is 3 cm?
questions.e: v = ω√(A² − x²) = 10 × √(25 − 9) cm/s = 10 × 4 = 40 cm/s = 0.4 m/s. 0.5 m/s is the maximum speed Aω, reached only at equilibrium, and 0.2 m/s uses ω(A − x).

questions.s: A simple pendulum has period T when at rest on the ground. It is placed in a lift that accelerates downward at 7.5 m/s². What is its period now? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: In a lift accelerating downward the effective gravity is g − a = 2.5 m/s², one quarter of g. Since T ∝ 1/√g, the period becomes T × √4 = 2T. T/2 would follow from using g + a, which applies to upward acceleration.

questions.s: A string fixed at both ends vibrates with 4 loops at a fixed driving frequency. The tension is then increased so that the wave speed doubles, while the driving frequency stays the same and a standing wave forms again. How many loops are there now?
questions.e: With f fixed, λ = v/f doubles, so each loop (λ/2) is twice as long. The string length is unchanged, so the number of loops halves from 4 to 2. 8 assumes a faster wave fits more loops, but faster waves at the same frequency have longer wavelengths.

questions.s: A pipe closed at one end resonates at 150 Hz and at 250 Hz, and at no frequency in between. What is its fundamental frequency?
questions.e: A closed pipe has only odd harmonics f₁, 3f₁, 5f₁, …, so neighbouring resonances differ by 2f₁. Here 2f₁ = 100 Hz and f₁ = 50 Hz (150 = 3 × 50, 250 = 5 × 50). 100 Hz assumes all harmonics are present, which is true for an open pipe.

questions.s: A transverse wave of wavelength 4 m travels in the +x direction. At t = 0 there is a crest at x = 1 m, and at t = 0.5 s there is a crest at x = 2 m. The period of the wave is longer than 0.5 s. What is the wave speed?
questions.e: Because T > 0.5 s, in 0.5 s the wave moves less than one wavelength, so the crest has moved from x = 1 m to x = 2 m: 1 m in 0.5 s gives v = 2 m/s. 10 m/s (a shift of 1 + 4 = 5 m) would need T < 0.5 s, and 6 m/s would need the wave to move 3 m in the −x direction.

questions.s: A 0.2 kg block on a spring of spring constant 80 N/m oscillates on a smooth horizontal surface with amplitude 0.05 m. What is its kinetic energy when its displacement is 0.03 m?
questions.e: Total energy ½kA² = 40 × 0.0025 = 0.1 J; potential energy at x = 0.03 m is ½kx² = 40 × 0.0009 = 0.036 J. So KE = 0.1 − 0.036 = 0.064 J. 0.036 J is the potential energy, and 0.128 J forgets the factor ½.

questions.s: Two pulses of the same shape and size, one upright and one inverted, travel towards each other on a rope. Which statement is correct at the instant they overlap exactly?
o: The rope is flat and its energy is all kinetic
The rope is flat and it has no energy at all
The pulses have cancelled each other permanently
The displacement is doubled at every point
