questions.e: The displacements add to zero, so the rope is momentarily straight, but its particles are still moving, so the energy is stored as kinetic energy. Afterwards the pulses pass through each other unchanged, so they are not destroyed.

questions.s: A particle moves according to x = 4 sin(πt/2), with x in centimetres and t in seconds. What distance does it travel from t = 0 to t = 3 s?
questions.e: ω = π/2 rad/s, so T = 4 s and 3 s is three quarters of a cycle. Starting at x = 0 it goes to +4, back to 0 and on to −4: distance 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 cm. 4 cm is the size of the displacement at t = 3 s, not the distance travelled.

questions.s: A string 0.6 m long, fixed at both ends, vibrates in its third harmonic at a frequency of 300 Hz. What is the speed of the waves on the string?
questions.e: The third harmonic has 3 loops: 3 × λ/2 = 0.6 m, so λ = 0.4 m and v = fλ = 300 × 0.4 = 120 m/s. 360 m/s treats the vibration as the fundamental (λ = 1.2 m), and 60 m/s takes the loop length 0.2 m as the wavelength.

questions.s: Two loudspeakers vibrate in phase with the same frequency. A listener stands at a point where the path difference from the two speakers is 0.85 m. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. What is the lowest frequency for which the listener hears a minimum?
questions.e: A minimum needs a path difference of (n + ½)λ. The lowest frequency means the longest wavelength: 0.85 = λ/2, so λ = 1.7 m and f = 340/1.7 = 200 Hz. 400 Hz gives λ = 0.85 m, a whole wavelength, which is a maximum.

questions.s: A mass on a spring of spring constant k oscillates with period T. The spring is cut into two equal halves, and the same mass is attached to both halves side by side (in parallel). What is the new period?
questions.e: Each half-spring has constant 2k (a shorter spring stretches less for the same force). Two in parallel give 4k, so T ∝ 1/√k gives T/√4 = T/2. T/√2 counts only one of the two effects.

questions.s: A mass on a spring makes 20 complete oscillations in 8 s. What is its period?
questions.e: The period is the time for one oscillation: T = 8/20 = 0.4 s. 2.5 s is the frequency in Hz (20/8), not the period.

questions.s: Water waves travel at 3 m/s and have a wavelength of 1.5 m. What is their frequency?
questions.e: f = v/λ = 3/1.5 = 2 Hz. 4.5 Hz multiplies v by λ, and 0.5 Hz divides λ by v.

questions.s: Which of the following is a longitudinal wave?
o: A wave on a guitar string
questions.e: In sound the air particles vibrate back and forth along the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions, so it is longitudinal. A wave on a guitar string is transverse: the string moves at right angles to the direction the wave travels along it.

questions.s: For a body in simple harmonic motion, which statement about its acceleration is correct?
o: Proportional to displacement and opposite in direction
Proportional to velocity and in the same direction
Constant in size and always towards equilibrium
Proportional to displacement and in the same direction
questions.e: SHM is defined by a = −ω²x: the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and always directed opposite to it, back towards equilibrium. 'Same direction' would push the body farther away, so it would not oscillate.

questions.s: The mass of the bob of a simple pendulum is doubled while its length stays the same. What happens to its period?
questions.e: T = 2π√(L/g) does not contain the mass, so the period is unchanged. A heavier bob feels a larger gravitational force, but it also has more inertia, and the two effects cancel.

questions.s: In a standing wave, an antinode is a point where
o: the particles stay at rest at all times
the wave energy moves the fastest
questions.e: Antinodes are the points of maximum amplitude in a standing wave; nodes are the points that stay at rest. Energy is not carried along a standing wave, and the wavelength is the same everywhere along it.

questions.s: A 0.9 kg mass on a light spring of spring constant 10 N/m oscillates horizontally on a smooth surface. What is its period?
questions.e: T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π√(0.09) = 2π × 0.3 = 0.6π s. 0.18π s forgets the square root, and (20π/3) s uses √(k/m) instead of √(m/k).

questions.s: What is the period of a simple pendulum of length 0.4 m? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: T = 2π√(L/g) = 2π√(0.04) = 2π × 0.2 = 0.4π s. 10π s inverts the ratio inside the root, and 0.2π s forgets the factor 2.

questions.s: A body performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude 0.04 m and angular frequency 5 rad/s. What is its maximum speed?
questions.e: v_max = Aω = 0.04 × 5 = 0.2 m/s, reached at the equilibrium position. 1 m/s is Aω², the maximum acceleration in m/s², and 0.4 m/s uses 2A, the full distance between the extremes, as the amplitude.

questions.s: A mass–spring oscillator has total energy E. Its amplitude is then reduced to half. What is its new maximum kinetic energy?
questions.e: The total energy ½kA² is proportional to A², so halving A gives E/4, and at equilibrium all of it is kinetic. E/2 forgets to square the amplitude.

questions.s: A string 0.9 m long is fixed at both ends and vibrates with 3 loops. What is the wavelength of the waves on the string?
questions.e: Each loop is half a wavelength, so 3 × λ/2 = 0.9 m and λ = 0.6 m. 0.3 m is the length of one loop, which is only half a wavelength.

questions.s: A tube 0.17 m long is closed at one end and open at the other. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. What is its fundamental frequency?
questions.e: The fundamental of a closed tube has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so L = λ/4 and λ = 0.68 m; f = 340/0.68 = 500 Hz. 1000 Hz uses λ = 2L, which is for a tube open at both ends.

questions.s: Which statement about the Doppler effect for sound is correct?
o: Waves ahead of a moving source are bunched closer together
The source itself emits a higher frequency when moving
The speed of sound in still air rises with the source's speed
Waves behind a moving source are bunched closer together
questions.e: A moving source partly catches up with the waves it sends ahead, so wavefronts in front are closer together (shorter wavelength) and those behind are spread out. The source's own frequency does not change, and the speed of sound depends on the air, not on the source.

questions.s: Two points along the path of a wave are 1.5 wavelengths apart. At any instant their displacements are
questions.e: A separation of 1.5λ gives a phase difference of 3π, which is equivalent to π: the points are in antiphase, so their displacements are always equal in size and opposite in sign. Points a whole number of wavelengths apart would be in phase.

questions.s: A wave travels along a rope at 24 m/s with a frequency of 8 Hz. What is the distance between a crest and the nearest trough?
questions.e: λ = v/f = 24/8 = 3 m, and a crest and the nearest trough are half a wavelength apart: 1.5 m. 3 m is the distance between two neighbouring crests.

questions.s: A ship's sonar sends a sound pulse straight down, and the echo from the sea bed returns 0.4 s later. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water. How deep is the sea there?
questions.e: The pulse travels down and back: total distance 1500 × 0.4 = 600 m, so the depth is 300 m. 600 m forgets the round trip, and 3750 m divides the speed by the time.

questions.s: A particle moves in simple harmonic motion with amplitude 10 cm. When its displacement is 6 cm its speed is 0.8 m/s. What is its period?
questions.e: v = ω√(A² − x²): 0.8 = ω × √(0.01 − 0.0036) = ω × 0.08, so ω = 10 rad/s and T = 2π/ω = 0.2π s. 0.25π s assumes 0.8 m/s is the maximum speed Aω.

questions.s: A block hangs at rest from a vertical spring, stretching it by 2.5 cm. It is pulled down a further 4 cm and released. What is the magnitude of its maximum acceleration? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.e: At equilibrium k/m = g/x₀ = 10/0.025 = 400 s⁻², so ω² = 400. The amplitude is 0.04 m, so a_max = ω²A = 400 × 0.04 = 16 m/s². 26 m/s² wrongly adds g; the weight is already balanced at the equilibrium position, so only the extra stretch gives the net force.

questions.s: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its third harmonic at 120 Hz. What is the frequency of its fifth harmonic?
questions.e: For a string fixed at both ends fₙ = nf₁, so f₁ = 120/3 = 40 Hz and f₅ = 5 × 40 = 200 Hz. 160 Hz is the fourth harmonic, and 40 Hz is the fundamental.

questions.s: A car sounding a siren moves at constant speed along a straight road directly towards an observer far ahead, passes close by and drives away. How does the frequency heard by the observer change?
o: Higher while approaching, then lower once it has passed
Rises steadily while approaching, then drops steadily
Lower while approaching, then higher once it has passed
Equal to the emitted frequency the whole time
questions.e: While the source approaches at constant speed the heard frequency is constant and higher than emitted; after it passes and moves away the frequency is constant and lower. The change happens quickly as the car goes by; the frequency does not keep rising while it approaches.

questions.s: Two point charges of +2.0 μC and +3.0 μC are 0.30 m apart in vacuum. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the magnitude of the electric force between them?
questions.e: F = kq₁q₂/r² = 9.0 × 10⁹ × (2.0 × 10⁻⁶)(3.0 × 10⁻⁶)/0.090 = 0.054/0.090 = 0.60 N. The value 0.18 N comes from dividing by r instead of r².

questions.s: Two point charges exert a force F on each other. Each charge is doubled and the distance between them is also doubled. What is the new force?
questions.e: F ∝ q₁q₂/r². Doubling both charges multiplies the force by 4; doubling r divides it by 2² = 4. The net factor is 1, so the force stays F. Choosing F/2 treats the force as inversely proportional to r rather than r².

questions.s: Which statement about electric field lines is correct?
o: They begin on negative charges and end on positive charges.
Two field lines may cross where two fields overlap.
A charge released from rest always moves along a field line.
They are drawn closer together where the field is stronger.
questions.e: The density of field lines shows the field strength, so lines are closer where the field is stronger. Lines start on positive and end on negative charges, and they never cross because the field has one direction at each point. A charge released from rest follows a field line only if the line is straight; on curved lines its inertia carries it off the line.

questions.s: A point charge of +4.0 × 10⁻⁹ C is in vacuum. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the electric field strength 0.20 m from the charge?
questions.e: E = kQ/r² = 9.0 × 10⁹ × 4.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.040 = 36/0.040 = 900 N/C. Dividing by r instead of r² gives 180 N/C.

questions.s: A test charge of 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C placed at point P in an electric field feels a force of 6.0 × 10⁻³ N. The test charge is replaced by one of 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ C. What is the field strength at P now?
questions.e: E = F/q = 6.0 × 10⁻³/2.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 3.0 × 10³ N/C. The field at P is set by the source charges, not by the test charge, so it is unchanged; only the force doubles. 6.0 × 10³ N/C wrongly assumes the field grows with the test charge.

questions.s: A charge +Q is fixed at x = 0 and a charge +4Q is fixed at x = 0.30 m. At which position on the x-axis is the electric field zero?
questions.e: For like charges the zero point lies between them, nearer the smaller charge. kQ/d² = k(4Q)/(0.30 − d)² gives 0.30 − d = 2d, so d = 0.10 m. The midpoint 0.15 m would only be correct for equal charges.

questions.s: Charges of +2.0 μC and −2.0 μC are fixed 0.60 m apart. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the electric field at the midpoint between them?
questions.e: Each charge gives E = kq/r² = 9.0 × 10⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁶/0.090 = 2.0 × 10⁵ N/C at the midpoint. The field of the positive charge points away from it and that of the negative charge points towards it, so both point towards the negative charge and add to 4.0 × 10⁵ N/C. Zero would be the answer for two equal like charges.

questions.s: Point A is at a potential of +150 V and point B is at −50 V. A charge of −2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C moves from A to B. What is the work done on it by the electric force?
questions.e: W = qU_AB = q(φA − φB) = (−2.0 × 10⁻⁶)(150 − (−50)) = −4.0 × 10⁻⁴ J. The field does negative work, so the charge's potential energy rises by 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ J. +4.0 × 10⁻⁴ J ignores the negative sign of the charge.

questions.s: A charge of −5.0 × 10⁻⁹ C is placed at a point where the electric potential is +300 V. What is its electric potential energy?
questions.e: Ep = qφ = (−5.0 × 10⁻⁹)(300) = −1.5 × 10⁻⁶ J. The sign matters: a negative charge at a positive potential has negative potential energy, so +1.5 × 10⁻⁶ J is wrong.

questions.s: Two large parallel plates are 4.0 cm apart. The negative plate is earthed (0 V) and the positive plate is at +200 V. What is the potential at a point between the plates that is 3.0 cm from the negative plate?
questions.e: E = U/d = 200/0.040 = 5000 V/m, and the potential rises steadily from the negative plate. φ = 5000 × 0.030 = 150 V. 50 V is the result of measuring the 3.0 cm from the wrong plate.

questions.s: A 20 μF capacitor is charged to a potential difference of 10 V. What is the charge on each plate?
questions.e: Q = CU = 20 × 10⁻⁶ × 10 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ C. The value 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C comes from dividing C by U instead of multiplying.

questions.s: An air-filled parallel-plate capacitor stays connected to a battery while the distance between its plates is doubled. Which statement is correct?
o: C halves and the charge on each plate halves.
C halves and the voltage between the plates doubles.
C doubles and the charge on each plate doubles.
C halves and the field between the plates is unchanged.
questions.e: C = εS/(4πkd), so doubling d halves C. The battery keeps U fixed, so Q = CU halves and E = U/d halves. A rising voltage happens only when the capacitor is disconnected and Q is fixed.

questions.s: A charged parallel-plate capacitor is disconnected from its battery, and then its plates are pulled further apart. Which statement is correct?
o: The field between the plates decreases.
The voltage between the plates is unchanged.
The field between the plates is unchanged.
The charge on each plate decreases.
questions.e: Isolated, Q stays fixed. C = εS/(4πkd) falls, so U = Q/C rises in proportion to d, and E = U/d = 4πkQ/(εS) does not depend on d. The voltage therefore increases rather than staying the same.

questions.s: An air-filled parallel-plate capacitor connected to a battery holds charge Q. With the battery still connected, the gap is completely filled with a dielectric of relative permittivity 3. What charge does it now hold?
questions.e: Filling the gap multiplies C by εr = 3. The battery keeps U fixed, so Q = CU becomes 3Q. Q/3 would describe the voltage of an isolated capacitor, not the charge of a connected one.

questions.s: An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What kinetic energy does it gain?
questions.e: The work done by the field is eU = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 100 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ J (that is, 100 eV). 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J is the energy for 1 V only.

questions.s: A proton and an alpha particle (charge 2e, mass 4 times that of the proton) start from rest and are accelerated through the same potential difference. What is the ratio of the proton's final speed to the alpha particle's final speed?
questions.e: qU = ½mv² gives v = √(2qU/m), so v ∝ √(q/m). q/m is 1 for the proton and 2/4 = 1/2 for the alpha particle (in proton units), so v_p : v_α = 1 : √(1/2) = √2 : 1. Choosing 2 : 1 forgets the square root.

questions.s: A charged particle enters the region between two parallel plates moving parallel to them and leaves with a sideways deflection y. The voltage across the plates is doubled and the particle's initial kinetic energy is also doubled. Ignore gravity. What is the new deflection?
questions.e: y = ½(qU/md)(L/v₀)² = qUL²/(4d·Ek), where Ek = ½mv₀². So y ∝ U/Ek, and doubling both leaves y unchanged. 2y considers only the voltage change.

questions.s: An oil drop of mass 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held at rest between two horizontal plates 2.0 cm apart when the potential difference between them is 600 V. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the magnitude of the charge on the drop?
questions.e: Balance: qU/d = mg, so q = mgd/U = 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 10 × 0.020/600 = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ C (20 electron charges). 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ C comes from using d = 2.0 instead of 0.020 m.

questions.s: Which unit is equivalent to the newton per coulomb (N/C), the unit of electric field strength?
questions.e: From E = U/d, field strength can be written in volts per metre: 1 V/m = 1 (J/C)/m = 1 N/C. J/C is the volt, the unit of potential, not of field strength.

questions.s: Two equal point charges +q are fixed at two corners of an equilateral triangle of side a. What is the magnitude of the electric field at the third corner? (k is Coulomb's constant.)
questions.e: Each charge gives kq/a² at the third corner, along the two sides, which meet at 60°. The resultant is 2(kq/a²)cos 30° = √3·kq/a². 2kq/a² would require the two fields to be in the same direction.

questions.s: Which statement about equipotential surfaces is correct?
o: The field strength is zero at every point on an equipotential surface.
Moving a charge along an equipotential surface needs positive work by the field.
The equipotential surfaces of an isolated point charge are flat planes.
Electric field lines cross equipotential surfaces at right angles.
questions.e: No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential, so the field has no component along the surface and must be perpendicular to it. The field need not be zero there (a constant potential along a surface says nothing about the potential change across it). A point charge has spherical equipotentials.

questions.s: A uniform electric field of 2000 V/m points in the +x direction. Point A is at (0, 0) and point B is at (0.03 m, 0.04 m). What is the potential difference U_AB = φA − φB?
questions.e: Only the displacement along the field matters: U_AB = E·Δx = 2000 × 0.03 = 60 V. 100 V uses the full distance of 0.05 m, which is not along the field.

questions.s: Two identical small metal spheres carry charges +5q and −q and attract each other with a force F when a distance r apart. They are touched together and then put back at distance r. What is the new force?
questions.e: On contact the total charge 5q − q = 4q is shared equally, so each sphere has +2q. Before: F ∝ 5q·q = 5q²; after: F′ ∝ 2q·2q = 4q², so F′ = 4F/5, and like charges now repel. Keeping 'attractive' ignores that both spheres end up positive.

questions.s: A small ball of mass 2.0 × 10⁻³ kg and charge +4.0 × 10⁻⁶ C hangs from an insulating thread in a horizontal uniform field of 5.0 × 10³ N/C. Take g = 10 m/s². At what angle to the vertical does the thread hang in equilibrium?

A particle of charge 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ C and mass 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ kg enters midway between two parallel plates at 200 m/s, moving parallel to them. The plates are 10 cm long, 5.0 cm apart and have 40 V across them. Ignore gravity. What is its sideways displacement as it leaves the plates?
questions.e: E = 40/0.050 = 800 V/m, a = qE/m = 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ × 800/1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 1.6 × 10⁵ m/s², t = 0.10/200 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ s. y = ½at² = ½ × 1.6 × 10⁵ × 2.5 × 10⁻⁷ = 0.020 m = 2.0 cm, which is less than the 2.5 cm to the plate, so it does leave. 4.0 cm forgets the ½ (and could not happen anyway, since the particle would hit the plate).

questions.s: Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Which of the following could be the charge on a small oil drop?
questions.e: Charge is quantised: any charge is a whole-number multiple of e. 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C = 3e. The others are 1.5e, 0.625e and 0.5e, which are impossible.

questions.s: A glass rod becomes positively charged when it is rubbed with a silk cloth. Which statement explains this?
o: Protons move from the silk to the glass.
Positive charge is created on the glass by friction.
Electrons move from the silk to the glass.
Electrons move from the glass to the silk.
questions.e: Rubbing transfers electrons, which are the mobile charges; protons stay in the nuclei. The glass loses electrons to the silk, so it is left positive and the silk becomes equally negative. Charge is conserved, so friction cannot create net positive charge.

questions.s: A charged metal object is in electrostatic equilibrium. Which statement is correct?
o: The electric field inside the metal is zero.
Excess charge spreads evenly through the volume of the metal.
Its sharpest points are at a higher potential than the rest of it.
Field lines meet its surface at an angle of 45°.
questions.e: In equilibrium the free charges are at rest, so there can be no field inside the metal. Excess charge sits on the outer surface, the whole conductor is one equipotential (sharp points have a higher charge density, not a higher potential), and field lines meet the surface at 90°.

questions.s: Charges +Q and +4Q are free to move and are a distance L apart, at points A and B. A third charge is placed on line AB so that all three charges are in equilibrium under their mutual forces. What is the third charge and where is it?
questions.e: The third charge must be negative and between A and B, nearer the smaller charge. For it to be in equilibrium, Q/x² = 4Q/(L − x)², so x = L/3. For A to be in equilibrium, k·Q·q/(L/3)² = k·Q·4Q/L², giving q = 4Q/9, so the charge is −4Q/9. A positive third charge would repel the charges at A and B outwards, so no equilibrium is possible.

questions.s: An electron is released from rest in a uniform electric field. Which statement describes what happens?
o: It moves along the field to lower potential, and its potential energy falls.
It moves against the field to higher potential, and its potential energy falls.
It moves against the field to higher potential, and its potential energy rises.
It moves along the field to lower potential, and its potential energy rises.
questions.e: The force on a negative charge is opposite to E, so the electron moves against the field, towards higher potential. The field does positive work on it, so its potential energy falls as its kinetic energy rises. A negative charge at higher potential has lower potential energy (Ep = qφ with q < 0).

questions.s: An external force does 8.0 × 10⁻⁶ J of work to move a charge of +4.0 × 10⁻⁸ C slowly from infinity (zero potential) to point A. What is the potential at A?
questions.e: Moving slowly, the external work equals the gain in potential energy, so Ep at A = +8.0 × 10⁻⁶ J. φA = Ep/q = 8.0 × 10⁻⁶/4.0 × 10⁻⁸ = +200 V. −200 V would follow from taking the external work as the work done by the field.

questions.s: Three equally spaced equipotential surfaces a, b and c lie in a uniform field, and b is at zero potential. A charged particle acted on only by the electric force crosses a with kinetic energy 50 J and reaches c with kinetic energy 20 J. What is its kinetic energy at the moment its electric potential energy is 5 J?
questions.e: In a uniform field equal spacing means equal changes of potential energy, so from a to b the particle loses 15 J of kinetic energy and has 35 J at b, where Ep = 0. The total energy is 35 J, so when Ep = 5 J, Ek = 35 − 5 = 30 J. 45 J wrongly uses the 50 J at a as the total energy, but Ep at a is not zero.

questions.s: For a parallel-plate capacitor of capacitance C, the area of the plates is doubled and the distance between them is halved. What is the new capacitance?
questions.e: C = εS/(4πkd) is proportional to S/d. Doubling S doubles C and halving d doubles it again, so the new value is 4C. Answering C assumes the two changes cancel, but they act in the same direction.

questions.s: Which statement about the capacitance of a given capacitor is correct?
o: The charge Q on it is proportional to the voltage U across it.
Its capacitance doubles when the charge on it doubles.
Its capacitance halves when the voltage across it doubles.
Its capacitance is zero when it is uncharged.
questions.e: C = Q/U is fixed by the capacitor's construction (plate area, gap, dielectric), so Q and U change in the same proportion. C is not changed by charging or discharging, even though it is calculated as Q/U.

questions.s: When the voltage across a capacitor is raised from 10 V to 15 V, the charge on it increases by 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ C. What is its capacitance?
questions.e: Since Q ∝ U, C = ΔQ/ΔU = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵/5 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁶ F = 6.0 μF. 2.0 μF comes from dividing ΔQ by the final voltage 15 V instead of by the change 5 V.

questions.s: The electric field strength 0.10 m from a point charge is 3600 N/C. What is the field strength 0.30 m from the same charge?
questions.e: E ∝ 1/r². Tripling the distance divides the field by 9: 3600/9 = 400 N/C. 1200 N/C treats E as proportional to 1/r.

questions.s: A charge of +9Q is fixed at x = 0 and a charge of −Q is fixed at x = 0.20 m. Where on the x-axis, apart from infinity, is the electric field zero?
questions.e: Between unlike charges the two fields point the same way, so the zero point lies outside, beyond the smaller charge. With d the distance beyond −Q: 9Q/(0.20 + d)² = Q/d², so 0.20 + d = 3d and d = 0.10 m, giving x = 0.30 m. x = 0.15 m solves the equation between the charges, where the fields add rather than cancel.

questions.s: A charge of +2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C moves 0.050 m in a straight line in a uniform field of 1.0 × 10⁴ N/C. Its path makes an angle of 60° with the field. How much work does the electric force do?
questions.e: W = qE·d·cos 60° = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.0 × 10⁴ × 0.050 × 0.5 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ J. Only the displacement along the field counts; leaving out cos 60° gives 1.0 × 10⁻³ J.

questions.s: In an electric field, U_AB = 20 V and U_BC = −50 V. If point C is taken as zero potential, what is the potential of point A?
questions.e: U_AC = U_AB + U_BC = 20 + (−50) = −30 V, and U_AC = φA − φC = φA − 0, so φA = −30 V. +70 V comes from subtracting U_BC instead of adding it.

questions.s: An electron at point P feels an electric force of 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ N directed north. Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the electric field at P?
questions.e: E = F/e = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.0 × 10⁴ N/C. The force on a negative charge is opposite to the field, so the field points south. Choosing north treats the electron as a positive charge.

questions.s: A small ball of mass m and charge +q is released from rest in a uniform field E that points horizontally, where qE = mg. Ignore air resistance. How does the ball move?
o: Along a downward-curving parabola, with acceleration g
In a straight line 45° below the horizontal, with acceleration √2·g
In a straight line 45° below the horizontal, with acceleration 2g
questions.e: Both forces are constant: mg down and qE = mg sideways, so the resultant is √2·mg at 45° below the horizontal. Starting from rest, the ball accelerates along this resultant in a straight line with a = √2·g. A parabola would need an initial velocity at an angle to the resultant force; 2g adds the two forces as if they were parallel.

questions.s: When the charge on a capacitor is increased by 50 %, the voltage across it rises by 6.0 V. What was the original voltage across it?
questions.e: U = Q/C, so a 50 % rise in Q gives a 50 % rise in U: 0.5U = 6.0 V and U = 12 V. 18 V is the final voltage, not the original one.

questions.s: An alpha particle (charge +2e) starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 1000 V. How much kinetic energy does it gain, in electronvolts?
questions.e: Ek = qU = 2e × 1000 V = 2000 eV. 1000 eV would be correct for a particle with a single elementary charge.

questions.s: In a field-line drawing for two point charges A and B, 16 lines leave A. Eight of them end on B and the other eight go off to infinity. Which statement is correct?
o: A is negative, B is positive, and A has the larger charge.
A is positive, B is negative, and A has the larger charge.
A is positive, B is negative, and B has the larger charge.
A and B are both positive, and A has the larger charge.
questions.e: Lines leave positive charges and end on negative ones, so A is positive and B is negative. The number of lines is proportional to the charge: 16 at A and 8 at B, so |qA| = 2|qB|. If B were positive, no lines could end on it.

questions.s: In a uniform field of 2.0 × 10⁴ N/C, a charge of +3.0 × 10⁻⁶ C is carried from A to B along a semicircle of radius 0.10 m. AB is a diameter of the semicircle and points in the direction of the field. How much work does the electric force do?
questions.e: The work done by an electric field does not depend on the path. W = qE·AB = 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 2.0 × 10⁴ × 0.20 = 1.2 × 10⁻² J. 6π × 10⁻³ J uses the length of the semicircle, which is not the displacement along the field.

questions.s: A particle with charge-to-mass ratio q/m = 1.0 × 10⁸ C/kg enters a uniform field of 4.0 × 10⁵ N/C between two parallel plates at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s, moving parallel to the plates. The plates are 0.10 m long and the particle does not hit them. Ignore gravity. At what angle to its original direction does it leave the plates?
questions.e: a = (q/m)E = 4.0 × 10¹³ m/s², t = L/v₀ = 0.10/2.0 × 10⁶ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁸ s, so v_y = at = 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s. tan θ = v_y/v₀ = 1, so θ = 45°. Using the displacement ratio y/L = 0.5 instead of the velocity ratio gives a smaller, wrong angle.

questions.s: A parallel-plate capacitor with plates 2.0 mm apart has a potential difference of 10 V across it. What is the field strength between the plates?
questions.e: E = U/d = 10/(2.0 × 10⁻³) = 5.0 × 10³ V/m. 5.0 V/m uses the gap in millimetres instead of metres.

questions.s: Square ABCD has side a. Charges +q, +q, −q and −q are fixed at A, B, C and D respectively. What is the magnitude of the electric field at the centre of the square? (k is Coulomb's constant.)
questions.e: Each corner is a/√2 from the centre, so each charge gives kq/(a²/2) = 2kq/a². Along diagonal AC, +q at A and −q at C both point from A to C: 4kq/a². Along BD the same: 4kq/a² from B to D. The diagonals are perpendicular, so E = √2 × 4kq/a² = 4√2·kq/a². 0 would require opposite corners to carry equal charges of the same sign.

questions.s: How does the electric potential change as you move along an electric field line in the direction of the field?
o: It depends on the sign of the test charge.
questions.e: Field lines point from high to low potential, so moving with the field the potential always decreases. The potential is a property of the field alone; the sign of a test charge affects its potential energy, not the potential.

questions.s: Two point charges of +1.0 × 10⁻⁸ C are fixed at (−0.30 m, 0) and (+0.30 m, 0). Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the magnitude of the electric field at the point (0, 0.40 m)?
questions.e: Each charge is 0.50 m away, giving E = 9.0 × 10⁹ × 1.0 × 10⁻⁸/0.25 = 360 N/C. The x-components cancel and the y-components add: 2 × 360 × (0.40/0.50) = 576 N/C. 720 N/C adds the magnitudes as if both fields pointed the same way.

questions.s: A positively charged rod is held near, but not touching, a neutral metal sphere on an insulating stand. While the rod is there, the sphere is briefly connected to earth. The earth connection is removed first and then the rod is taken away. What charge does the sphere now have?
o: Positive on one side and negative on the other, with no net charge
questions.e: The rod attracts electrons from earth onto the sphere while it is earthed. Breaking the earth connection before removing the rod traps these extra electrons, so the sphere ends up negative (charging by induction gives the opposite sign to the rod). The separated-charge picture only applies while the rod is nearby and the sphere is isolated.

questions.s: A negatively charged rod is brought near, but not touching, the cap of an uncharged gold-leaf electroscope. Which statement is correct?
o: The leaves diverge and carry negative charge.
The leaves diverge and carry positive charge.
The leaves stay closed because no charge is transferred.
The leaves collapse and the cap becomes negative.
questions.e: The rod repels electrons from the cap down to the leaves, so the cap becomes positive and both leaves negative; the leaves repel and diverge. No charge needs to be transferred for this separation by induction, so 'stay closed' is wrong.

questions.s: A closed, uncharged hollow metal box is placed in a strong uniform electric field. Which statement is correct once equilibrium is reached?
o: The field in the cavity equals the field outside the box.
Charges are induced on the inner surface of the box.
The box gains a net negative charge.
The field in the empty cavity is zero.
questions.e: Induced charges collect on the outer surface and their field cancels the external field everywhere inside the metal and in the empty cavity: this is electrostatic shielding. No charge appears on the inner surface, and the box stays neutral overall because induction only separates charge.

questions.s: Points A and B are at distances r and 2r from an isolated positive point charge. Which statement about the field strengths E and potentials φ is correct (zero potential at infinity)?
questions.e: E ∝ 1/r², so halving the distance gives four times the field: E_A = 4E_B. Field lines point away from a positive charge and the potential falls along them, so the nearer point A is at the higher potential. E_A = 2E_B treats the field as 1/r.

questions.s: A charged particle moves past a fixed positive point charge, acted on only by the electric force. Its curved path bends away from the fixed charge. Which statement is correct?
o: The particle is negative, and its speed is greatest at the point closest to the fixed charge.
The particle is positive, and its speed is greatest at the point closest to the fixed charge.
The particle is negative, and its speed is least at the point closest to the fixed charge.
The particle is positive, and its speed is least at the point closest to the fixed charge.
questions.e: A path curving away from the charge means the force is repulsive, so the particle is positive. As it approaches, the repulsion does negative work and slows it, so its kinetic energy is least at the closest point and its potential energy greatest. 'Greatest speed' would be true for an attracting, negative particle.

questions.s: Along the x-axis, the electric potential falls steadily (linearly) from 60 V at x = 0 to 0 V at x = 30 cm. What is the electric field along this part of the axis?
questions.e: E = ΔU/Δx = 60/0.30 = 200 V/m, and the field points towards lower potential, which is the +x direction. 2.0 V/m comes from leaving the distance in centimetres.

questions.s: A graph of electric potential φ against position x along a line has a maximum at x = x₀. Which statement about the point x = x₀ is correct?
o: The component of the field along x is zero there.
Any charge placed there has its greatest potential energy there.
The field strength is greatest there.
A positive charge placed there is pushed in the +x direction.
questions.e: The field component along x equals minus the gradient of the φ–x graph, which is zero at a maximum. Potential energy is qφ, so only a positive charge has its greatest potential energy there; a negative charge has its least. On either side the field points away from x₀, so a positive charge there feels no force along x.

questions.s: A proton and an alpha particle start from rest and are accelerated through the same voltage. Both then enter the same deflecting field between parallel plates, moving parallel to the plates along the same line. Ignore gravity. Which statement is correct?
o: The proton is deflected twice as much as the alpha particle.
The alpha particle is deflected twice as much as the proton.
They follow the same path through the deflecting plates.
The proton is deflected √2 times as much as the alpha particle.
questions.e: Acceleration gives ½mv₀² = qU₁. In the plates y = qU₂L²/(2dmv₀²) = U₂L²/(4dU₁), which contains neither q nor m. So every positive particle accelerated from rest through the same U₁ follows the same path. The proton is faster, but the alpha particle feels a proportionally larger force, so the speed difference does not change the path.

questions.s: An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through 500 V. It then enters midway between two parallel plates 2.0 cm apart and 10 cm long, moving parallel to them, with 20 V across the plates. Ignore gravity. What is its sideways displacement as it leaves the plates?
questions.e: Combining ½mv₀² = eU₁ with y = ½(eU₂/md)(L/v₀)² gives y = U₂L²/(4dU₁) = 20 × 0.010/(4 × 0.020 × 500) = 0.20/40 = 5.0 × 10⁻³ m = 0.50 cm. This is less than the 1.0 cm to a plate, so the electron gets through. 1.0 cm comes from dropping the factor 4 down to 2.

questions.s: Coulomb's law, F = kq₁q₂/r², applies directly to which situation?
o: Any two charged bodies at any distance apart
Two point charges at rest in a vacuum
Two charges only if they have the same sign
Two charges only when r is very small
questions.e: The law is stated for point charges at rest in vacuum (and holds well in air). For extended bodies close together the charge distribution matters and r is not well defined. It applies to both like and unlike charges.

questions.s: Two small charged balls A and B attract each other with force F. The distance between them is reduced to one third and the charge on A is halved. What is the new force?
questions.e: F ∝ q₁q₂/r². Dividing r by 3 multiplies the force by 9, and halving one charge halves it: 9/2 × F = 9F/2. 3F/2 uses 1/r instead of 1/r².

questions.s: A charge has electric potential energy 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ J at point A and −1.0 × 10⁻⁶ J at point B. How much work does the electric force do on it as it moves from A to B?
questions.e: Work done by the field = decrease in potential energy = EpA − EpB = 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ − (−1.0 × 10⁻⁶) = +4.0 × 10⁻⁶ J. −4.0 × 10⁻⁶ J reverses the subtraction; ±2.0 × 10⁻⁶ J ignores the minus sign of EpB.

questions.s: A graph of the charge Q on a capacitor against the voltage U across it is a straight line through the origin, passing through Q = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ C at U = 12 V. What is the capacitance?
questions.e: C = Q/U = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴/12 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ F = 50 μF. 7.2 × 10³ μF comes from multiplying Q by U instead of dividing.

questions.s: A charged parallel-plate capacitor is isolated. One plate is slid sideways so that the area where the plates overlap is halved, while the gap stays the same. What happens to the voltage U between the plates and the field E between them?
o: U doubles and E is unchanged
U is unchanged and E doubles
questions.e: Isolated, Q is fixed. C ∝ S/d halves, so U = Q/C doubles, and with d unchanged E = U/d also doubles (the same charge is crowded onto half the area). 'E unchanged' is the result for changing d, not S.

questions.s: A charged ball hangs at rest from an insulating thread in a horizontal uniform electric field, with the thread at 37° to the vertical. The thread is then cut. Take g = 10 m/s², sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8 and ignore air resistance. What is the magnitude of the ball's acceleration just after the thread is cut?
questions.e: Before cutting, the resultant of mg and qE balanced the tension, so it lies along the thread with magnitude mg/cos 37°. After cutting, this resultant acts alone: a = g/cos 37° = 10/0.8 = 12.5 m/s², along the line of the thread. 10 m/s² ignores the electric force, which is still acting.

questions.s: A particle with charge-to-mass ratio 2.0 × 10⁸ C/kg starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. What is its final speed?
questions.e: qU = ½mv² gives v² = 2(q/m)U = 2 × 2.0 × 10⁸ × 100 = 4.0 × 10¹⁰ m²/s², so v = 2.0 × 10⁵ m/s. 4.0 × 10¹⁰ m/s is v², with the square root forgotten (and is faster than light).

questions.s: Which describes the electric field lines around an isolated negative point charge?
o: Radial straight lines pointing outwards, away from the charge
Radial straight lines pointing inwards, towards the charge
questions.e: Field lines show the direction of the force on a positive test charge, which is attracted to a negative charge, so the lines point radially inwards and end on the charge. Outward lines describe a positive charge; parallel equally spaced lines describe a uniform field.

questions.s: Two parallel plates 5.0 cm apart have a potential difference of 1000 V. Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the electric force on an electron between the plates?
questions.e: E = U/d = 1000/0.050 = 2.0 × 10⁴ V/m, and F = eE = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁴ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ N. 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ N uses d = 5.0 instead of 0.050 m; 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ is eU, an energy in joules, not a force.

questions.s: Charges +Q and −Q are fixed a short distance apart. Taking zero potential at infinity, which is correct at the midpoint between them?
questions.e: Potential is a scalar: the contributions of +Q and −Q are equal and opposite at the midpoint, so φ = 0. Field is a vector: both fields point towards −Q there and add, so E ≠ 0. A zero potential does not imply a zero field.

questions.s: A small ball of mass 0.10 kg and charge +1.0 × 10⁻⁴ C is thrown vertically upwards at 15 m/s in a uniform electric field of 5.0 × 10³ N/C pointing vertically downwards. Take g = 10 m/s² and ignore air resistance. What maximum height does it reach?
questions.e: Both mg = 1.0 N and qE = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 5.0 × 10³ = 0.50 N act downwards, so a = 1.5/0.10 = 15 m/s². h = v²/(2a) = 225/30 = 7.5 m. 11.25 m ignores the electric force, and 22.5 m takes it as acting upwards.

questions.s: An electron leaves the negative plate of a pair of parallel plates with negligible speed and reaches the positive plate with speed v. The voltage is then made 4 times larger and the plate separation is doubled. With what speed does the electron now reach the positive plate?
questions.e: eU = ½mv², so v ∝ √U and the separation does not matter: the field is weaker but acts over a longer distance, and the work done is eU either way. Four times the voltage gives √4 = 2 times the speed. √2·v wrongly lets the doubled separation halve the effect.

questions.s: The electric potential at a point P is zero. Which statement must be true?
o: A charge placed at P has zero electric potential energy.
The electric field strength at P is zero.
There are no charges near P.
A charge placed at P feels no electric force.
questions.e: Ep = qφ, so with φ = 0 any charge there has zero potential energy. The potential's zero depends on the chosen reference, and the field (the rate of change of potential) need not be zero; for example, the midpoint between +Q and −Q has φ = 0 but a strong field.

questions.s: A charge of +1.0 μC is at the origin. A charge of +3.0 μC is fixed at (0.30 m, 0) and a charge of +4.0 μC is fixed at (0, 0.30 m). Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the magnitude of the resultant electric force on the charge at the origin?
questions.e: The 3.0 μC charge exerts 9.0 × 10⁹ × 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.0 × 10⁻⁶/0.090 = 0.30 N along −x, and the 4.0 μC charge exerts 0.40 N along −y. These are perpendicular, so F = √(0.30² + 0.40²) = 0.50 N. 0.70 N adds the magnitudes directly.

questions.s: The farad (F) is the unit of capacitance. Which combination of units is equal to 1 F?
questions.e: C = Q/U, so 1 F = 1 C/V: a one-farad capacitor stores one coulomb per volt. 1 J/C is the volt, and 1 C·V is the joule.

questions.s: Charges +Q and −Q are fixed a short distance apart. A small positive test charge is moved from point M to point N, both on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining the two charges. How much work does the electric force do on it?
o: Zero, because the bisector is an equipotential line
Positive, because the field near the bisector points from +Q towards −Q
Negative, because the charge moves against the field
It depends on the speed at which the charge is moved
questions.e: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from +Q and −Q, so their potentials cancel and the bisector is an equipotential. Moving along it, the field (perpendicular to the bisector) does no work. The field does point from +Q towards −Q, but that direction is at right angles to the motion.

questions.s: A charged dust particle is at rest between the horizontal plates of a parallel-plate capacitor that stays connected to a battery. The upper plate is then moved slightly upwards. What happens to the particle?
o: It moves downwards at constant speed.
questions.e: At first qE = mg with E = U/d. The battery keeps U fixed, so increasing d reduces E and the electric force, and gravity now wins: the particle accelerates downwards. It would stay at rest only if the capacitor were disconnected, because then E does not depend on d.

questions.s: A charge of +2.0 × 10⁻⁷ C moves 0.20 m along the +x direction in a uniform electric field, and its electric potential energy falls by 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ J. What is the electric field along the x-axis?
questions.e: The field does work W = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ J = qEd, so E = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵/(2.0 × 10⁻⁷ × 0.20) = 1000 N/C. A positive charge loses potential energy when it moves with the field, so the field points along +x. 200 is the potential difference in volts, obtained by forgetting to divide by the distance.

questions.s: Rectangle ABCD (vertices in that order) lies in a uniform electric field that is parallel to the plane of the rectangle. The potentials at A, B and C are 12 V, 4 V and −4 V. What is the potential at D?
questions.e: In a uniform field, equal and parallel displacements give equal potential differences. AB and DC are equal and parallel, so φA − φB = φD − φC: 12 − 4 = φD − (−4), giving φD = 4 V. 0 V assumes D is simply 'halfway' between the other values without using the geometry.

questions.s: Two identical small balls, each of mass 1.8 × 10⁻³ kg and carrying equal charges q, hang from the same point on insulating threads 0.10 m long. In equilibrium each thread makes 45° with the vertical. Take g = 10 m/s² and k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is q?
questions.e: At 45°, the electric force equals the weight: F = mg tan 45° = 0.018 N. The separation is r = 2L sin 45° = √2 × 0.10 m, so r² = 0.020 m². q² = Fr²/k = 0.018 × 0.020/9.0 × 10⁹ = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ C², so q = 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ C. 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ C is q² with the square root forgotten.

questions.s: Plate A is at +100 V and plate B is earthed (0 V); the plates are parallel and 5.0 cm apart. What is the electric potential energy of an electron at the midpoint between the plates?
questions.e: The field is uniform, so the midpoint is at φ = 50 V. Ep = qφ = (−e)(50 V) = −50 eV. +50 eV forgets that the electron's charge is negative.

questions.s: Two point charges of +1.0 μC and +4.0 μC are 0.20 m apart. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the force between them?
questions.e: F = kq₁q₂/r² = 9.0 × 10⁹ × 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 4.0 × 10⁻⁶/0.040 = 0.036/0.040 = 0.90 N. 0.18 N comes from dividing by r = 0.20 instead of r² = 0.040.

questions.s: The distance between two point charges is tripled, and the charges are unchanged. The force between them was F. What is it now?
questions.e: F ∝ 1/r², so tripling r divides the force by 3² = 9. F/3 forgets to square the distance.

questions.s: A charge of 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ C feels a force of 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ N at a point in an electric field. What is the field strength at that point?
questions.e: E = F/q = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴/2.0 × 10⁻⁸ = 2.0 × 10⁴ N/C. 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ N/C is q/F, the ratio upside down; 8.0 × 10⁻¹² is the product.

questions.s: Two parallel plates are 1.5 cm apart with a potential difference of 300 V. What force acts on a charge of +3.0 × 10⁻⁹ C between them?
questions.e: E = U/d = 300/0.015 = 2.0 × 10⁴ V/m and F = qE = 3.0 × 10⁻⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁴ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ N. 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ N uses the gap in centimetres; 9.0 × 10⁻⁷ is qU, which is an energy, not a force.

questions.s: A charge of +5.0 × 10⁻⁶ C moves from A to B, where U_AB = 40 V. How much work does the electric force do on it?
questions.e: W = qU_AB = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 40 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ J. Dividing q by U gives 1.25 × 10⁻⁷, which is not a work at all.

questions.s: Point A is at +10 V and point B is at −20 V. An electron moves from A to B. How does its electric potential energy change?
questions.e: ΔEp = qΔφ = (−e)(−20 − 10) V = +30 eV, so the potential energy increases by 30 eV: the electron moves to lower potential, against the force on it. 'Decreases' would be right for a positive charge.

questions.s: A 50 μF capacitor holds a charge of 1.0 × 10⁻³ C. What is the voltage across it?
questions.e: U = Q/C = 1.0 × 10⁻³/5.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 20 V. 0.05 V is C/Q, the ratio inverted.

questions.s: A parallel-plate capacitor stays connected to a battery while the area of overlap of its plates is halved, with the gap unchanged. What happens to the charge Q on each plate and the field E between the plates?
o: Q is unchanged and E doubles.
Q doubles and E is unchanged.
Q halves and E is unchanged.
questions.e: C ∝ S/d halves. The battery fixes U, so Q = CU halves, while E = U/d stays the same because neither U nor d changed. E halving would need U or d to change.

questions.s: An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through 50 V. Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What kinetic energy does it gain?
questions.e: Ek = eU = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 50 = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ J doubles this by wrongly inserting a factor 2 from ½mv²; the work done by the field is simply eU.

questions.s: A charge +Q is fixed at x = 0 and a charge +9Q at x = 0.40 m. At what position on the x-axis is the electric field zero?
questions.e: For like charges the point lies between them, nearer the smaller one: Q/d² = 9Q/(0.40 − d)², so 0.40 − d = 3d and d = 0.10 m. 0.04 m splits the distance in the ratio 1 : 9, forgetting that the field depends on 1/r².

questions.s: How are the field lines of a uniform electric field drawn?
o: As radial lines spreading out from a point
As parallel lines that get closer together
As parallel lines that are equally spaced
As circles around a central point
questions.e: A uniform field has the same strength and direction everywhere, so its lines are parallel (same direction) and equally spaced (same strength). Lines getting closer would mean the field is getting stronger.

questions.s: A charge of 2.0 μC is moved from one point to another point on the same equipotential surface, which is at 50 V. How much work does the electric force do?
questions.e: W = qU and the potential difference between two points on one equipotential is 0, so no work is done. 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ J multiplies q by the potential 50 V, but work depends on a potential difference, not a potential.

questions.s: Plate A is earthed (0 V) and plate B is at −120 V; the plates are parallel and 6.0 cm apart. What is the potential at a point between them 2.0 cm from plate A?
questions.e: The field is uniform, so the potential changes by 120 V/6.0 cm = 20 V per cm, falling from A towards B. 2.0 cm from A it is 0 − 40 = −40 V. −80 V measures the 2.0 cm from plate B.

questions.s: A particle with charge-to-mass ratio 5.0 × 10⁷ C/kg enters a uniform field of 2.0 × 10⁴ N/C between parallel plates at 1.0 × 10⁶ m/s, moving parallel to the plates. The plates are 10 cm long and the particle does not hit them. Ignore gravity. What is its sideways displacement on leaving?
An oil drop is held at rest between two horizontal plates. The voltage between the plates is then doubled. What is the drop's acceleration now? (g is the acceleration due to gravity.)
questions.e: At first qE = mg. Doubling the voltage doubles E, so the electric force becomes 2mg upwards against mg downwards: net force mg upwards, a = g upwards. 2g ignores the weight that still acts.

questions.s: Two identical small metal spheres carry charges +3q and +q and repel each other with force F. They are touched together and then returned to their original positions. What is the force now?
questions.e: The total charge 4q is shared equally, so each sphere has +2q. F ∝ q₁q₂: before 3q², after 4q², so the new force is 4F/3, still repulsive. Answering F assumes the force depends only on the total charge.

questions.s: A particle of mass 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ kg and charge −2.0 × 10⁻⁵ C moves only under an electric force. It passes point A (potential 100 V) at 10 m/s. Point B is at potential 300 V. What is its speed at B?
questions.e: W = qU_AB = (−2.0 × 10⁻⁵)(100 − 300) = +4.0 × 10⁻³ J, so the negative particle gains energy moving to higher potential. Ek at A is ½ × 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 100 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ J, so Ek at B = 4.5 × 10⁻³ J and v² = 900, v = 30 m/s. 'It cannot reach B' treats the charge as positive.

questions.s: Which change increases the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor?
o: Increasing the voltage between the two plates
Inserting a dielectric between the plates
Reducing the overlapping area of the two plates
questions.e: C = εr·S/(4πkd), so a dielectric (εr > 1) increases C. Wider spacing or smaller area decreases C, and the voltage does not affect C at all.

questions.s: A charge of +4q is fixed at x = 0 and a charge of −q at x = L. Where on the x-axis, apart from infinity, is the electric field zero?
questions.e: Between unlike charges the fields add, so the zero point lies outside, beyond the smaller charge. With distance d beyond −q: 4q/(L + d)² = q/d², so L + d = 2d and d = L, giving x = 2L. x = 2L/3 solves the equation between the charges, where the fields actually point the same way.

questions.s: A proton is in a uniform electric field of 3.0 × 10⁴ N/C pointing east. Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and the proton mass as 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Ignore gravity. What is its acceleration?
questions.e: F = eE = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 3.0 × 10⁴ = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁵ N, and a = F/m = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁵/1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ = 3.0 × 10¹² m/s², in the field direction because the proton is positive. 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁵ is the force, not the acceleration.

questions.s: A steady current of 0.50 A flows in a wire for 2.0 minutes. How much charge passes any cross-section of the wire?
questions.e: Q = It = 0.50 × 120 = 60 C. 1.0 C comes from leaving the time in minutes instead of converting to 120 s.

questions.s: A current of 0.32 A flows through a lamp for 10 s. Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. How many electrons pass through the lamp?
questions.e: Q = It = 0.32 × 10 = 3.2 C, and n = Q/e = 3.2/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.0 × 10¹⁹. 5.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ multiplies by e instead of dividing; 2.0 × 10¹⁸ forgets the 10 s.

questions.s: A potential difference of 12 V across a resistor drives a current of 0.40 A through it. What is its resistance?
questions.e: R = U/I = 12/0.40 = 30 Ω. 4.8 Ω is U × I, which is the power in watts, not a resistance; 0.033 Ω is I/U.

questions.s: A uniform metal wire of resistance R is drawn out evenly to twice its original length; its volume and resistivity do not change. What is its new resistance?
questions.e: R = ρL/S. Doubling L at constant volume halves the cross-sectional area S, so R is multiplied by 2 × 2 = 4. 2R accounts for the longer length but forgets that the wire also became thinner.

questions.s: Which statement about the resistivity of a metal is correct?
o: It doubles when the length of the wire is doubled.
It depends only on the material and its temperature.
It halves when the cross-sectional area is doubled.
It has the same value for all metals at room temperature.
questions.e: Resistivity is a property of the material (and changes with temperature); it does not depend on the shape of the sample. The resistance R = ρL/S changes with length and area, but ρ does not. Different metals have different resistivities, which is why copper is used for wiring.

questions.s: Resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in series across a 20 V supply with negligible internal resistance. What is the voltage across the 6 Ω resistor?
questions.e: I = 20/(4 + 6) = 2 A, so U = 2 × 6 = 12 V. In series the voltage divides in the ratio of the resistances (4 : 6). 8 V is the voltage across the 4 Ω resistor.

questions.s: What is the combined resistance of a 3 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor connected in parallel?
questions.e: 1/R = 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω (or R = 3 × 6/(3 + 6) = 2 Ω). A parallel combination is always smaller than the smallest resistor; 9 Ω is the series value.

questions.s: A 6 Ω resistor is connected in series with a parallel pair made of a 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor. The whole arrangement is connected to a 24 V supply with negligible internal resistance. What is the current in the 3 Ω resistor?
questions.e: The parallel pair is 6 × 3/9 = 2 Ω, so the total is 8 Ω and the supply current is 24/8 = 3 A. The voltage across the pair is 3 × 2 = 6 V, so the 3 Ω resistor carries 6/3 = 2 A. 3 A is the total current, which splits between the two branches.

questions.s: A battery of EMF 6.0 V and internal resistance 1.0 Ω is connected to a 5.0 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the battery's terminals?
questions.e: I = E/(R + r) = 6.0/6.0 = 1.0 A, so the terminal voltage is IR = 5.0 V (or E − Ir = 6.0 − 1.0). 6.0 V would be the reading only with no current flowing; 1.0 V is the 'lost volts' inside the battery.

questions.s: When a battery is connected to a 2.0 Ω resistor the current is 1.0 A; when it is connected to a 5.0 Ω resistor the current is 0.50 A. What are the EMF E and internal resistance r of the battery?
questions.e: E = I(R + r): E = 1.0(2.0 + r) and E = 0.50(5.0 + r). Equating, 2.0 + r = 2.5 + 0.5r, so r = 1.0 Ω and E = 3.0 V. Check: 0.50 × 6.0 = 3.0 V. Taking E = 2.5 V uses only the second reading and ignores the internal resistance.

questions.s: An electric heater is marked '220 V, 1100 W'. What is its resistance when it works at its rated voltage?
questions.e: P = U²/R gives R = U²/P = 220²/1100 = 48 400/1100 = 44 Ω. 5.0 Ω is the current in amperes (P/U), not the resistance.

questions.s: An appliance rated at 1500 W is used for 2.0 hours every day for 30 days. How much electrical energy does it use in total?
questions.e: Energy = Pt = 1.5 kW × (2.0 h × 30) = 1.5 × 60 = 90 kWh. 3.0 kWh is one day's use only, and 45 kWh uses 1 hour per day.

questions.s: Two lamps marked '220 V, 40 W' and '220 V, 100 W' are connected in series to a 220 V supply. Assume their resistances are constant. Which lamp is brighter?
o: The 100 W lamp, because its rated power is larger
The 40 W lamp, because its resistance is larger
Neither; they are equally bright because the current is the same
The 40 W lamp, because its resistance is smaller
questions.e: R = U²/P, so the 40 W lamp has the larger resistance (1210 Ω against 484 Ω). In series the current is the same, so P = I²R is larger for the larger resistance and the 40 W lamp is brighter. The rated power only applies at the rated voltage, which neither lamp now gets.

questions.s: Lamps marked '6 V, 3 W' and '6 V, 6 W' are connected in series to a 9 V supply with negligible internal resistance. Assume the resistances of the lamps are constant. What is the power of the '6 V, 6 W' lamp?
questions.e: R = U²/P gives 12 Ω and 6 Ω. The current is 9/18 = 0.5 A, so the 6 W lamp has P = I²R = 0.25 × 6 = 1.5 W (and the 3 W lamp is exactly at its rating: 0.25 × 12 = 3 W). 6.0 W assumes the lamp gets its rated voltage, but it only has 3 V across it.

questions.s: A galvanometer has resistance 100 Ω and gives full-scale deflection at 1.0 mA. How can it be converted into a voltmeter with a range of 0–3 V?
o: Connect a 2900 Ω resistor in series with it
Connect a 3000 Ω resistor in series with it
Connect a 2900 Ω resistor in parallel with it
Connect a 0.033 Ω resistor in parallel with it
questions.e: At full scale the total resistance must be U/Ig = 3/0.001 = 3000 Ω. The galvanometer provides 100 Ω, so a series resistor of 2900 Ω is needed. 3000 Ω forgets the galvanometer's own resistance; a parallel resistor would make an ammeter.

questions.s: A galvanometer has resistance 99 Ω and gives full-scale deflection at 1.0 mA. How can it be converted into an ammeter with a range of 0–0.10 A?
o: Connect a 1.0 Ω resistor in series with it
Connect a 99 Ω resistor in parallel with it
Connect a 1.0 Ω resistor in parallel with it
Connect a 0.99 Ω resistor in parallel with it
questions.e: At full scale the shunt carries 0.10 − 0.001 = 0.099 A at the same voltage as the galvanometer, 0.001 × 99 = 0.099 V. R = 0.099/0.099 = 1.0 Ω, connected in parallel. 0.99 Ω divides by the full 0.10 A, forgetting that 1 mA still goes through the galvanometer.

questions.s: A battery with internal resistance is connected to resistor R₁ in series with a parallel pair made of resistor R₂ and a variable resistor R₃. The resistance of R₃ is increased. What happens to the current in R₂ and to the battery's terminal voltage?
o: The current in R₂ decreases and the terminal voltage increases.
The current in R₂ increases and the terminal voltage decreases.
The current in R₂ decreases and the terminal voltage decreases.
The current in R₂ increases and the terminal voltage increases.
questions.e: Increasing R₃ increases the total resistance, so the battery current falls and the terminal voltage E − Ir rises. The voltage across R₁ (IR₁) falls, so the voltage across the parallel pair rises, and the current in R₂ increases. The current in R₃ itself must fall, since the total fell while R₂'s share rose.

questions.s: By mistake, an ideal voltmeter is connected in series with a small lamp across a battery. What happens?
o: The lamp lights normally and the voltmeter reads zero.
The lamp does not light and the voltmeter reads about the EMF.
The voltmeter is damaged by a very large current.
The lamp does not light and the voltmeter reads zero.
questions.e: An ideal voltmeter has a very large resistance, so almost no current flows and the lamp stays dark. With almost no current, the lamp has almost no voltage across it and nearly the whole EMF appears across the voltmeter. A large current would flow only if an ammeter were connected directly across the battery.

questions.s: A battery of EMF 12 V and internal resistance 2.0 Ω is connected to a variable resistor R. For what value of R is the power delivered to R greatest, and what is that power?
questions.e: The output power is greatest when R = r = 2.0 Ω. Then I = 12/4.0 = 3.0 A and P = I²R = 9.0 × 2.0 = 18 W. With R = 0 the large current produces heat only inside the battery and the power in R is zero; R = 4.0 Ω gives 2.0² × 4.0 = 16 W, which is less.

questions.s: The I–U graphs (current on the vertical axis) of two resistors A and B are straight lines through the origin, and A's line is steeper. Which resistor has the larger resistance?
o: A, because a steeper line means a larger resistance
B, because the gradient of the line equals 1/R
They have equal resistance, because both lines pass through the origin
It cannot be decided without knowing the voltage
questions.e: With I plotted against U, the gradient is I/U = 1/R. A steeper line means a larger current for the same voltage, so smaller resistance; B has the larger resistance. The answer A would be correct only for a U–I graph, with U on the vertical axis.

questions.s: The I–U graph of a filament lamp (current on the vertical axis) curves towards the U-axis as the voltage increases. What is the reason?
o: Its resistance falls because its temperature rises.
Its resistance is constant, so the line is really straight.
Its resistance rises because its temperature rises.
Its resistance rises because the current falls.
questions.e: As U increases, the filament gets hotter and the resistivity of the metal increases, so each extra volt produces less extra current and the curve flattens towards the U-axis. The current does not fall; it keeps rising, only more slowly.

questions.s: The same current flows through two wires made of the same metal; wire Y has twice the cross-sectional area of wire X. What is the ratio of the drift speeds of the electrons, v_X : v_Y?
questions.e: I = nqvS with the same n, q and I, so v ∝ 1/S. X has half the area, so its electrons drift twice as fast: v_X : v_Y = 2 : 1. 1 : 1 assumes the drift speed depends only on the material.

questions.s: A small electric motor has a coil resistance of 0.50 Ω. When running from a 12 V supply it draws a current of 2.0 A. What mechanical power does it produce, ignoring friction?
questions.e: Input power UI = 12 × 2.0 = 24 W; heat in the coil I²R = 4.0 × 0.50 = 2.0 W; mechanical output 24 − 2.0 = 22 W. 288 W uses U²/R, which is wrong for a running motor: only IR = 1.0 V of the 12 V drives current through the coil's resistance, so Ohm's law does not apply to the whole motor.

questions.s: Resistors of 10 kΩ and 20 kΩ are connected in series across a 12 V supply with negligible internal resistance. A voltmeter of resistance 20 kΩ is connected across the 20 kΩ resistor. What does it read?
questions.e: The voltmeter in parallel with the 20 kΩ resistor makes 10 kΩ, so the supply sees 10 kΩ + 10 kΩ and the voltage divides equally: 6 V. 8 V is the reading of an ideal (infinite-resistance) voltmeter; a real meter with resistance comparable to the circuit lowers the voltage it measures.

questions.s: A high-resistance voltmeter connected directly across a battery reads 1.50 V. When a 2.5 Ω resistor is also connected across the battery, the voltmeter reads 1.25 V. What is the internal resistance of the battery?
questions.e: With no current the reading equals the EMF, E = 1.50 V. With the resistor, I = 1.25/2.5 = 0.50 A and the lost volts are 1.50 − 1.25 = 0.25 V, so r = 0.25/0.50 = 0.50 Ω. 0.25 Ω is the lost voltage in volts, not the resistance.

questions.s: What is the direction of the conventional current in a metal wire?
o: The direction in which the free electrons drift
From the negative to the positive terminal in the external circuit
The direction in which the metal ions drift
The direction in which positive charge would flow
questions.e: Conventional current is defined as the direction of flow of positive charge, which is from the positive to the negative terminal through the external circuit. In a metal the moving charges are electrons, which drift the opposite way; the metal ions stay fixed in the lattice.

questions.s: A copper wire is 100 m long and has a cross-sectional area of 1.0 mm². The resistivity of copper is 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m. What is the resistance of the wire?
questions.e: S = 1.0 mm² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m², so R = ρL/S = 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ × 100/1.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.6 Ω. 1.6 × 10⁻³ Ω comes from converting 1 mm² to 10⁻³ m², but area scales with the square of length: 1 mm² = (10⁻³ m)².

questions.s: A uniform wire of resistance R is cut into two equal halves, and the two halves are connected in parallel. What is the resistance of the combination?
questions.e: Each half has resistance R/2. Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one: (R/2)/2 = R/4. R/2 is the resistance of one half alone.

questions.s: The current through a fixed resistor is 0.20 A when the voltage across it is 3.0 V. What is the current when the voltage is raised to 4.5 V?
questions.e: For a fixed resistor I ∝ U (R = 3.0/0.20 = 15 Ω), so I = 4.5/15 = 0.30 A. 0.13 A comes from making the current inversely proportional to the voltage.

questions.s: Three 6 Ω resistors must all be used together in a circuit. Which total resistance is impossible to obtain?
questions.e: All in parallel: 2 Ω. Two in series (12 Ω) in parallel with the third: 12 × 6/18 = 4 Ω. Two in parallel (3 Ω) in series with the third: 9 Ω. All in series: 18 Ω. 12 Ω uses only two of the resistors, so it is not possible with all three.

questions.s: Resistors of 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply with negligible internal resistance. What is the total current drawn from the supply?
questions.e: Each resistor has the full 12 V: currents 3 A, 2 A and 1 A, which add to 6 A (the combination is 2 Ω). 0.55 A comes from adding the resistances (22 Ω) as if they were in series.

questions.s: Two branches are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply with negligible internal resistance. Branch 1 is a 2 Ω resistor followed by a 4 Ω resistor; branch 2 is a 2 Ω resistor followed by a 6 Ω resistor; in each branch the 2 Ω resistor is joined to the positive terminal. P is the junction between the resistors in branch 1 and Q the junction in branch 2. What is the magnitude of the potential difference between P and Q?
questions.e: Take the negative terminal as 0 V. Branch 1: the 4 Ω resistor has 12 × 4/6 = 8 V across it, so φP = 8 V. Branch 2: the 6 Ω resistor has 12 × 6/8 = 9 V, so φQ = 9 V. |φP − φQ| = 1 V. 0 would need the two branches to divide the voltage in the same ratio.

questions.s: A graph of terminal voltage U against current I for a battery is a straight line. It meets the U-axis at 3.0 V and passes through the point I = 1.0 A, U = 2.4 V. What is the internal resistance of the battery?
questions.e: U = E − Ir, so the intercept is E = 3.0 V and the magnitude of the gradient is r = (3.0 − 2.4)/1.0 = 0.6 Ω. 2.4 Ω is U/I at that point, which is the external resistance, not the internal one.

questions.s: A cell has EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω. Its terminals are accidentally joined by a thick wire of negligible resistance. What current flows?
questions.e: With no external resistance only r limits the current: I = E/r = 1.5/0.50 = 3.0 A. 0.75 A multiplies E by r instead of dividing.

questions.s: A current of 2.0 A flows through a 5.0 Ω resistor for 1.0 minute. How much heat is produced in the resistor?
questions.e: Q = I²Rt = 4.0 × 5.0 × 60 = 1200 J = 1.2 × 10³ J. 6.0 × 10² J uses I instead of I² (and 20 J is the power in watts, the heat in one second only).

questions.s: A battery of internal resistance 1.0 Ω supplies a 4.0 Ω external resistor. What fraction of the total electrical energy produced by the battery is delivered to the resistor?
questions.e: The same current flows through R and r, so the useful fraction is IU/(IE) = R/(R + r) = 4.0/5.0 = 80 %. 100 % ignores the heat produced inside the battery.

questions.s: A battery of EMF 12 V and internal resistance 1.0 Ω is connected to resistors of 3.0 Ω and 2.0 Ω in series. A 10 μF capacitor is connected across the 2.0 Ω resistor. Once steady conditions are reached, what is the charge on the capacitor?
questions.e: In the steady state no current flows into the capacitor, so I = 12/(1.0 + 3.0 + 2.0) = 2.0 A and the voltage across the 2.0 Ω resistor is 4.0 V. Q = CU = 10 × 10⁻⁶ × 4.0 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ C. 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ C uses the full EMF, ignoring the voltage shared with the other resistances.

questions.s: Two lamps L₁ and L₂ are connected in series with a battery and a closed switch, but neither lamp lights. A voltmeter connected across L₁ reads almost the battery EMF, and across L₂ it reads zero. What is the fault?
questions.e: Across a break in a series circuit, the voltmeter completes the circuit through the other components and reads nearly the full EMF; across an intact lamp with no current it reads zero. So L₁ is open. A short circuit in either lamp would let the other one light.

questions.s: Which statement about resistors connected in parallel is correct?
o: The voltage across each resistor is the same.
The current in each resistor is the same.
The total resistance is the sum of the resistances.
The largest resistor carries the largest current.
questions.e: Parallel resistors are connected between the same two points, so they have the same voltage. The currents divide in inverse proportion to the resistances, so the largest resistor carries the smallest current. Adding resistances is the rule for series.

questions.s: Resistors of 2 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel to a supply. What is the ratio of the power in the 2 Ω resistor to the power in the 3 Ω resistor?
questions.e: In parallel the voltage is the same, so P = U²/R and P₁ : P₂ = 1/2 : 1/3 = 3 : 2. 2 : 3 uses P = I²R as if the current were the same, which is the series case.

questions.s: A 2.0 kW electric kettle heats 1.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.2 × 10³ J/(kg·°C). Assuming no heat is lost, how long does this take?
questions.e: Q = mcΔT = 1.0 × 4.2 × 10³ × 80 = 3.36 × 10⁵ J, and t = Q/P = 3.36 × 10⁵/2000 = 168 s. 336 s comes from dividing by 1000 W instead of 2000 W.

questions.s: A battery of EMF E and internal resistance r is connected to a variable resistor R. A voltmeter measures the terminal voltage U and an ammeter measures the current I. As R is changed, what is the magnitude of the ratio ΔU/ΔI of the changes in the two readings?
questions.e: U = E − Ir with E and r fixed, so ΔU = −rΔI and |ΔU/ΔI| = r for any change of R. U/I gives R, which changes as the resistor is adjusted; it is not the ratio of the changes.

questions.s: A voltmeter with a range of 0–3 V has a resistance of 3 kΩ. How can its range be extended to 0–15 V?
o: Connect a 12 kΩ resistor in series with it
Connect a 15 kΩ resistor in series with it
Connect a 3 kΩ resistor in series with it
Connect a 12 kΩ resistor in parallel with it
questions.e: Full-scale current is 3/3000 = 1 mA. For 15 V the total resistance must be 15/0.001 = 15 kΩ, so 15 − 3 = 12 kΩ is added in series. 15 kΩ forgets the meter's own 3 kΩ.

questions.s: How many joules are there in one kilowatt-hour (1 kWh)?
questions.e: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. 3.6 × 10³ J is one watt-hour, and 6.0 × 10⁴ J would be 1 kW for one minute.

questions.s: To measure an unknown resistance R, a voltmeter is connected directly across R, and an ammeter measures the total current flowing into R and the voltmeter together. How does the value U/I compare with the true value of R?
o: Smaller than R, because the voltmeter takes some of the current
Larger than R, because the ammeter itself has some resistance
Smaller than R, because the ammeter has some resistance
Equal to R, because both meters are ideal enough to ignore
questions.e: The voltmeter reads the true voltage across R, but the ammeter reads the current through R plus the small current through the voltmeter. I is therefore too large, and U/I is smaller than R. The ammeter's resistance does not matter here, because the ammeter is outside the part whose voltage is measured.

questions.s: A battery delivers the same power to a 4.0 Ω resistor as it does to a 1.0 Ω resistor (each connected alone). What is the internal resistance of the battery?
questions.e: P = E²R/(R + r)². Setting 4/(4 + r)² = 1/(1 + r)² gives 2(1 + r) = 4 + r, so r = 2.0 Ω (equivalently r² = R₁R₂ = 4). 2.5 Ω is just the average of the two resistances.

questions.s: A lamp marked '12 V, 24 W' is to work normally from an 18 V supply of negligible internal resistance. What resistor must be connected in series with it?
questions.e: At normal working I = P/U = 24/12 = 2 A, and the resistor must take the remaining 18 − 12 = 6 V: R = 6/2 = 3 Ω. 6 Ω is the lamp's own resistance, and 9 Ω divides the whole 18 V by 2 A.

questions.s: A battery of EMF 9.0 V and internal resistance 1.0 Ω is connected to two 4.0 Ω resistors in parallel. What is the current in each 4.0 Ω resistor?
questions.e: The parallel pair is 2.0 Ω, so I = 9.0/(2.0 + 1.0) = 3.0 A, which splits equally: 1.5 A each. 2.25 A puts the full 9.0 V across one resistor, ignoring the internal resistance.

questions.s: Which of these has a resistance that decreases noticeably as its temperature rises?
questions.e: In a semiconductor, heating frees many more charge carriers, so its resistance falls; thermistors use this. The resistance of metals such as copper and tungsten rises with temperature, and constantan is an alloy chosen because its resistance hardly changes.

questions.s: A battery of EMF 6.0 V and internal resistance 1.0 Ω is connected in series with a fixed 2.0 Ω resistor and a variable resistor R. What is the greatest power that can be delivered to the variable resistor?
questions.e: Treat the battery and the 2.0 Ω resistor as one source with internal resistance 3.0 Ω. The power in R is greatest when R = 3.0 Ω: I = 6.0/6.0 = 1.0 A and P = 1.0² × 3.0 = 3.0 W. 8.0 W is the power in the fixed resistor when R = 0, and with R = 0 the variable resistor gets no power at all.

questions.s: How should an ammeter be connected in a circuit, and what kind of resistance should it have?
o: In series, with a very large resistance
In series, with a very small resistance
In parallel, with a very small resistance
In parallel, with a very large resistance
questions.e: An ammeter must carry the current it measures, so it goes in series, and its resistance must be very small so that it hardly changes that current. In parallel with a very small resistance it would short-circuit the component; a very large resistance is the requirement for a voltmeter.

questions.s: Wires A and B are made of the same metal. B is twice as long as A and has twice the diameter. What is the ratio of their resistances, R_A : R_B?
questions.e: R = ρL/S and S ∝ d². For B, the length factor is 2 and the area factor is 4, so R_B = (2/4)R_A = R_A/2, giving R_A : R_B = 2 : 1. 1 : 1 forgets that doubling the diameter quadruples the area.

questions.s: A 4 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel pair made of a 12 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor, connected to a 12 V supply with negligible internal resistance. What power is dissipated in the 12 Ω resistor?
questions.e: The pair is 12 × 6/18 = 4 Ω, so the total is 8 Ω, I = 1.5 A and the pair has 1.5 × 4 = 6 V across it. P = U²/R = 36/12 = 3 W. 12 W puts the whole 12 V across the 12 Ω resistor.

questions.s: A battery has an EMF of 1.5 V. What does this mean?
o: Its terminal voltage stays at 1.5 V whatever current is drawn from it.
It can deliver a current of up to 1.5 A to any circuit connected to it.
It gives 1.5 J of electrical energy to each coulomb of charge passing through it.
It holds a total of 1.5 J of chemical energy that can be turned into electricity.
questions.e: EMF is the energy converted into electrical energy per unit charge passing through the source: 1.5 V = 1.5 J/C. The terminal voltage falls below the EMF when current flows because of the internal resistance, and the EMF says nothing about the total energy stored or the maximum current.

questions.s: A battery of EMF 12 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω supplies a current of 4.0 A. How much power is wasted as heat inside the battery?
questions.e: P = I²r = 16 × 0.50 = 8.0 W. The battery produces EI = 48 W in total, of which 40 W reaches the external circuit (terminal voltage 10 V). 2.0 W uses Ir instead of I²r.

questions.s: A 20 Ω rheostat is used as a potential divider: its two ends are connected to a 12 V supply with negligible internal resistance. A 10 Ω load is connected between one end of the rheostat and its slider, which is at the midpoint. What is the voltage across the load?
questions.e: The load (10 Ω) is in parallel with the 10 Ω lower half, giving 5 Ω, in series with the 10 Ω upper half. The voltage divides 5 : 10, so the load gets 12 × 5/15 = 4.0 V. 6.0 V would be the reading with no load, and 8.0 V is the voltage across the upper half.

questions.s: A battery with significant internal resistance lights lamp A. An identical lamp B is then connected in parallel with A. What happens to the brightness of A?
o: It stays the same, because A and B are in parallel.
It increases, because the total current increases.
It decreases, because the terminal voltage falls.
It decreases, because the current in A is now shared with B.
questions.e: Adding B lowers the external resistance, so the battery current rises and the lost volts Ir increase; the terminal voltage, which is the voltage across A, falls and A dims. The current is not 'shared': each lamp has its own branch current set by the terminal voltage. With an ideal battery A would stay the same.

questions.s: A battery of EMF 12 V and internal resistance 1.0 Ω is connected in series with a 2.0 Ω resistor and a small motor whose coil resistance is 0.50 Ω. When the motor runs, a voltmeter across the 2.0 Ω resistor reads 4.0 V. What mechanical power does the motor produce, ignoring friction?
