questions.e: Before opening, the coil carries a larger current than the lamp because its resistance is smaller. When the switch opens, the self-induced EMF keeps the coil's current flowing for a moment, and the only path is back through the lamp, so the lamp briefly carries a larger current than before, in the opposite direction, and flashes. It does not go out at once because the inductor opposes the sudden drop in current.

questions.s: A rod slides along parallel rails 0.5 m apart, joined by a 2 Ω resistor, in a uniform 0.4 T field perpendicular to the plane of the rails. Other resistances are negligible. At what speed must the rod move for a current of 0.5 A to flow?
questions.e: The EMF needed is E = IR = 0.5 × 2 = 1 V. Since E = BLv, v = E/(BL) = 1/(0.4 × 0.5) = 5 m/s. Forgetting the resistor and setting BLv = I gives 2.5 m/s.

questions.s: A 50-turn coil of area 0.1 m² rotates at ω = 100π rad/s in a uniform 0.2 T field, about an axis perpendicular to the field. At t = 0 the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field. Which expression gives the induced EMF?
questions.e: E_max = NBAω = 50 × 0.2 × 0.1 × 100π = 100π V. At t = 0 the flux is maximum and changing least, so the EMF is zero and the expression is a sine. The cosine form would apply if the coil started parallel to the field; 100 V forgets the factor π in ω.

questions.s: Which device works mainly by inducing eddy currents in a metal object?
o: An electric kettle with a heating element
questions.e: An induction cooker uses a rapidly alternating magnetic field that induces eddy currents in the metal base of the pan, heating it directly. A kettle element and a lamp filament are heated by a current passed through them, and a battery works by chemical reactions.

questions.s: Why is the iron core of a transformer made of thin insulated sheets (laminations) rather than a solid block?
o: To increase the magnetic flux in the core
To reduce energy lost to eddy currents
To make the core lighter for transport
To change the turns ratio of the coils
questions.e: The alternating flux induces eddy currents in the core. Thin insulated sheets break up their paths, cutting the current and the heat loss I²R. Laminating does not increase the flux, and the turns ratio depends only on the windings.

questions.s: Which quantity is the same in the primary and secondary circuits of an ideal transformer?
questions.e: Both coils link the same alternating flux, so the induced voltages alternate at the same frequency. The voltages and currents are changed in the ratio of the turns, and the numbers of turns generally differ.

questions.s: A square loop of side 0.2 m and resistance 0.02 Ω lies perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field that varies as B = (0.2 + 0.1t) T, with t in seconds. What is the induced current?
questions.e: ΔB/Δt = 0.1 T/s and A = 0.04 m², so E = AΔB/Δt = 0.004 V and I = 0.004/0.02 = 0.2 A. Using the field value 0.2 T instead of its rate of change gives 0.4 A; only the changing part of B induces an EMF.

questions.s: A square loop of side 0.2 m lies in the plane of the page with exactly half of its area (a 0.2 m × 0.1 m part) inside a region of uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the page. The field increases at 0.5 T/s. What EMF is induced in the loop?
questions.e: Only the area inside the field carries flux: A = 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.02 m², so E = AΔB/Δt = 0.02 × 0.5 = 0.01 V. Using the whole loop area 0.04 m² gives 0.02 V.

questions.s: A rod starts from rest on smooth horizontal rails 0.5 m apart, joined by a 0.5 Ω resistor, in a uniform vertical field of 0.5 T. A constant horizontal force of 0.5 N pulls the rod along the rails. Other resistances are negligible. What is the rod's final constant speed?
questions.e: As the rod speeds up the current I = BLv/R grows, and so does the opposing force B²L²v/R. The speed stops rising when B²L²v/R = F: v = FR/(B²L²) = 0.5 × 0.5/(0.25 × 0.25) = 0.25/0.0625 = 4 m/s. Forgetting to square B and L gives 1 m/s.

questions.s: A circular loop of radius 0.2 m lies perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. What is the flux through the loop?
questions.e: A = πr² = 0.04π m², so Φ = BA = 0.5 × 0.04π = 0.02π Wb. Using the diameter instead of the radius gives 0.08π Wb, and 0.04π Wb is the area without multiplying by B.

questions.s: A rod 0.5 m long moves at 10 m/s perpendicular to its length and to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. What EMF is induced between its ends?
questions.e: E = BLv = 0.2 × 0.5 × 10 = 1 V. Dividing by the length instead of multiplying gives 4 V, and BL alone gives 0.1 V.

questions.s: The N pole of a bar magnet is pulled away from one end of a coil connected to a meter. What magnetic pole does that end of the coil become while the magnet moves away?
o: A north pole, repelling the magnet
A south pole, attracting the magnet
No pole, because the flux is decreasing
A north pole, attracting the magnet
questions.e: The flux from the magnet through the coil is decreasing, so the induced current opposes the decrease by trying to keep the magnet close: the near end becomes a south pole and attracts the receding N pole. A north pole there would push the magnet away and speed up the change, which breaks energy conservation.

questions.s: The flux through each turn of a 500-turn coil falls uniformly from 4 × 10⁻³ Wb to zero in 0.02 s. What is the induced EMF?
questions.e: E = NΔΦ/Δt = 500 × 4 × 10⁻³/0.02 = 500 × 0.2 = 100 V. Forgetting the number of turns gives 0.2 V.

questions.s: A sinusoidal alternating voltage has a peak value of 10√2 V. What is its rms value?
questions.e: For a sinusoid U_rms = U_max/√2 = 10√2/√2 = 10 V. Dividing by 2 instead of √2 gives 5√2 V, and 10√2 V is the peak itself.

questions.s: An ideal transformer has 200 turns on the primary and 1000 turns on the secondary. The primary voltage is 12 V AC. What is the secondary voltage?
questions.e: Us = Up × Ns/Np = 12 × 1000/200 = 60 V; it is a step-up transformer. Inverting the ratio gives 2.4 V.

questions.s: The frequency of an AC supply is 50 Hz. What is its angular frequency ω?
questions.e: ω = 2πf = 2π × 50 = 100π rad/s (about 314 rad/s). 50π rad/s forgets the factor 2, and 100 rad/s forgets the π.

questions.s: The page is the x–y plane with +x to the right and +y toward the top. A rod lies parallel to the y axis across two rails along the x direction and moves in the −x direction (to the left) in a uniform field pointing out of the page. In which direction does the induced current flow in the rod?
o: No current flows in the rod
questions.e: For positive charges in the rod, q(v × B) = q((−x̂) × ẑ) = −q(x̂ × ẑ) = +qŷ, so the current flows toward the top of the page. −y would be the answer for a rod moving to the right; the current cannot be along the motion because the rod lies along y.

questions.s: A single loop of area 0.1 m² and resistance 0.5 Ω lies perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field that decreases at a steady 0.2 T/s. What is the induced current?
questions.e: E = AΔB/Δt = 0.1 × 0.2 = 0.02 V, so I = E/R = 0.02/0.5 = 0.04 A. Multiplying by R instead of dividing gives 0.01 A.

questions.s: Which statement about a coil with self-inductance in a circuit is correct?
o: It opposes any steady current through it
It produces an EMF that is largest when its current is largest
It opposes changes in the current through it
It makes the current change instantly when switched on
questions.e: The self-induced EMF is E = L ΔI/Δt, so it depends on how fast the current changes, not on its size. The coil slows down both the rise and the fall of the current; a steady current is opposed only by the coil's resistance.

questions.s: An ideal transformer has turns ratio Np : Ns = 4 : 1. The primary current is 0.5 A. What is the secondary current?
questions.e: Power balance UpIp = UsIs with Us = Up/4 gives Is = 4Ip = 2 A: the step-down side carries the larger current. Applying the turns ratio directly to the current gives 0.125 A.

questions.s: An AC generator coil has 100 turns of area 0.05 m² and rotates at 50 rad/s in a uniform magnetic field of 0.1 T. What is the peak EMF?
questions.e: E_max = NBAω = 100 × 0.1 × 0.05 × 50 = 25 V. Forgetting the number of turns gives 0.25 V, and 12.5 V divides by 2 as if taking an average.

questions.s: A sinusoidal voltage of peak value 40 V is applied across a 20 Ω resistor. What is the average power dissipated?
questions.e: U_rms = 40/√2 = 20√2 V, so P = U_rms²/R = 800/20 = 40 W. Using the peak value gives 1600/20 = 80 W, which is the maximum instantaneous power.

questions.s: A fixed power is sent along a transmission line. If the transmission voltage is doubled, what happens to the power lost in the line?
questions.e: At fixed power the line current I = P/U halves when U doubles, and the loss I²R falls to (1/2)² = 1/4. 'It halves' forgets that the loss depends on the square of the current.

questions.s: A rod moves at 10 m/s along smooth rails 0.4 m apart, joined by a 1 Ω resistor, in a uniform 0.5 T field perpendicular to the plane of the rails. Other resistances are negligible. What is the magnetic force on the rod?
questions.e: E = BLv = 0.5 × 0.4 × 10 = 2 V, I = E/R = 2 A and F = BIL = 0.5 × 2 × 0.4 = 0.4 N, opposing the motion. 2 N confuses the EMF in volts with the force.

questions.s: A rod of mass 0.02 kg slides without friction down two long vertical rails 0.2 m apart, joined at the top by a 0.4 Ω resistor. A uniform horizontal field of 1 T is perpendicular to the plane of the rails. What is the rod's terminal speed? (g = 10 m/s², other resistances negligible)
questions.e: At terminal speed the magnetic force balances the weight: B²L²v/R = mg. B²L²/R = 1 × 0.04/0.4 = 0.1, so v = 0.2/0.1 = 2 m/s. Forgetting to square L gives a coefficient of 0.5 and a speed five times too small.

questions.s: A metal rod 1 m long rotates at 10 rad/s about one end, in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. What is the EMF between the ends of the rod?
questions.e: The speed rises linearly from 0 at the axis to ωL = 10 m/s at the tip, so the average speed is 5 m/s and E = ½BωL² = 0.5 × 0.2 × 10 × 1 = 1 V. Using the tip speed gives 2 V, which overestimates the EMF by a factor of 2.

questions.s: The flux through a single loop of resistance 0.2 Ω changes by 0.004 Wb. How much charge flows around the loop?
questions.e: q = IΔt = (ΔΦ/Δt)(Δt/R) = ΔΦ/R = 0.004/0.2 = 0.02 C, independent of how quickly the flux changes. Multiplying by R instead of dividing gives 0.0008 C.

questions.s: A coil rotates steadily in a uniform magnetic field about an axis perpendicular to the field. At the instant the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field, which statement is correct?
o: The flux is zero and the EMF is maximum
The flux is zero and the EMF is zero
The flux is maximum and the EMF is maximum
The flux is maximum and the EMF is zero
questions.e: With the plane perpendicular to the field, the whole area faces the field, so the flux is maximum. At that instant the flux is momentarily not changing (the top of a cosine curve), so the EMF is zero. Maximum EMF occurs a quarter turn later, when the plane is parallel to the field and the flux is zero.

questions.s: A voltage across a resistor is 6 V for the first third of each period and zero for the remaining two thirds. What is the rms value of this voltage?
questions.e: The rms value gives the same heating: U²T = 6²(T/3), so U² = 12 and U = 2√3 V. The average value is 2 V, which underestimates the heating because power depends on U².

questions.s: Under a microscope, tiny pollen grains suspended in still water are seen to jiggle about irregularly and without stopping. What does this motion directly show?
o: The pollen grains are living and swim by themselves
Water molecules move randomly and strike each grain unevenly
The molecules inside each pollen grain vibrate randomly
The grains are pulled about by attractive forces from the water
questions.e: This is Brownian motion: a small grain is hit by water molecules from all sides, and at any instant the impacts do not balance, so the grain jerks about. It is indirect evidence of the random thermal motion of the liquid molecules. The motion is not of the grain's own molecules, and dead pollen or dust shows it just the same.

questions.s: A room is at 27 °C. What is this temperature on the thermodynamic (kelvin) scale?
questions.e: T = t + 273 = 27 + 273 = 300 K. Subtracting (273 − 27 = 246 K) is a sign error, and 273 K is only 0 °C.

questions.s: The temperature of a liquid rises by 20 °C. By how much does its thermodynamic temperature rise?
questions.e: A kelvin and a degree Celsius are the same size, so a change of 20 °C is a change of 20 K. Adding 273 (293 K) converts a temperature value, not a temperature difference.

questions.s: A fixed amount of ideal gas is heated from 300 K to 600 K. By what factor does the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules change?
o: It increases by a factor of √2
It increases by a factor of 2
It increases by a factor of 4
questions.e: The average translational kinetic energy of a molecule is proportional to the thermodynamic temperature, so doubling T from 300 K to 600 K doubles it. The factor √2 applies to the rms speed, not to the kinetic energy.

questions.s: The thermodynamic temperature of a gas is raised from 300 K to 1200 K. By what factor does the root-mean-square speed of its molecules change?
questions.e: Average kinetic energy ½mv² is proportional to T, so v_rms ∝ √T. T increases 4 times, so v_rms increases √4 = 2 times. Choosing 4 confuses the speed with the kinetic energy.

questions.s: Two molecules are at their equilibrium separation r₀. Which statement about the forces between them is correct?
o: Both the attractive and the repulsive forces are zero
The attractive and repulsive forces are equal, so the net force is zero
Only an attractive force acts between them
Only a repulsive force acts between them
questions.e: Attraction and repulsion act together at every separation. At r₀ they have equal size, so the net force is zero. Neither force is zero itself; for r < r₀ repulsion is larger and for r > r₀ attraction is larger.

questions.s: The separation of two molecules is increased slowly from much less than r₀ (the equilibrium separation) to a very large distance. How does their molecular potential energy change?
questions.e: For r < r₀ the net force is repulsive, so moving apart lets the force do positive work and the potential energy falls. For r > r₀ the net force is attractive, so pulling apart needs work and the potential energy rises. The potential energy is therefore a minimum at r₀.

questions.s: For a fixed mass of an ideal gas, the internal energy depends only on which quantity?
questions.e: In an ideal gas the molecules exert no forces on each other except in collisions, so there is no molecular potential energy. The internal energy is the total molecular kinetic energy, which depends only on temperature. Volume would matter only for a real gas.

questions.s: A gas occupies 2.0 L at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. It is compressed slowly at constant temperature to 0.50 L. What is its new pressure?
questions.e: Boyle's law: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂, so p₂ = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 2.0/0.50 = 4.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Multiplying by 0.50/2.0 instead gives 2.5 × 10⁴ Pa, which wrongly predicts a pressure drop on compression.

questions.s: A gas at constant pressure has a volume of 6.0 L at 27 °C. It is heated to 127 °C. What is its new volume?
questions.e: At constant pressure V/T is constant with T in kelvin: V₂ = 6.0 × 400/300 = 8.0 L. Using Celsius values (6.0 × 127/27 ≈ 28 L) is the classic error; 4.5 L uses the ratio upside down.

questions.s: A sealed rigid steel tank holds air at 2.8 × 10⁵ Pa when its temperature is 7 °C. The tank warms to 37 °C. What is the new pressure of the air?
questions.e: At constant volume p/T is constant: p₂ = 2.8 × 10⁵ × 310/280 = 3.1 × 10⁵ Pa. The ratio 37/7 in Celsius gives the absurd 14.8 × 10⁵ Pa; 2.5 × 10⁵ Pa inverts the temperature ratio.

questions.s: What volume does 1.0 mol of an ideal gas occupy at 27 °C and 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa? Take R = 8.3 J/(mol·K).
questions.e: V = nRT/p = 1.0 × 8.3 × 300/(1.0 × 10⁵) = 2.49 × 10⁻² m³ = 24.9 L. Using 27 instead of 300 K gives about 2.2 L, and 2.5 L or 249 L come from slipping a power of ten in the m³ to L conversion (1 m³ = 1000 L).

questions.s: A fixed mass of gas has volume 3.0 L at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 300 K. It is changed to 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 400 K. What is its new volume?
questions.e: pV/T is constant: V₂ = V₁ × (p₁/p₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 3.0 × ½ × 4/3 = 2.0 L. Inverting the pressure ratio gives 8.0 L; inverting the temperature ratio gives about 1.1 L.

questions.s: A long uniform glass tube, closed at the bottom and open at the top, stands vertically. A 15 cm column of mercury traps a 30 cm column of air. Atmospheric pressure is 75 cmHg. The tube is slowly turned upside down (open end down) with no mercury escaping and the temperature constant. What is the new length of the air column?
questions.e: Open end up: p₁ = 75 + 15 = 90 cmHg. Open end down: p₂ = 75 − 15 = 60 cmHg. Boyle's law with uniform cross-section: L₂ = 90 × 30/60 = 45 cm. Answering 20 cm swaps the two pressures, as if the air were compressed.

questions.s: A uniform glass tube closed at one end lies horizontally. A 25 cm thread of mercury traps 20 cm of air; atmospheric pressure is 75 cmHg. The tube is slowly turned to vertical with the open end up, at constant temperature. What is the new length of the air column?
questions.e: Horizontal: the air is at 75 cmHg. Open end up: p = 75 + 25 = 100 cmHg. L = 75 × 20/100 = 15 cm. 30 cm is the result for open end down (p = 50 cmHg), and about 27 cm inverts the pressure ratio.

questions.s: An air bubble rises from the bottom of a lake 10 m deep to the surface. The water temperature is the same everywhere. Atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, the density of water is 1.0 × 10³ kg/m³ and g = 10 m/s². How does the volume of the bubble change?
questions.e: At the bottom p = p₀ + ρgh = 1.0 × 10⁵ + 1.0 × 10³ × 10 × 10 = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa; at the surface p = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. With constant temperature pV is constant, so the volume doubles. A factor of 10 wrongly scales with the depth itself instead of with the absolute pressure.

questions.s: How much heat is needed to warm 2.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 70 °C? The specific heat capacity of water is 4.2 × 10³ J/(kg·°C).
questions.e: Q = mcΔT = 2.0 × 4.2 × 10³ × 50 = 4.2 × 10⁵ J. Using the final temperature 70 °C instead of the change 50 °C gives 5.9 × 10⁵ J, and forgetting the mass gives 2.1 × 10⁵ J.

questions.s: Amina mixes 0.20 kg of water at 80 °C with 0.30 kg of water at 20 °C in an insulated flask. Ignoring heat exchange with the flask, what is the final temperature?
questions.e: Heat lost = heat gained: 0.20 × c × (80 − T) = 0.30 × c × (T − 20), so 16 − 0.2T = 0.3T − 6 and T = 44 °C. The simple average 50 °C ignores the different masses, and 56 °C attaches the masses to the wrong temperatures.

questions.s: How much heat is needed to melt 0.50 kg of ice already at 0 °C into water at 0 °C? The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.3 × 10⁵ J/kg.
questions.e: Q = mL = 0.50 × 3.3 × 10⁵ = 1.65 × 10⁵ J. Dividing by the mass instead of multiplying gives 6.6 × 10⁵ J.

questions.s: 0.10 kg of ice at 0 °C is dropped into 0.40 kg of water at 50 °C in an insulated container. The latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.36 × 10⁵ J/kg and the specific heat capacity of water is 4.2 × 10³ J/(kg·°C). What is the final temperature?
questions.e: Melting the ice needs 0.10 × 3.36 × 10⁵ = 33 600 J; cooling the water to 0 °C could give 0.40 × 4200 × 50 = 84 000 J, so all the ice melts. The remaining 50 400 J warms all 0.50 kg: ΔT = 50 400/(0.50 × 4200) = 24 °C. Ignoring the latent heat gives 40 °C, and heating only the 0.40 kg gives 30 °C.

questions.s: A crystalline solid is melting at its melting point while still absorbing heat, and its temperature stays constant. Which statement about its molecules is correct?
o: Average kinetic energy increases; potential energy is unchanged
Average kinetic energy is unchanged; potential energy increases
Both the average kinetic energy and the potential energy increase
Neither the average kinetic energy nor the potential energy changes
questions.e: Temperature measures average molecular kinetic energy, so a constant temperature means it does not change. The absorbed heat still raises the internal energy, so it goes into molecular potential energy as the ordered structure breaks up.

questions.s: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and at the same time does 200 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?
questions.e: First law: ΔU = Q + W, with Q = +500 J (absorbed) and W = −200 J (work done by the gas). ΔU = +300 J. Adding the two magnitudes (+700 J) treats the work as if it were done on the gas.

questions.s: 300 J of work is done on a gas to compress it, and during the compression the gas gives out 100 J of heat. What is the change in the internal energy of the gas?
questions.e: ΔU = W + Q = (+300) + (−100) = +200 J, an increase. +400 J forgets that heat released is negative.

questions.s: Air in a bicycle pump is compressed very quickly, so there is no time for heat exchange with the surroundings. What happens to the air?
o: Its temperature rises, because work done on it increases its internal energy
Its temperature stays constant, because no heat enters it
Its temperature falls, because its volume decreases
Its internal energy stays constant, because Q = 0
questions.e: For an adiabatic process Q = 0, so ΔU = W. The work done on the air is positive, so its internal energy and temperature rise, which is why a pump barrel gets warm. Q = 0 does not mean ΔU = 0, because work can still change U.

questions.s: A fixed mass of ideal gas expands slowly at constant temperature. Which statement is correct?
o: Its internal energy is unchanged and it absorbs heat equal to the work it does
Its internal energy is unchanged and it exchanges no heat with the surroundings
Its internal energy decreases by the amount of work it does
Its internal energy is unchanged and it releases heat equal to the work it does
questions.e: Constant temperature means ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas. Expanding, it does work (W < 0), so Q = −W > 0: it must absorb exactly that much heat. Saying no heat is exchanged confuses an isothermal process with an adiabatic one.

questions.s: A gas kept at a constant pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa expands from 3.0 L to 5.0 L. How much work does the gas do on its surroundings?
questions.e: W = pΔV = 2.0 × 10⁵ × (5.0 − 3.0) × 10⁻³ = 400 J. Using the initial volume (pV₁ = 600 J) instead of the change in volume is the common slip; 40 J comes from writing 1 L = 10⁻⁴ m³.

questions.s: A gas in a cylinder expands at a constant pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, its volume increasing by 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³, while it absorbs 500 J of heat. What is the change in its internal energy?
questions.e: Work done by the gas = pΔV = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 2.0 × 10⁻³ = 200 J, so W = −200 J. ΔU = Q + W = 500 − 200 = +300 J. +700 J adds the work instead of subtracting it.

questions.s: On a p–V diagram, an ideal gas is taken clockwise round a rectangle whose corners are at pressures 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa and volumes 1.0 L and 4.0 L. How much net heat does the gas absorb in one complete cycle?
questions.e: The net work done by the gas in a clockwise cycle is the enclosed area: (3.0 − 1.0) × 10⁵ × (4.0 − 1.0) × 10⁻³ = 600 J. After a full cycle ΔU = 0, so the net heat absorbed equals 600 J. 1200 J uses the full 4.0 L and 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa instead of the side lengths of the rectangle.

questions.s: Which statement agrees with the second law of thermodynamics?
o: A heat engine without friction could turn all the heat it absorbs into work
Heat can never be moved from a colder body to a hotter body by any means
Heat cannot flow by itself from a colder body to a hotter body
The total entropy of an isolated system tends to decrease over time
questions.e: The Clausius statement says heat does not flow spontaneously from cold to hot. A refrigerator does move heat from cold to hot, but only because work is done, so 'never by any means' is wrong. No engine, even without friction, converts all absorbed heat into work, and the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

questions.s: In each cycle a heat engine absorbs 2000 J from a hot source and rejects 1500 J to a cold sink. What is its efficiency?
questions.e: Work per cycle W = 2000 − 1500 = 500 J, so η = W/Q_in = 500/2000 = 25 %. 75 % is the ratio of rejected to absorbed heat, and 33 % divides the work by the rejected heat.

questions.s: A drop of ink spreads through a glass of hot water faster than through a glass of cold water. What is the best explanation?
o: Hot water has a lower density, so the ink sinks faster
Ink molecules are larger in hot water
Hot water molecules attract the ink molecules more strongly
Molecular motion is faster at higher temperature, so diffusion is faster
questions.e: Diffusion is caused by the random thermal motion of molecules, and the average molecular speed increases with temperature. The spreading is not driven by density or by attraction, and molecules do not grow when heated.

questions.s: The molar mass of water is 18 g/mol and the Avogadro constant is 6.0 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. What is the mass of one water molecule?
questions.e: m = M/N_A = 18 × 10⁻³ kg/mol ÷ 6.0 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 3.0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg. 3.0 × 10⁻²³ is the value in grams written as kilograms, and 3.3 × 10²² is N_A/18, the number of molecules in one gram.

questions.s: How many molecules are there in 36 g of water? Molar mass of water is 18 g/mol; Avogadro constant is 6.0 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
questions.e: n = 36/18 = 2.0 mol, so N = 2.0 × 6.0 × 10²³ = 1.2 × 10²⁴. 2.2 × 10²⁵ multiplies the mass in grams directly by N_A without converting to moles.

questions.s: In an oil-film experiment, a drop containing 4.0 × 10⁻¹¹ m³ of oil spreads on water into a single-molecule layer of area 0.20 m². Estimate the diameter of an oil molecule.
questions.e: For a monolayer, thickness = volume/area = 4.0 × 10⁻¹¹/0.20 = 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, which is the molecular diameter. Multiplying volume by area gives 8.0 × 10⁻¹² m, and area/volume gives the impossible 5.0 × 10⁹ m.

questions.s: A gas is heated in a sealed rigid container. From the molecular point of view, why does its pressure increase?
o: The number of molecules per unit volume increases
The molecules hit the walls more often and with larger average force
The molecules become larger and fill more of the container
The attractive forces between the molecules become weaker
questions.e: The volume and number of molecules are fixed, so the number density is unchanged. Higher temperature means higher average molecular speed, so each collision with the wall transfers more momentum and collisions happen more often; both raise the pressure.

questions.s: Two containers hold the same ideal gas at the same temperature. The number of molecules per unit volume in container B is twice that in container A. What is the ratio p_B : p_A?
questions.e: Pressure depends on the number density of molecules and their average kinetic energy. At the same temperature the average kinetic energy is the same, so pressure is proportional to number density: p_B : p_A = 2 : 1. Answering 1 : 1 assumes temperature alone fixes pressure.

questions.s: A container holds a mixture of hydrogen (molar mass 2 g/mol) and oxygen (molar mass 32 g/mol) in thermal equilibrium. Which statement is correct?
o: Their average kinetic energies are equal; hydrogen's rms speed is 4 times oxygen's
Their average kinetic energies are equal; hydrogen's rms speed is 16 times oxygen's
Hydrogen's average kinetic energy is 16 times oxygen's; their rms speeds are equal
Hydrogen's average kinetic energy is 4 times oxygen's; its rms speed is also 4 times
questions.e: At the same temperature molecules have the same average translational kinetic energy, ½mv². Then v_rms ∝ 1/√m, so v_H/v_O = √(32/2) = √16 = 4. The factor 16 forgets the square root.

questions.s: A 20 L steel cylinder contains gas at 1.5 × 10⁶ Pa. It is used to fill balloons, each to 2.0 L at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, until the cylinder pressure falls to 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Temperature is constant. How many balloons can be filled?
questions.e: At 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa the gas would occupy 1.5 × 10⁶ × 20/1.0 × 10⁵ = 300 L. 20 L of this must stay in the cylinder, leaving 280 L, which fills 280/2.0 = 140 balloons. 150 forgets that the cylinder keeps 20 L of gas at the final pressure.

questions.s: A tyre has a fixed volume of 8.0 L and contains air at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Each stroke of a pump pushes in 0.40 L of air taken at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. What is the tyre pressure after 20 strokes, if the temperature stays constant?
questions.e: The 20 strokes add 20 × 0.40 = 8.0 L of air at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Boyle's law for all the air: 1.0 × 10⁵ × (8.0 + 8.0) = p × 8.0, so p = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa. 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa adds the original pressure a second time, and 2.1 × 10⁶ Pa adds 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa per stroke.

questions.s: Which statement about absolute zero is correct?
o: It equals −273 K and can be reached with a good refrigerator
It equals 0 °C, the freezing point of water
It equals about −273 °C and can be approached but never reached
It equals about −273 °C and is reached when a gas is liquefied
questions.e: Absolute zero is 0 K, about −273.15 °C, and the third law says it cannot be reached in a finite number of steps, only approached. −273 K is a confusion of the two scales, and liquefying a gas happens far above absolute zero.

questions.s: Compare 1 kg of ice at 0 °C with 1 kg of water at 0 °C. Which statement is correct?
o: The ice has the greater internal energy, because it is a solid
Both have the same internal energy, because their temperatures are equal
Neither has any internal energy at 0 °C
The water has the greater internal energy, because melting absorbs heat
questions.e: Ice must absorb latent heat to become water at the same temperature, so the water has more internal energy (more molecular potential energy). Equal temperature only means equal average kinetic energy, not equal internal energy.

questions.s: For a fixed mass of gas at constant volume, pressure is plotted against Celsius temperature t and gives a straight line. Extended backwards, at what temperature does this line meet the t-axis?
questions.e: At constant volume p ∝ T (kelvin), so p = 0 when T = 0 K, which is about −273 °C. On a p–T graph with T in kelvin the same line passes through the origin; on the Celsius axis it does not pass through 0 °C.

questions.s: For a fixed mass of ideal gas, isotherm T₁ passes through the point (2.0 L, 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa) and isotherm T₂ passes through (3.0 L, 4.0 × 10⁵ Pa). What is T₂/T₁?
questions.e: For fixed mass, pV ∝ T. p₁V₁ = 6.0 × 10² J and p₂V₂ = 12 × 10² J, so T₂/T₁ = 2. 1/2 inverts the ratio; 4/3 compares pressures only.

questions.s: An ideal gas goes from state A (1.0 L, 4.0 × 10⁵ Pa) to state B (4.0 L, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa) along a straight line on a p–V diagram. How much heat does the gas absorb?
questions.e: pV = 400 J at A and at B, so T_A = T_B and ΔU = 0. The work done by the gas is the trapezium area: ½(4.0 + 1.0) × 10⁵ × 3.0 × 10⁻³ = 750 J, so Q = 750 J absorbed. Answering 0 J assumes the path is isothermal-like with no heat flow, but equal end temperatures only fix ΔU, not Q.

questions.s: A gas is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 450 K. Its new density is what fraction of its original density?
questions.e: At constant pressure V ∝ T, so V increases by 450/300 = 3/2. The mass is unchanged, so density falls to 2/3 of its original value. 3/2 gives the volume ratio, not the density ratio.

questions.s: A gas in a sealed rigid container is heated. Which quantity stays the same?
o: The number of molecules per unit volume
The average kinetic energy of the molecules
The average speed of the molecules
questions.e: The container is sealed and rigid, so both the number of molecules and the volume are fixed, and the number density cannot change. Heating raises the temperature, so the average kinetic energy, the average speed and therefore the pressure all increase.

questions.s: Two bodies are placed in thermal contact. The net flow of heat between them stops when they have equal values of which quantity?
questions.e: Thermal equilibrium is defined by equal temperature: heat flows from higher to lower temperature until the temperatures match. A large cool body can have more internal energy than a small hot one, so equal internal energy is not the condition.

questions.s: Equal masses of water and cooking oil absorb the same amount of heat. The water temperature rises by 10 °C and the oil temperature rises by 20 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.2 × 10³ J/(kg·°C). What is the specific heat capacity of the oil?
questions.e: Q = mcΔT is the same for both with equal m, so c is inversely proportional to ΔT: c_oil = 4.2 × 10³ × 10/20 = 2.1 × 10³ J/(kg·°C). 8.4 × 10³ uses the ratio the wrong way round: the liquid that warms more has the smaller specific heat capacity.

questions.s: A 1000 W electric kettle heats 1.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C. Only 80 % of the electrical energy goes into the water. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.2 × 10³ J/(kg·°C). How long does this take?
questions.e: Heat needed: Q = 1.0 × 4.2 × 10³ × 80 = 3.36 × 10⁵ J. Useful power is 0.80 × 1000 = 800 W, so t = 3.36 × 10⁵/800 = 420 s. 336 s ignores the efficiency, and 269 s multiplies by 0.80 instead of dividing.

questions.s: 0.020 kg of steam at 100 °C condenses to water and then cools to 50 °C. How much heat is released? Specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.3 × 10⁶ J/kg; specific heat capacity of water is 4.2 × 10³ J/(kg·°C).
questions.e: Condensing: mL = 0.020 × 2.3 × 10⁶ = 4.6 × 10⁴ J. Cooling: mcΔT = 0.020 × 4.2 × 10³ × 50 = 4.2 × 10³ J. Total 5.02 × 10⁴ J. Stopping at 4.6 × 10⁴ J forgets the cooling stage, and 5.44 × 10⁴ J cools through 100 °C instead of 50 °C.

questions.s: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the ideal gas model?
o: Molecules are in continuous random motion
Molecules attract each other strongly at all separations
Collisions of molecules are perfectly elastic
The volume of the molecules themselves is negligible
questions.e: The ideal gas model assumes no intermolecular forces except during collisions, which is why its internal energy has no potential energy part. Random motion, elastic collisions and negligible molecular volume are all assumptions of the model.

questions.s: Both the pressure and the volume of a fixed mass of ideal gas are doubled. What happens to its thermodynamic temperature?
questions.e: pV/T is constant for a fixed mass, so T ∝ pV. Doubling p and V multiplies pV by 4, so T becomes 4 times as large. Answering 'unchanged' wrongly applies Boyle's law, which needs constant temperature.

questions.s: A vertical cylinder, open at the top, contains gas under a smooth piston of mass 10 kg and area 50 cm². Atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 10 m/s². What is the pressure of the gas when the piston is at rest?
questions.e: Balance on the piston: pS = p₀S + mg, so p = 1.0 × 10⁵ + 100/(5.0 × 10⁻³) = 1.0 × 10⁵ + 2.0 × 10⁴ = 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa. 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa comes from converting 50 cm² to 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² instead of 5.0 × 10⁻³ m², and 0.8 × 10⁵ Pa subtracts the piston's weight.

questions.s: In a vertical cylinder open at the top, gas is held at a constant 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa under a free, smooth piston of area 50 cm². The gas column is 30 cm high at 300 K. The gas is heated slowly to 400 K. How much work does the gas do?
questions.e: At constant pressure h ∝ T, so the column grows to 30 × 400/300 = 40 cm, a rise of 0.10 m. W = pSΔh = 1.2 × 10⁵ × 5.0 × 10⁻³ × 0.10 = 60 J. 50 J uses only atmospheric pressure, as if the piston had no weight.

questions.s: Which statement about a working household refrigerator is correct?
o: It moves heat from cold to hot without any energy input
It releases less heat to the kitchen than it removes from the inside
It shows that heat flows by itself from cold to hot bodies
It moves heat from inside to the room because work is done on it
questions.e: Heat does not flow from cold to hot by itself; the compressor does work so the refrigerator can pump heat out. By energy conservation the heat released to the room equals the heat removed plus the work done, so it is more than the heat removed, not less.

questions.s: A running refrigerator stands with its door open in a sealed, well-insulated room. What happens to the room temperature over a long time?
o: It rises, as the electrical energy supplied becomes heat in the room
It falls, because the refrigerator keeps removing heat from the room air
It stays the same, because the heat taken in equals the heat given out
It falls at first and then returns to its starting value
questions.e: With the door open the refrigerator only moves heat around inside the room, while the electrical energy it uses is finally converted into internal energy of the room. No heat leaves the insulated room, so its internal energy and temperature rise. The cold air near the door is outweighed by the heat released at the back.

questions.s: A fixed mass of ideal gas in state A is heated at constant volume until its pressure doubles (state B), and then heated at constant pressure until its volume doubles (state C). What is T_C/T_A?
questions.e: A → B at constant volume: T doubles. B → C at constant pressure: T doubles again. So T_C = 4T_A, as also follows from pV ∝ T with both p and V doubled. 2 counts only one of the two steps.

questions.s: An ideal gas is compressed slowly at constant temperature, and 200 J of work is done on it. Which statement about heat is correct?
o: The gas absorbs 200 J of heat
The gas releases 200 J of heat
The gas releases 400 J of heat
questions.e: Constant temperature gives ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so Q = −W = −200 J: the gas releases 200 J. Saying no heat is exchanged would make the compression adiabatic, which would warm the gas.

questions.s: A gas in an insulated cylinder pushes a piston outward and does 150 J of work, with no heat exchanged. Which statement is correct?
o: ΔU = −150 J and its temperature falls
ΔU = +150 J and its temperature rises
ΔU = 0, because no heat is exchanged
ΔU = −150 J, but its temperature is unchanged
questions.e: Adiabatic: Q = 0, and W = −150 J because the gas does work, so ΔU = −150 J. The internal energy of a gas depends on its temperature, so the temperature falls; this is how expanding gas cools. ΔU = 0 wrongly treats 'no heat' as 'no change'.

questions.s: A 'perpetual motion machine of the second kind' would take heat from a single reservoir, such as the ocean, and turn all of it into work. Which statement is correct?
o: A machine of the first kind is impossible only because friction cannot be removed
A machine of the second kind would break the law of conservation of energy
An engine turning heat from the sea fully into work breaks the first law
A machine of the second kind obeys energy conservation but breaks the second law
questions.e: Turning heat fully into work conserves energy, so it does not violate the first law; it is forbidden by the Kelvin statement of the second law. A machine of the first kind, producing work from nothing, is impossible because it violates energy conservation, not merely because of friction.

questions.s: Water boils at 100 °C at standard pressure. What is this temperature in kelvin?
questions.e: T = t + 273 = 100 + 273 = 373 K. 173 K comes from subtracting 100 from 273 instead of adding.

questions.s: A gas sample is cooled to −73 °C. What is its thermodynamic temperature?
questions.e: T = t + 273 = −73 + 273 = 200 K. 346 K ignores the minus sign, and no thermodynamic temperature can be negative, so −200 K is impossible.

questions.s: A gas has volume 4.0 L at 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa. At constant temperature its pressure is reduced to 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. What is its new volume?
questions.e: Boyle's law: V₂ = p₁V₁/p₂ = 3.0 × 10⁵ × 4.0/1.0 × 10⁵ = 12 L. Lower pressure means larger volume, so 1.3 L (dividing instead of multiplying) cannot be right.

questions.s: A gas at constant pressure occupies 0.60 m³ at 27 °C. It is cooled to −73 °C. What is its new volume?
questions.e: V/T is constant with T in kelvin: V₂ = 0.60 × 200/300 = 0.40 m³. Using Celsius gives a negative volume, which is impossible, and 0.90 m³ inverts the ratio.

questions.s: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of a 0.50 kg aluminium block by 20 °C? The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/(kg·°C).
questions.e: Q = mcΔT = 0.50 × 900 × 20 = 9000 J. Leaving out the mass gives 18 000 J, and leaving out the temperature change gives 450 J.

questions.s: Kwame pours 1.0 kg of water at 90 °C into 2.0 kg of water at 30 °C. Ignoring heat losses, what is the final temperature?
questions.e: 1.0 × c × (90 − T) = 2.0 × c × (T − 30) gives 90 − T = 2T − 60, so T = 50 °C. 60 °C is the plain average, which ignores that there is twice as much cold water; 70 °C pairs the masses with the wrong temperatures.

questions.s: A gas absorbs 400 J of heat while 400 J of work is done on it. What is the change in its internal energy?
questions.e: ΔU = Q + W = (+400) + (+400) = +800 J, since both heat absorbed and work done on the gas add energy. 0 J treats the work as done by the gas.

questions.s: A gas does 250 J of work on its surroundings and its internal energy decreases by 100 J. What heat exchange took place?
questions.e: ΔU = Q + W with ΔU = −100 J and W = −250 J, so Q = −100 + 250 = +150 J: the gas absorbed 150 J. It did more work than its loss of internal energy, so the extra 150 J must have come in as heat.

questions.s: Which observation is an example of diffusion caused by molecular motion?
o: Dust particles swirling in a beam of sunlight
Water boiling vigorously in an open kettle
An ice cube melting slowly on a warm plate
The smell of perfume spreading through a still room
questions.e: Perfume molecules spread through still air by their own random thermal motion, which is diffusion. Swirling dust is moved by air currents, and boiling and melting are changes of state, not diffusion.

questions.s: Helium and neon gases are kept at the same temperature. Which statement is correct?
o: Their molecules have equal average kinetic energy
Neon molecules have greater average kinetic energy
Helium molecules have greater average kinetic energy
Their molecules have equal average speed
questions.e: Average translational kinetic energy depends only on temperature, not on the type of molecule. Because helium atoms are lighter, they move faster on average to have the same kinetic energy, so the average speeds are not equal.

questions.s: A sealed rigid container holds gas at 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa and 27 °C. It is heated to 127 °C. What is the new pressure?
questions.e: At constant volume p/T is constant: p₂ = 1.5 × 10⁵ × 400/300 = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa. The Celsius ratio 127/27 gives about 7.1 × 10⁵ Pa, which is wrong because gas laws need kelvin.

questions.s: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa from 2.0 L to 6.0 L. How much work does it do?
questions.e: W = pΔV = 1.5 × 10⁵ × 4.0 × 10⁻³ = 600 J. 6.0 × 10⁵ J forgets to convert litres to cubic metres, and 900 J uses the final volume instead of the change.

questions.s: A long uniform tube, closed at one end, is held vertical with its open end down. A 15 cm column of mercury traps 30 cm of air. Atmospheric pressure is 75 cmHg. The tube is slowly turned so the open end is up, with no mercury lost and the temperature constant. What is the new length of the air column?
questions.e: Open end down: p₁ = 75 − 15 = 60 cmHg. Open end up: p₂ = 75 + 15 = 90 cmHg. L₂ = 60 × 30/90 = 20 cm. 45 cm swaps the two pressures, and 24 cm treats the final pressure as 75 cmHg.

questions.s: How much heat must be supplied to melt 0.20 kg of ice at 0 °C completely? The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.3 × 10⁵ J/kg.
questions.e: Q = mL = 0.20 × 3.3 × 10⁵ = 6.6 × 10⁴ J. 1.65 × 10⁶ J divides by the mass, and 3.3 × 10⁵ J is the value for 1 kg.

questions.s: In each cycle a heat engine does 300 J of useful work and rejects 900 J of heat to its cold sink. What is its efficiency?
questions.e: Heat absorbed = 300 + 900 = 1200 J, so η = 300/1200 = 25 %. 33 % divides the work by the rejected heat instead of by the heat absorbed.

questions.s: Which everyday process is consistent with the second law of thermodynamics?
o: A hot cup of tea in a cool room can warm up by taking heat from the room air
Gas that has spread through a room will gather back into its bottle by itself
Friction heat can turn back by itself into the same amount of kinetic energy
Heat flows by itself from a hot cup of tea into the cooler room air
questions.e: Natural processes go one way: heat flows by itself from hot to cold, gas spreads out, and friction turns kinetic energy into internal energy. None of these reverses by itself, even though the reverse would conserve energy. That is the content of the second law.

questions.s: A tightly capped bottle of air is moved from a warm room into a refrigerator, and the pressure inside falls. What is the molecular explanation?
o: Some molecules escape through the cap, so fewer of them remain inside
Molecules move more slowly and hit the walls less hard and less often
The molecules shrink as they cool and fill less of the space
The molecules are pulled more strongly towards the cold glass walls
questions.e: The bottle is sealed and rigid, so the number density is fixed. Lower temperature means lower average molecular speed, so collisions with the walls are both gentler and less frequent, and the pressure falls. Molecules do not shrink, and no gas escapes from a tight cap.

questions.s: A container of volume 0.030 m³ holds an ideal gas at 1.66 × 10⁵ Pa and 27 °C. How many moles of gas does it contain? Take R = 8.3 J/(mol·K).
questions.e: n = pV/(RT) = 1.66 × 10⁵ × 0.030/(8.3 × 300) = 4980/2490 = 2.0 mol. Using 27 instead of 300 K gives about 22 mol.

questions.s: Two molecules are farther apart than their equilibrium separation r₀ and are pulled further apart. Which statement is correct?
o: Net force attractive; potential energy increases
Net force attractive; potential energy decreases
Net force repulsive; potential energy increases
Net force repulsive; potential energy decreases
questions.e: For r > r₀ the attraction exceeds the repulsion, so the net force is attractive. Separating them works against this force, so the potential energy increases. It decreases only when they move towards r₀ from either side.

questions.s: An ideal gas goes round a cycle A → B → C → A on a p–V diagram. A is (1.0 L, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa), B is (1.0 L, 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa) and C is (3.0 L, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa); each step is a straight line. What net work does the gas do in one cycle?
questions.e: The net work equals the area of the triangle: ½ × (3.0 − 1.0) × 10⁻³ × (3.0 − 1.0) × 10⁵ = 200 J, positive because the cycle runs clockwise. 400 J forgets the factor ½ for a triangle.

questions.s: A light ray strikes a plane mirror making an angle of 30° with the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.e: Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal, not from the surface. The angle of incidence is 90° − 30° = 60°, and the angle of reflection equals it, 60°. Choosing 30° uses the angle with the mirror surface instead of the normal.

questions.s: A plane mirror is turned through 15° about an axis lying in its surface, while the incident ray stays fixed. Through what angle does the reflected ray turn?
questions.e: Turning the mirror by 15° turns the normal by 15°, so the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection each change by 15°. The reflected ray therefore turns by 2 × 15° = 30°. Answering 15° forgets that both angles change.

questions.s: Glass has a refractive index of 3/2. What is the speed of light in this glass? (Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.)
questions.e: n = c/v, so v = c/n = (3.0 × 10⁸)/(3/2) = 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Light is slower in an optically denser medium. 4.5 × 10⁸ m/s comes from multiplying by n instead of dividing, and would exceed c.

questions.s: A ray of light passes from air into a transparent plastic. The angle of incidence is 60° and the angle of refraction is 30°. What is the refractive index of the plastic?
questions.e: Snell's law: n = sin i / sin r = sin 60° / sin 30° = (√3/2)/(1/2) = √3. The tempting answer 2 is the ratio of the angles, 60°/30°, but Snell's law uses the sines of the angles, not the angles themselves. √3/3 is the inverted ratio, which would be less than 1.

questions.s: Light in air strikes the flat surface of a glass block at an angle of incidence of 45°. The refractive index of the glass is √2. What is the angle of refraction?
questions.e: sin r = sin 45° / n = (√2/2)/√2 = 1/2, so r = 30°. The ray bends towards the normal as it enters the denser glass. 15° is the deviation of the ray (45° − 30°), not the angle of refraction, and 60° would mean bending away from the normal.

questions.s: The critical angle for light travelling from a transparent crystal into air is 30°. What is the refractive index of the crystal?
questions.e: At the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the surface, so sin C = 1/n. Then n = 1/sin 30° = 1/(1/2) = 2. The value 1/2 is sin C itself, and √2 would correspond to a critical angle of 45°.

questions.s: Monochromatic light has a wavelength of 600 nm in vacuum. What is its wavelength in water of refractive index 4/3?
questions.e: The frequency does not change on entering water, but the speed falls to c/n, so λ = λ₀/n = 600 nm × 3/4 = 450 nm. 800 nm comes from multiplying by n instead of dividing; 400 nm would need n = 3/2, the value for glass.

questions.s: A beam of monochromatic light passes obliquely from air into water. Which property of the light stays the same?
questions.e: The frequency is set by the source and cannot change at a boundary, otherwise wave crests would pile up or vanish there. The speed falls to c/n and the wavelength falls in the same ratio, and for oblique incidence the ray changes direction. Wavelength is the usual wrong choice: it does change, because λ = v/f and v changes.

questions.s: A swimming pool is filled with water (refractive index 4/3) to a depth of 2.0 m. Seen from directly above, how deep does the pool appear to be?
questions.e: For viewing at near-normal incidence, apparent depth = real depth / n = 2.0 ÷ 4/3 = 1.5 m. The bottom appears raised by 0.5 m, which is the shift, not the apparent depth. 8/3 m comes from multiplying by n, which would make the pool look deeper than it is.

questions.s: Under which conditions can total internal reflection occur?
o: Light goes from glass into air, angle of incidence above the critical angle
Light goes from air into glass, angle of incidence above the critical angle
Light goes from glass into air, angle of incidence below the critical angle
Light goes from air into water, at any angle of incidence
questions.e: Total internal reflection needs two conditions: light must travel from the optically denser medium to the less dense one (glass to air), and the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle. Light going from air into glass bends towards the normal and always has a refracted ray, so it can never be totally reflected. Below the critical angle part of the light is still refracted out.

questions.s: A layer of liquid with refractive index √2 lies on a flat block of glass with refractive index 2. What is the critical angle for light travelling inside the glass towards the glass–liquid boundary?
questions.e: At the critical angle, n_glass sin C = n_liquid sin 90°, so sin C = √2/2 and C = 45°. The value 30° is the critical angle for a glass–air boundary (sin C = 1/2), which ignores the liquid. 60° would need sin C = √3/2.

questions.s: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a thin converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Where is the image formed, and what kind of image is it?
questions.e: With 1/u + 1/v = 1/f (real distances positive): 1/v = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30, so v = +30 cm, a real image on the other side of the lens. Because the object is between f and 2f, the image is real, inverted and enlarged. 6 cm comes from adding 1/10 + 1/15 instead of subtracting.

questions.s: An object 1.5 cm tall stands 30 cm from a thin converging lens of focal length 20 cm. How tall is the image?
questions.e: 1/v = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60, so v = 60 cm. Magnification m = v/u = 60/30 = 2, so the image is 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 cm tall (and inverted). 0.75 cm uses u/v instead of v/u; 1.0 cm uses f/u, which is not the magnification.

questions.s: What is the power of a thin converging lens of focal length 25 cm?
questions.e: Power P = 1/f with f in metres: P = 1/0.25 m = +4 D (dioptres). +0.04 D comes from using f = 25 in centimetres, and +0.25 D is the focal length in metres rather than its reciprocal.

questions.s: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror whose radius of curvature is 20 cm. Where is the image?
o: 7.5 cm in front of the mirror
15 cm in front of the mirror
60 cm in front of the mirror
questions.e: f = R/2 = 10 cm. Then 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30, so v = 15 cm, a real image in front of the mirror. 60 cm comes from using R = 20 cm as the focal length, and 7.5 cm from adding the reciprocals.

questions.s: A convex mirror forms an image of a real object. Which description of the image is always correct?
questions.e: A convex mirror spreads reflected rays out, so they only appear to come from a point behind the mirror: the image is virtual and upright. It always lies between the mirror and the focal point, so it is smaller than the object. This is why convex mirrors give a wide field of view in shops and on roads.

questions.s: When white light passes through a glass prism, violet light is deviated more than red light. Which statement explains this?
o: Glass has a larger refractive index for violet light than for red
Glass has a larger refractive index for red light than for violet
Glass slows red and violet light down by exactly the same amount
Glass absorbs red light much more strongly than violet light
questions.e: This is dispersion: the refractive index of glass depends on frequency and is larger for violet than for red. A larger n means more bending at each face, so violet is deviated most. If the indices were equal (same slowing), all colours would bend together and no spectrum would form.

questions.s: In a double-slit experiment the slit separation is 0.20 mm, the screen is 1.0 m from the slits and the light has a wavelength of 600 nm. What is the distance between adjacent bright fringes?
questions.e: Δx = Lλ/d = (1.0 × 6.0 × 10⁻⁷)/(2.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m = 3.0 mm. 1.5 mm is the distance from a bright fringe to the next dark fringe, and 30 mm comes from a power-of-ten slip when converting 0.20 mm to metres.

questions.s: In a double-slit experiment the slit separation is halved and the distance to the screen is doubled, with the same light. What happens to the fringe spacing?
o: It becomes four times as large
questions.e: Fringe spacing Δx = Lλ/d. Doubling L doubles Δx, and halving d doubles it again, so Δx becomes 2 × 2 = 4 times as large. Thinking the two changes cancel gives 'stays the same', but both changes act in the same direction.

questions.s: In a double-slit experiment with light of wavelength 600 nm, the path difference from the two slits to a point P on the screen is 1.5 μm. Which description of P is correct?
o: A bright fringe, the second from the centre
A dark fringe, the third from the centre
A bright fringe, the third from the centre
A dark fringe, the second from the centre
questions.e: Path difference / λ = 1.5 μm / 0.60 μm = 2.5, an odd number of half-wavelengths, so P is dark. Dark fringes occur at 0.5λ, 1.5λ, 2.5λ, …, so 2.5λ is the third dark fringe from the centre. Answering 'second' counts 2.5 as the second because of the 2, but 0.5λ is already the first dark fringe.

questions.s: In a double-slit experiment, red light is replaced by blue light while everything else stays the same. What happens to the interference fringes?
questions.e: Fringe spacing Δx = Lλ/d is proportional to wavelength. Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red light, so the fringes move closer together. They do not disappear, because light from the two slits is still coherent.

questions.s: Which observation shows that light is a transverse wave?
questions.e: Only transverse waves can be polarised, because only they have a direction of vibration perpendicular to the direction of travel that a filter can select. Refraction, interference and diffraction happen to all waves, including longitudinal sound waves, so they show that light is a wave but not that it is transverse.

questions.s: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through a polariser and then through an analyser whose transmission axis is at 60° to that of the polariser. What is the intensity of the light leaving the analyser?
questions.e: The first polariser passes half of unpolarised light: I₀/2. Malus's law then gives I = (I₀/2)cos² 60° = (I₀/2)(1/4) = I₀/8. I₀/4 comes from using cos 60° without squaring, and 3I₀/8 from using sin² 60° instead of cos² 60°.

questions.s: A plane wave passes through a narrow slit. When is diffraction most noticeable?
o: When the slit width is far larger than the wavelength
When the slit width is close to the wavelength
When the wave has a very large amplitude
When the wave has been plane polarised first
questions.e: Diffraction spreading is significant when the slit width is comparable to (or smaller than) the wavelength. A slit much wider than the wavelength lets the wave pass almost straight through with sharp shadows. Amplitude and polarisation do not control how much a wave spreads.

questions.s: A glass prism has an apex angle of 30° and refractive index √2. A ray of light enters the first face along the normal. What is the total angle of deviation of the ray after it leaves the second face?
questions.e: The ray enters undeviated, so it meets the second face at an angle of incidence equal to the apex angle, 30° (below the critical angle of 45°). There sin r = √2 × sin 30° = √2/2, so it leaves at 45° to the normal. The deviation is 45° − 30° = 15°. 45° is the angle of emergence, not the deviation.

questions.s: Ahmed stands 2.0 m in front of a large plane mirror. He walks 0.5 m straight towards the mirror. What is the distance between Ahmed and his image now?
questions.e: He is now 2.0 − 0.5 = 1.5 m from the mirror, and a plane mirror forms the image the same distance behind it, 1.5 m. The distance between him and the image is 1.5 + 1.5 = 3.0 m. 1.5 m is only his distance to the mirror, and 4.0 m was the separation before he moved.

questions.s: Amina is 1.80 m tall. What is the minimum height of a vertical plane mirror in which she can see her whole body at once, from head to feet?
questions.e: Rays from her feet and from the top of her head reflect into her eyes at points halfway (in height) between her eyes and each of those parts. So the mirror needs only half her height: 1.80/2 = 0.90 m, whatever her distance from the mirror. 1.80 m assumes the mirror must be as tall as the person.

questions.s: Light travels inside glass of refractive index √3 and meets the glass–air boundary at an angle of incidence of 30°. At what angle to the normal does the light leave the glass?
questions.e: Snell's law: √3 sin 30° = 1 × sin r, so sin r = √3/2 and r = 60°. The light bends away from the normal as it enters the less dense air. 90° would only occur at the critical angle (sin C = 1/√3), which is larger than 30°, so the ray does escape.

questions.s: Light travels in water (refractive index 4/3) towards the water–air surface. What is the sine of the critical angle?
questions.e: sin C = n_air/n_water = 1/(4/3) = 3/4. A sine can never exceed 1, so 4/3 is impossible; it is the refractive index itself. 2/3 would be the value for glass of refractive index 3/2.

questions.s: A ray of light in air strikes a flat glass surface at an angle of incidence of 60°. The glass has refractive index √3. Part of the light is reflected and part is refracted. What is the angle between the reflected ray and the refracted ray?
questions.e: The reflected ray makes 60° with the normal. For the refracted ray, sin r = sin 60°/√3 = 1/2, so r = 30°. The reflected ray is 90° − 60° = 30° above the surface and the refracted ray is 90° − 30° = 60° below it, so the angle between them is 30° + 60° = 90°. 120° comes from 180° − 60°, which ignores the bending of the refracted ray.

questions.s: A small mark on a sheet of paper is covered by a glass block 6.0 cm thick with refractive index 3/2. Viewed from directly above, how far does the mark appear to be raised?
questions.e: Apparent depth = real depth/n = 6.0/1.5 = 4.0 cm below the top surface. The mark therefore appears raised by 6.0 − 4.0 = 2.0 cm. 4.0 cm is the apparent depth, not the shift; 9.0 cm comes from multiplying by n.

questions.s: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a thin diverging lens of focal length 15 cm. Where is the image, and what kind is it?
questions.e: For a diverging lens f = −15 cm. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/15 − 1/30 = −3/30, so v = −10 cm: a virtual image 10 cm from the lens on the same side as the object. A diverging lens always gives a virtual, upright, diminished image of a real object. 30 cm comes from treating the lens as converging.

questions.s: To use a converging lens as a magnifying glass, where must the object be placed?
o: Between the lens and its focal point
Between f and 2f from the lens
questions.e: With the object inside the focal length, the rays leaving the lens diverge and appear to come from a larger, upright, virtual image on the same side. Between f and 2f the lens forms a real, inverted image, as in a projector. At the focal point the rays leave parallel and no image forms at a finite distance.

questions.s: An object and a screen are fixed 90 cm apart. A thin converging lens of focal length 20 cm is moved between them. There are two lens positions that give a sharp image on the screen. How far apart are these two positions?
questions.e: We need u + v = 90 and 1/u + 1/v = 1/20, so (u + v)/(uv) = 1/20 and uv = 1800. u and v are the roots of x² − 90x + 1800 = 0, giving 30 cm and 60 cm. The lens can sit 30 cm or 60 cm from the object, so the positions are 60 − 30 = 30 cm apart. 45 cm is simply half of 90 cm and has no physical meaning here.

questions.s: A concave mirror of focal length 15 cm forms an upright image that is 3 times the size of the object. How far is the object from the mirror?
questions.e: An upright image from a concave mirror is virtual, so v = −3u. Then 1/u − 1/(3u) = 1/15, giving 2/(3u) = 1/15 and u = 10 cm. Check: 1/v = 1/15 − 1/10 = −1/30, v = −30 cm, m = 30/10 = 3. 20 cm gives a real, inverted image three times the size, which is not upright.

questions.s: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 40 cm. What is its focal length?
questions.e: For a spherical mirror the focal point lies halfway between the pole and the centre of curvature, so f = R/2 = 40/2 = 20 cm. 80 cm comes from doubling instead of halving, and 40 cm confuses the radius with the focal length.

questions.s: White light enters a glass prism. Which colour of light travels most slowly inside the glass?
questions.e: Glass has its largest refractive index for violet light, and v = c/n, so violet travels most slowly. This is also why violet is deviated most by a prism. Red has the smallest refractive index and travels fastest in glass.

questions.s: Red light and violet light travel in the same glass towards a glass–air boundary. Which colour has the larger critical angle, and why?
o: Red, because glass has a smaller refractive index for red light
Violet, because glass has a smaller refractive index for violet light
Red, because red light has a higher frequency than violet light
Violet, because violet light travels faster in glass than red light
questions.e: sin C = 1/n, so a smaller refractive index gives a larger critical angle. Glass has a smaller refractive index for red light than for violet light, so red has the larger critical angle. Red has the lower frequency, and violet is the slower colour in glass, so the other reasons are false.

questions.s: In a double-slit experiment the slits are 0.25 mm apart and the screen is 1.0 m away. Adjacent bright fringes are 2.4 mm apart. What is the wavelength of the light?
questions.e: λ = dΔx/L = (2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m)(2.4 × 10⁻³ m)/1.0 m = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m = 600 nm, which is visible orange light. 300 nm results from taking half the fringe spacing (bright to dark), and 60 nm or 6000 nm come from power-of-ten slips with millimetres.

questions.s: In a double-slit experiment the slit separation is 0.40 mm and the screen is 1.2 m away. The distance from the central bright fringe to the fourth bright fringe on one side is 6.0 mm. What is the wavelength?
questions.e: From the centre to the fourth bright fringe there are 4 fringe spacings, so Δx = 6.0/4 = 1.5 mm. λ = dΔx/L = (4.0 × 10⁻⁴)(1.5 × 10⁻³)/1.2 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm. Dividing by 5 (counting fringes instead of gaps) gives 400 nm, and using the whole 6.0 mm gives 2000 nm.

questions.s: A double-slit experiment in air gives a fringe spacing of 1.2 mm. The whole apparatus is then immersed in water of refractive index 4/3, with nothing else changed. What is the new fringe spacing?
questions.e: In water the wavelength becomes λ/n, and Δx = Lλ/d is proportional to the wavelength, so Δx = 1.2 × 3/4 = 0.9 mm. 1.6 mm comes from multiplying by n, and 0.3 mm is the decrease in spacing, not the new spacing.

questions.s: Monochromatic light passes through a single narrow slit onto a screen. The slit is then made narrower. What happens to the central bright band?
questions.e: The angular half-width of the central maximum is given by sin θ = λ/a, where a is the slit width. A smaller a gives a larger angle, so the central band spreads out and becomes wider (and dimmer). Expecting a narrower band treats the light like a beam passing straight through, ignoring diffraction.

questions.s: A diffraction grating has 1000 lines per millimetre. Light at normal incidence produces its first-order maximum at 30° from the straight-through direction. What is the wavelength?
questions.e: The line spacing is d = 1 mm/1000 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. The grating equation d sin θ = mλ with m = 1 gives λ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 1/2 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm. 1000 nm is d itself (forgetting sin 30°), and 2000 nm comes from dividing by sin 30° instead of multiplying.

questions.s: Two ideal polarising filters are crossed (axes at 90°), so no light gets through. A third filter is placed between them with its axis at 45° to each. Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ falls on the first filter. What intensity emerges from the last filter?
questions.e: After the first filter: I₀/2. After the middle filter at 45°: (I₀/2)cos² 45° = I₀/4. After the last filter, also at 45° to the middle one: (I₀/4)cos² 45° = I₀/8. Zero would be correct without the middle filter, but it rotates the polarisation so some light passes the last one.

questions.s: Polarising sunglasses reduce the glare from a calm lake. This works because light reflected from the water surface is
questions.e: Reflection from a horizontal surface such as water partly polarises the light, with its vibrations mainly parallel to the surface, i.e. horizontal. Polarising sunglasses have vertical transmission axes, so they block much of this horizontally polarised glare. If the reflected light were unpolarised, the glasses would only halve it like any other light.

questions.s: Unpolarised light in air falls on a flat glass surface of refractive index √3. At what angle of incidence is the reflected light completely plane polarised?
questions.e: Complete polarisation of the reflected light happens when the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular (Brewster's angle), which gives tan θ = n. tan θ = √3, so θ = 60°; the refracted ray is then at 30° and 60° + 30° = 90°. 30° would be the angle of refraction, not of incidence.

questions.s: Two thin lenses with powers +5 D and −3 D are placed in contact. What is the focal length of the combination?
questions.e: Powers of thin lenses in contact add: P = +5 + (−3) = +2 D. Then f = 1/P = 0.50 m = 50 cm, a converging combination. 12.5 cm comes from adding the magnitudes (8 D), and 20 cm is the focal length of the +5 D lens alone.

questions.s: Light travelling in glass of refractive index 3/2 strikes the glass–air boundary at an angle of incidence of 45°. What happens to the light?
o: It refracts into the air at about 28°
It refracts along the surface at 90°
It passes into the air without bending
questions.e: sin C = 1/n = 2/3 ≈ 0.67, while sin 45° ≈ 0.71 is larger, so 45° exceeds the critical angle and the light is totally internally reflected. Snell's law would need sin r = 1.5 × 0.71 ≈ 1.06, which is impossible. The 28° value comes from dividing by n, as if light were entering the glass.

questions.s: Light in air strikes a horizontal layer of water (refractive index 4/3) at an angle of incidence of 60°. Below the water is a parallel-sided layer of glass with refractive index √3. What is the angle of refraction in the glass?
questions.e: At each parallel boundary n sin θ is unchanged, so n_air sin 60° = n_glass sin θ_glass, and the water layer drops out. sin θ = (√3/2)/√3 = 1/2, so θ = 30°. About 40° is the angle in the water (sin θ = 3√3/8 ≈ 0.65), not in the glass.

questions.s: A transparent medium has a refractive index of 2. Compared with the same light in vacuum, the light in the medium has
o: half the speed and half the wavelength
half the speed and the same wavelength
double the speed and half the wavelength
the same speed and half the wavelength
questions.e: v = c/n = c/2, and since the frequency is unchanged, λ = v/f is also halved. Keeping the same wavelength would require the frequency to halve, but frequency never changes at a boundary. Light can never travel faster than c, so 'double the speed' is impossible.

questions.s: A light ray passes through an equilateral glass prism (apex angle 60°) of refractive index √2 at minimum deviation, so it travels inside the prism parallel to the base. What is the angle of minimum deviation?
questions.e: At minimum deviation the path is symmetric, so the refraction angle at each face is A/2 = 30°. Then sin i = √2 × sin 30° = √2/2, so i = 45°. The deviation is D = 2i − A = 90° − 60° = 30°. 45° is the angle of incidence, not the deviation.

questions.s: An object is placed 24 cm from a thin converging lens of focal length 12 cm. Which describes the image?
o: Virtual, upright and the same size
Real, inverted and the same size
Real, inverted and twice the size
Real, upright and half the size
questions.e: The object is at 2f, so 1/v = 1/12 − 1/24 = 1/24 and v = 24 cm, also at 2f on the other side. The magnification is v/u = 1, so the image is real, inverted and the same size. A converging lens gives a virtual image only when the object is inside f.

questions.s: An object is placed 10 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Where is the image, and is it upright or inverted?
o: 20 cm in front of the mirror, inverted
6.7 cm in front of the mirror, inverted
questions.e: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/20 − 1/10 = −1/20, so v = −20 cm: a virtual image 20 cm behind the mirror. It is upright and magnified, m = 20/10 = 2, as in a shaving mirror. 10 cm behind is what a plane mirror would give, and 6.7 cm comes from adding the reciprocals.

questions.s: Light travels at 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a certain liquid. What is the refractive index of the liquid? (Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.)
questions.e: n = c/v = (3.0 × 10⁸)/(2.0 × 10⁸) = 1.5. 0.67 is v/c, the inverted ratio, and a refractive index below 1 would mean light travels faster than in vacuum. 6.0 comes from multiplying the speeds.

questions.s: Light travels from medium A (refractive index √3) into medium B (refractive index √2). The angle of incidence at the boundary is 45°. What is the angle of refraction in B?
questions.e: n_A sin i = n_B sin r: √3 × (√2/2) = √2 sin r, so sin r = √3/2 and r = 60°. The light bends away from the normal because B is less dense optically. 90° would occur only at the critical angle (sin C = √2/√3 ≈ 0.82), which is larger than 45°, so the ray does refract; 30° comes from swapping the two indices.

questions.s: Three transparent materials X, Y and Z have critical angles (to air) of 60°, 45° and 30° respectively. In which material does light travel fastest?
o: The speed is the same in all three
questions.e: sin C = 1/n, so the largest critical angle means the smallest refractive index. Since v = c/n, the smallest n gives the largest speed: X, with C = 60°. Choosing Z links a small critical angle to high speed, which is the reverse of the true relation.

questions.s: A small lamp lies on the flat bottom of a tank filled to a depth of 2 m with a liquid of refractive index √2. Seen from above, light leaves the surface only through a circle directly above the lamp. What is the radius of this circle?
questions.e: Light escapes only where it meets the surface at less than the critical angle: sin C = 1/√2, so C = 45°. The edge of the circle is where the ray hits at exactly 45°, so radius = depth × tan 45° = 2 × 1 = 2 m. 4 m is the diameter of the circle, and 2√2 m is the slant length of the edge ray.

questions.s: During a double-slit experiment with monochromatic light, one of the two slits is covered. What is now seen on the screen?
o: No light at all on the screen
Equally spaced fringes twice as wide
questions.e: Two-slit interference needs light from both slits to overlap. With one slit covered, only the diffraction of that single slit remains: a wide, bright central band with weaker side bands. The 'same fringes but dimmer' answer forgets that the equally spaced fringes come from interference between the two slits.

questions.s: In a double-slit experiment the slit separation is 0.50 mm, the screen is 1.5 m away and the wavelength is 500 nm. How far is the third bright fringe from the central bright fringe?
questions.e: Fringe spacing Δx = Lλ/d = (1.5 × 5.0 × 10⁻⁷)/(5.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.5 × 10⁻³ m = 1.5 mm. The third bright fringe is 3 spacings from the centre: 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 mm. 3.75 mm is the position of the third dark fringe (2.5 spacings), and 1.5 mm is only one spacing.

questions.s: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ falls on a single ideal polarising filter. What is the intensity of the light that passes through?
questions.e: Unpolarised light vibrates equally in all directions perpendicular to its path. An ideal polariser passes only the component along its axis, and averaging cos² θ over all directions gives 1/2, so I₀/2 passes. Zero intensity needs two crossed polarisers, not one.

questions.s: A light ray is reflected by a plane mirror, and the reflected ray is perpendicular to the incident ray. What is the angle of incidence?
questions.e: The angle between the incident and reflected rays equals i + r = 2i. If this is 90°, then i = 45°. 90° is the angle between the two rays, not the angle of incidence measured from the normal.

questions.s: Light travels at 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s in water. What is the refractive index of water? (Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.)
questions.e: n = c/v = 3.0/2.25 = 4/3. 3/4 is v/c, the inverted ratio, and any value below 1 is impossible for a material. 3/2 is the typical index of glass, not water.

questions.s: A ray passes from air into water of refractive index 4/3. The sine of the angle of refraction is 0.6. What is the angle of incidence? (Take sin 37° = 0.6 and sin 53° = 0.8.)
questions.e: sin i = n sin r = (4/3)(0.6) = 0.8, so i = 53°. Entering water the ray bends towards the normal, so the angle in air must be larger than the angle in water. 37° ignores refraction, and 27° comes from dividing by n instead of multiplying.

questions.s: A crystal has a refractive index of 2. What is the critical angle for light going from the crystal into air?
questions.e: sin C = 1/n = 1/2, so C = 30°. 60° is the angle whose cosine is 1/2, a common slip. 45° would need n = √2.

questions.s: Looking straight down into water of refractive index 4/3, Kwame sees a coin that appears to be 9 cm below the surface. How deep is the coin really?
questions.e: Apparent depth = real depth/n, so real depth = n × apparent depth = 4/3 × 9 = 12 cm. Objects under water look shallower than they are. 6.75 cm comes from dividing by n again, and 13.5 cm uses n = 3/2 for glass.

questions.s: An object is placed 5 cm from a thin converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Where is the image, and what kind is it?
questions.e: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/10 − 1/5 = −1/10, so v = −10 cm: a virtual image on the same side as the object. It is upright and magnified twice (10/5 = 2), as in a magnifying glass. 10/3 cm comes from adding the reciprocals.

questions.s: An optician prescribes a lens of power −2.5 D. What kind of lens is it, and what is its focal length?
questions.e: A negative power means a diverging lens. f = 1/P = 1/(−2.5) m = −0.40 m, so its focal length is 40 cm. Answers with 2.5 m take the power value as the focal length instead of its reciprocal.

questions.s: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 20 cm. Where is the image?
o: 10 cm in front of the mirror
questions.e: For a convex mirror f = −20 cm. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/20 − 1/20 = −1/10, so v = −10 cm: a virtual image 10 cm behind the mirror, upright and half the size. 'At infinity' would be the result for a concave mirror with the object at its focus.

questions.s: What is the name of the effect in which a glass prism splits white light into a spectrum of colours?
questions.e: Dispersion is the spreading of white light into colours because the refractive index of glass depends on the colour (frequency) of the light. Diffraction and interference can also produce colours, but a prism works by refraction with different indices for each colour.

questions.s: Light of wavelength 400 nm passes through two slits 0.30 mm apart. The screen is 1.5 m away. What is the spacing between adjacent bright fringes?
questions.e: Δx = Lλ/d = (1.5 × 4.0 × 10⁻⁷)/(3.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.0 × 10⁻³ m = 2.0 mm. 1.0 mm is the distance from a bright fringe to the next dark one, and 0.2 mm or 20 mm come from power-of-ten slips in converting units.

questions.s: Two coherent light sources vibrate in phase. At which points do they produce dark fringes (destructive interference)?
o: Where the path difference is zero
Where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths
Where the path difference is exactly one wavelength
Where the path difference is an odd number of half-wavelengths
questions.e: Destructive interference needs the waves to arrive half a cycle out of step, so the path difference must be λ/2, 3λ/2, 5λ/2, …, an odd number of half-wavelengths. A path difference of zero or a whole number of wavelengths brings crest on crest, giving bright fringes.

questions.s: Which condition must two light sources meet to produce a stable interference pattern?
o: The same frequency and a constant phase difference
The same amplitude but different frequencies
The same brightness and any frequencies at all
Different frequencies but a constant phase difference
questions.e: Stable fringes need coherent sources: the same frequency and a phase difference that does not change with time. With different frequencies the phase difference changes continuously, so the fringes move too fast to see. Equal amplitude only improves the contrast; it is not required.

questions.s: Plane-polarised light of intensity I₀ passes through a polarising filter whose axis is at 30° to the plane of polarisation. What is the transmitted intensity?
