questions.e: Malus's law: I = I₀cos² 30° = I₀ × (√3/2)² = 3I₀/4. √3I₀/2 forgets to square the cosine, and I₀/4 uses sin² 30° instead of cos² 30°. The light is already polarised, so there is no extra factor of 1/2.

questions.s: A glass prism has a cross-section that is a right-angled isosceles triangle. Light enters one of the short faces along the normal and meets the long face (hypotenuse) inside the glass. What is the least refractive index the glass needs for the light to be totally internally reflected there?
questions.e: The light enters undeviated and meets the hypotenuse at an angle of incidence of 45°. Total internal reflection needs 45° ≥ C, i.e. sin C = 1/n ≤ sin 45° = √2/2, so n ≥ √2. Ordinary glass (n ≈ 1.5) meets this, which is why such prisms are used as reflectors in binoculars. n = 2 works but is not the least value.

questions.s: Light of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz and wavelength 600 nm in vacuum enters glass of refractive index 3/2. What is its frequency in the glass?
questions.e: Frequency is fixed by the source and does not change on entering a new medium, so it stays 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. It is the speed and wavelength that fall by the factor n: the wavelength in glass is 400 nm. 3.3 × 10¹⁴ Hz wrongly divides the frequency by n.

questions.s: Li Wei walks straight towards a plane mirror at 1 m/s. At what speed does his image approach him?
questions.e: The image is always as far behind the mirror as Li Wei is in front. If his distance to the mirror falls by 1 m each second, the image's distance also falls by 1 m each second, so the gap between them shrinks by 2 m each second. 1 m/s is the image's speed relative to the mirror, not relative to him.

questions.s: Fatima can hear a radio playing in the next room through an open door but cannot see it. Which reason, based on diffraction, explains this?
o: Sound waves travel much more slowly than light
Sound wavelengths are close to door widths
Light waves are transverse, sound waves are not
Light has a much larger amplitude than sound
questions.e: Waves diffract strongly through a gap comparable in size to their wavelength. Audible sound has wavelengths from centimetres to metres, similar to a door, so it spreads round the corner; light's wavelength (about 500 nm) is far smaller, so it travels almost straight. Speed and polarisation do not decide how much a wave diffracts.

questions.s: A thin converging lens forms a sharp real image on a screen. The image is 3 times the size of the object, and the object is 80 cm from the screen. What is the focal length of the lens?
questions.e: Magnification 3 means v = 3u, and u + v = 80 cm, so u = 20 cm and v = 60 cm. Then 1/f = 1/20 + 1/60 = 4/60, so f = 15 cm. 20 cm is the object distance, not the focal length, and 40 cm is just half of 80 cm.

questions.s: Sunlight is reflected from a calm water surface (refractive index 4/3). At what angle of incidence is the reflected light completely plane polarised? (Take tan 53° = 4/3 and sin 49° ≈ 3/4.)
questions.e: Full polarisation by reflection occurs at Brewster's angle, where tan θ = n = 4/3, so θ = 53°. At this angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular (the refracted ray is at 37°). 49° is the critical angle for water (sin C = 3/4), which is a different condition and applies only to light inside the water.

questions.s: Red and violet light travel through the same piece of glass. Their speeds in the glass are v(red) and v(violet), and the refractive indices are n(red) and n(violet). Which statement is correct?
questions.e: Glass has a smaller refractive index for red light than for violet, and since v = c/n, red light travels faster. So v(red) > v(violet) and n(red) < n(violet). The last option is impossible because a larger n always means a smaller speed.

questions.s: What is the energy of a photon of light of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz? Take h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
questions.e: E = hν = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5.0 × 10¹⁴ = 33 × 10⁻²⁰ = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Dividing h by ν gives 1.3 × 10⁻⁴⁸ J, and 3.3 × 10⁻²⁰ J is a slip when tidying 33 × 10⁻²⁰.

questions.s: What is the energy of one photon of ultraviolet light of wavelength 300 nm? Take h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
questions.e: E = hc/λ = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸/(3.0 × 10⁻⁷) = 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Putting λ = 300 m (forgetting 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m) gives 6.6 × 10⁻²⁸ J; 2.0 × 10⁻²⁵ J is hc alone.

questions.s: A metal has a work function of 2.3 eV. Photons of energy 3.5 eV fall on it. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons?
questions.e: Einstein's photoelectric equation: E_k,max = hν − W = 3.5 − 2.3 = 1.2 eV. Adding the two (5.8 eV) wrongly treats the work function as extra energy given to the electron.

questions.s: Light whose photons each carry 4.5 eV falls on a metal with work function 2.5 eV. What is the stopping (cut-off) voltage for the photoelectrons?
questions.e: E_k,max = 4.5 − 2.5 = 2.0 eV, and eU_c = E_k,max, so U_c = 2.0 V. 1.8 V divides the energies instead of subtracting them.

questions.s: Light above the threshold frequency shines on a metal surface. Its intensity is increased while its frequency is kept the same. What happens?
o: The maximum kinetic energy of each emitted photoelectron increases
The threshold frequency of the metal decreases
The number of photoelectrons emitted per second increases
questions.e: Higher intensity at the same frequency means more photons per second, each with the same energy hν, so more electrons are emitted per second (larger saturation current). The maximum kinetic energy, and therefore the stopping voltage, depends only on frequency, and the threshold frequency is a property of the metal.

questions.s: Light below the threshold frequency of a metal shines on it, and its intensity is then greatly increased. What happens?
o: Electrons are emitted after a short delay
Electrons are emitted with smaller kinetic energy
No electrons are emitted at all
Electrons are emitted once the light is bright enough
questions.e: Each electron absorbs one photon, and below the threshold frequency hν is less than the work function, so no single photon can free an electron however many photons arrive. This is what the wave theory could not explain.

questions.s: The work function of a metal is 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is its threshold frequency? Take h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
questions.e: At threshold hν₀ = W, so ν₀ = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹/6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ Hz is h/W, the ratio upside down, and 2.2 × 10⁻⁵² Hz multiplies them.

questions.s: For two different metals, graphs of the maximum kinetic energy E_k of photoelectrons against light frequency ν are drawn on the same axes. Which statement is correct?
o: The two lines have different slopes, each equal to the work function
The two lines are parallel, each with slope equal to h
Both lines pass through the origin of the graph
The line for the metal with larger work function is steeper
questions.e: E_k = hν − W is a straight line of slope h for every metal, so the lines are parallel. They cut the ν-axis at the threshold frequency W/h, not at the origin, and the metal with the larger work function is shifted to higher frequency, not made steeper.

questions.s: When photons of energy 3.0 eV fall on a metal, the stopping voltage is 1.0 V. What is the stopping voltage when photons of energy 5.0 eV fall on the same metal?
questions.e: From the first case W = 3.0 − 1.0 = 2.0 eV. Then E_k,max = 5.0 − 2.0 = 3.0 eV, so U_c = 3.0 V. 1.7 V assumes the stopping voltage is proportional to the photon energy, which ignores the work function.

questions.s: An electron has momentum 3.3 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s. What is its de Broglie wavelength? Take h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
questions.e: λ = h/p = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴/3.3 × 10⁻²⁴ = 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, about the size of an atom, which is why electrons diffract from crystals. 5.0 × 10⁹ m is p/h, the ratio inverted.

questions.s: A beam of electrons passing through a thin crystal produces a diffraction pattern of rings. What does this experiment demonstrate?
o: Atoms have a small dense nucleus
questions.e: Diffraction is a wave effect, so the ring pattern shows that electrons, usually thought of as particles, have a wave nature, as de Broglie predicted. It says nothing about the charge of the electron or about the photon nature of light.

questions.s: Which property of light does the photoelectric effect most directly demonstrate?
questions.e: The photoelectric effect is explained by light arriving in packets (photons) of energy hν, each absorbed by one electron, which shows the particle nature of light. Being transverse and being polarisable are wave properties shown by polarisation experiments.

questions.s: A proton and an electron have the same kinetic energy (non-relativistic). Which has the shorter de Broglie wavelength, and why?
o: The electron, because it moves faster
The proton, because it has the larger momentum
Neither: equal kinetic energy gives equal wavelength
The electron, because it has the smaller mass
questions.e: p = √(2mE_k), so with equal E_k the heavier proton has the larger momentum, and λ = h/p is shorter for the proton. The electron does move faster, but wavelength depends on momentum, not speed alone.

questions.s: A particle has de Broglie wavelength λ. Its kinetic energy is increased to 4 times its original value (non-relativistic). What is its new de Broglie wavelength?
questions.e: p = √(2mE_k), so 4 times the kinetic energy gives 2 times the momentum, and λ = h/p halves to λ/2. λ/4 forgets that momentum grows only with the square root of kinetic energy.

questions.s: The energy levels of hydrogen are E_n = −13.6/n² eV. What photon energy is emitted when an electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2?
questions.e: E₃ = −13.6/9 = −1.51 eV and E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.40 eV, so the photon carries −1.51 − (−3.40) = 1.89 eV (the red Balmer line). 1.51 eV is just |E₃|, and 12.09 eV is the 3 → 1 transition.

questions.s: The energy levels of hydrogen are E_n = −13.6/n² eV. What minimum energy is needed to ionise a hydrogen atom whose electron is in the n = 2 level?
questions.e: Ionisation means raising the electron to E = 0. From E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV this needs 3.4 eV. 13.6 eV is the ionisation energy from the ground state, and 6.8 eV divides by n instead of n².

questions.s: A large number of hydrogen atoms are excited to the n = 4 level. As they return to the ground state, at most how many different spectral lines can be emitted?
questions.e: Any pair of levels among n = 1, 2, 3, 4 gives a line: the number of pairs is 4 × 3/2 = 6. Answering 3 counts only the direct step-by-step jumps 4 → 3 → 2 → 1.

questions.s: Hydrogen levels are E₁ = −13.6 eV, E₂ = −3.4 eV, E₃ = −1.51 eV and E₄ = −0.85 eV. A hydrogen atom is in its ground state. A photon of which energy can it absorb?
questions.e: A photon below the ionisation energy is absorbed only if its energy exactly equals a level difference from n = 1: 10.2 eV (to n = 2), 12.09 eV, 12.75 eV and so on. 10.2 eV matches; 11.0 eV and 12.5 eV fall between levels, and 3.4 eV is the gap from n = 2 to ionisation, not from the ground state.

questions.s: Hydrogen atoms are in the n = 3 level, where E_n = −13.6/n² eV. What is the largest photon energy they can emit?
questions.e: The largest energy is from the largest drop, n = 3 → 1: −1.51 − (−13.6) = 12.09 eV. 13.6 eV would need the electron to come from E = 0, and 1.89 eV is the smallest line (3 → 2).

questions.s: In the Bohr model, the electron of a hydrogen atom jumps from the n = 2 orbit to the n = 4 orbit. Which statement is correct?
o: It emits a photon, and its kinetic energy increases
It absorbs a photon, and its kinetic energy increases
It absorbs a photon, and its kinetic energy decreases
It emits a photon, and its orbit radius increases
questions.e: Moving to a higher level raises the total energy, so the atom must absorb a photon. In a larger orbit the Coulomb force is weaker and the electron moves more slowly, so its kinetic energy decreases while the potential energy increases by more.

questions.s: Hot hydrogen gas emits light only at certain sharp wavelengths (a line spectrum). What does this show?
o: Electrons in atoms can orbit at any radius
Atoms have only certain allowed energy levels
Light is a wave with a continuous range of frequencies
questions.e: Each line comes from a jump between two fixed energy levels, giving a photon of exactly hν = E_m − E_n. If any orbit or energy were allowed, the spectrum would be continuous, not a set of lines.

questions.s: How many protons and neutrons are in a nucleus of ²³⁵₉₂U?
questions.e: The lower number is the proton number Z = 92 and the upper number is the mass number A = 235, so N = A − Z = 143 neutrons. 235 is the total number of nucleons, not the number of neutrons.

questions.s: Which description fits two isotopes of the same element?
o: Same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons
Same number of neutrons, different numbers of protons
Same mass number, different numbers of protons
Same number of nucleons, different numbers of electrons
questions.e: An element is fixed by its proton number, so isotopes share Z but differ in neutron number and hence in mass number, for example ¹²C and ¹⁴C. Nuclei with the same mass number but different Z are different elements.

questions.s: Which statement about nuclear radiations is correct?
o: α particles are fast electrons that can penetrate several mm of aluminium
γ rays are helium nuclei and are stopped by a sheet of paper
β particles are the most strongly ionising of the three
α particles are helium nuclei and are stopped by a sheet of paper
questions.e: α particles are ⁴₂He nuclei: heavily charged and slow, they ionise most strongly and are stopped by paper. β particles are fast electrons stopped by a few mm of aluminium, and γ rays are electromagnetic waves, the most penetrating and least ionising.

questions.s: The nucleus ²³⁴₉₀Th undergoes β⁻ decay. What nucleus is formed?
questions.e: In β⁻ decay a neutron changes into a proton and emits an electron (⁰₋₁e). The mass number stays 234 and the proton number rises by 1 to 91, giving ²³⁴₉₁Pa. Lowering Z to 89 is the result for positron emission.

questions.s: Radium-226 (²²⁶₈₈Ra) undergoes α decay. Which nucleus is produced?
questions.e: An α particle is ⁴₂He, so A falls by 4 to 222 and Z falls by 2 to 86, which is radon: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He. Raising Z to 90 adds the α particle's charge instead of removing it.

questions.s: Uranium-238 (²³⁸₉₂U) decays through a series of α and β⁻ decays to the stable lead isotope ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb. How many α decays and how many β⁻ decays occur?
questions.e: Only α decay changes the mass number: (238 − 206)/4 = 8 α decays. These lower Z by 16, to 76, but the final Z is 82, so 6 β⁻ decays (each +1) are needed. 8 α and 10 β forgets that β⁻ decay raises Z rather than lowering it.

questions.s: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 5 days. A sample contains 80 g of it. How much of the isotope remains undecayed after 15 days?
questions.e: 15 days is 3 half-lives, so the mass halves three times: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 g. 27 g wrongly removes a third of the sample per 5 days in equal steps, as if decay were linear.

questions.s: After 24 hours only 1/16 of the original nuclei of a radioactive sample remain undecayed. What is the half-life?
questions.e: 1/16 = (1/2)⁴, so 24 h is 4 half-lives and T½ = 6 h. 1.5 h divides 24 by 16 instead of by the number of halvings.

questions.s: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 10 days. What fraction of its nuclei has decayed after 30 days?
questions.e: 30 days = 3 half-lives, so (1/2)³ = 1/8 remains and 1 − 1/8 = 7/8 has decayed. 1/8 is the fraction remaining, not the fraction decayed.

questions.s: How can the half-life of a given radioactive isotope be changed?
o: It stays the same whatever is done physically or chemically
Heating the sample strongly shortens its half-life
Combining it in a chemical compound always lengthens its half-life
Halving the mass of the sample halves its half-life
questions.e: Radioactive decay is a property of the nucleus, which is not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical bonding (these involve only the outer electrons). The half-life is also independent of the amount of sample.

questions.s: A narrow beam containing α, β⁻ and γ radiation passes through a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the beam. What is observed?
o: α and β rays bend the same way; γ rays are undeflected
Only γ rays are deflected, because they carry the most energy
All three are deflected, β rays the least
α and β rays bend in opposite directions; γ rays are undeflected
questions.e: α particles are positive and β⁻ particles negative, so the magnetic force pushes them to opposite sides. γ rays are uncharged electromagnetic waves and are not deflected. β particles actually bend the most, because of their tiny mass.

questions.s: In Rutherford's reaction ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + X, what is particle X?
questions.e: Mass number: 14 + 4 = 17 + A gives A = 1. Charge: 7 + 2 = 8 + Z gives Z = 1. So X is ¹₁H, a proton. A neutron has Z = 0 and would leave the charge unbalanced.

questions.s: In the reaction ⁹₄Be + ⁴₂He → ¹²₆C + X, what is particle X?
questions.e: Mass number: 9 + 4 = 12 + A gives A = 1. Charge: 4 + 2 = 6 + Z gives Z = 0. So X is a neutron, ¹₀n (this is how Chadwick's neutron was produced). A proton would make the total charge 7 on the right.

questions.s: How much energy is equivalent to a mass of 1.0 g? Take c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
questions.e: E = mc² = 1.0 × 10⁻³ × (3.0 × 10⁸)² = 9.0 × 10¹³ J. 9.0 × 10¹⁶ J is the value for 1 kg, and 3.0 × 10⁵ J forgets to square c.

questions.s: A proton has mass 1.0073 u, a neutron 1.0087 u and a deuteron (²₁H nucleus) 2.0136 u. Taking 1 u equivalent to 931 MeV, what is the binding energy of the deuteron, approximately?
questions.e: Mass defect Δm = 1.0073 + 1.0087 − 2.0136 = 0.0024 u, so the binding energy is 0.0024 × 931 ≈ 2.2 MeV. 1.1 MeV is the binding energy per nucleon, and 1.9 × 10³ MeV converts the whole deuteron mass instead of the mass defect.

questions.s: Which of the following is a nuclear fusion reaction?
questions.e: Fusion joins light nuclei into a heavier one: deuterium and tritium fuse into helium. The uranium–neutron reaction is fission, and the other two are α decay and β⁻ decay.

questions.s: Which statement about the binding energy per nucleon of nuclei is correct?
o: It is largest for the heaviest nuclei, such as uranium-238 and thorium
It is larger for fission fragments than for uranium, so fission absorbs energy
It peaks near iron, so both fission and fusion can release energy
It is the same for all nuclei, so mass defect depends only on nucleon number
questions.e: The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve peaks near iron (A ≈ 56). Splitting a heavy nucleus or joining light ones moves towards the peak, so the products are more tightly bound and energy is released in both cases. Fragments being more tightly bound means fission releases energy, not absorbs it.

questions.s: Which statement about a nuclear fission reactor is correct?
o: Control rods slow neutrons down so that more fission occurs
A chain reaction can occur in uranium of any size or mass
The moderator absorbs neutrons to stop the chain reaction
Control rods absorb neutrons to control the reaction rate
questions.e: Control rods (e.g. cadmium or boron) absorb neutrons, and moving them in or out sets the reaction rate. The moderator (water or graphite) slows neutrons down so they cause fission more easily. A chain reaction needs at least the critical mass.

questions.s: In Rutherford's α-scattering experiment on thin gold foil, most α particles passed straight through, but a very few were deflected through more than 90°. What did he conclude?
o: The positive charge is spread out evenly through the whole atom
Nearly all the mass and positive charge sit in a tiny nucleus
Electrons occupy only certain allowed orbits
Most α particles bounce straight back from the gold foil
questions.e: Most particles passing straight through means the atom is mostly empty; the rare large deflections need a strong force from a tiny, massive, positive centre. A spread-out positive charge (Thomson's model) could only cause small deflections. Allowed orbits came later from Bohr, not from this experiment.

questions.s: What is the energy of a photon of frequency 1.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz? Take h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
questions.e: E = hν = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 1.5 × 10¹⁵ = 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. 4.4 × 10⁻⁴⁹ J divides h by ν, and 9.9 × 10⁻²⁰ J slips a power of ten.

questions.s: Photons of energy 6.0 eV strike a metal whose work function is 4.5 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons?
questions.e: E_k,max = hν − W = 6.0 − 4.5 = 1.5 eV. Part of the photon energy is used to free the electron, so the electron cannot have the full 6.0 eV, and adding W (10.5 eV) is the wrong direction.

questions.s: A metal has a work function of 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Photons of energy 3.0 eV fall on it. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons in joules? Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
questions.e: Photon energy = 3.0 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so E_k,max = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ − 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (that is, 1.0 eV). 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J is the whole photon energy, forgetting the work function.

questions.s: Which statement about wave–particle duality is correct?
o: Light behaves only as a wave and electrons only as particles
Both light and matter particles show wave and particle properties
Only objects heavier than atoms can have a de Broglie wavelength
A photon carries energy but has no momentum
questions.e: Light shows interference (wave) and the photoelectric effect (particle); electrons show diffraction (wave) as well as particle behaviour. Every moving particle has λ = h/p, and a photon has momentum p = h/λ even though it has no rest mass.

questions.s: The energy levels of hydrogen are E_n = −13.6/n² eV. What photon energy is emitted when the electron drops from n = 2 to n = 1?
questions.e: E₂ = −3.4 eV and E₁ = −13.6 eV, so the photon energy is −3.4 − (−13.6) = 10.2 eV (the first Lyman line). 17.0 eV adds the two level values instead of subtracting.

questions.s: Many hydrogen atoms are excited to the n = 3 level. As they return to the ground state, at most how many different spectral lines can be emitted?
questions.e: The possible jumps are 3 → 2, 3 → 1 and 2 → 1, so 3 lines (number of pairs = 3 × 2/2). Answering 2 counts only the direct jumps from n = 3 and misses 2 → 1.

questions.s: How many neutrons are in the nucleus ¹⁴₆C?
questions.e: N = A − Z = 14 − 6 = 8. 14 is the total number of nucleons, and 6 is the number of protons.

questions.s: Carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C) is a β⁻ emitter. Which nucleus does it decay into?
questions.e: In β⁻ decay a neutron becomes a proton, so Z rises by 1 and A is unchanged: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e. ¹⁴₅B lowers Z, which would need positron emission.

questions.s: An isotope has a half-life of 10 days. How long does it take until only 1/8 of the original nuclei remain undecayed?
questions.e: 1/8 = (1/2)³, so 3 half-lives are needed: 3 × 10 = 30 days. 80 days multiplies the half-life by 8, treating the decay as linear.

questions.s: A sample contains 64 mg of an isotope with a half-life of 2 hours. What mass of the isotope remains after 8 hours?
questions.e: 8 h is 4 half-lives, so 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 mg. 16 mg divides by 4 (the number of half-lives) instead of by 2⁴ = 16.

questions.s: Which of the following radiations is the most penetrating?
questions.e: γ rays are uncharged electromagnetic waves that ionise weakly, so they lose energy slowly and need thick lead or concrete to absorb them. α particles are the least penetrating and are stopped by paper.

questions.s: In the fission reaction ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + x ¹₀n, what is the value of x?
questions.e: Mass number: 235 + 1 = 141 + 92 + x, so x = 236 − 233 = 3. The charges already balance (92 = 56 + 36). Forgetting the incoming neutron gives x = 2.

questions.s: In the fusion reaction ²₁H + ²₁H → ³₂He + X, what is X?
questions.e: Mass number: 2 + 2 = 3 + A gives A = 1. Charge: 1 + 1 = 2 + Z gives Z = 0. So X is a neutron. A proton would make the total charge 3 on the right.

questions.s: In the reaction ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n, the masses are: ²₁H 2.0141 u, ³₁H 3.0160 u, ⁴₂He 4.0026 u and ¹₀n 1.0087 u. Taking 1 u equivalent to 931 MeV, how much energy is released?
questions.e: Mass before = 5.0301 u, mass after = 5.0113 u, so Δm = 0.0188 u and E = 0.0188 × 931 ≈ 17.5 MeV. Answering 1.75 × 10³ MeV comes from a decimal-place slip in Δm.

questions.s: A metal has a work function of 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is the longest wavelength of light that can eject photoelectrons from it? Take h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
questions.e: At the threshold hc/λ₀ = W, so λ₀ = hc/W = 1.98 × 10⁻²⁵/3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m (600 nm). Longer wavelengths have less photon energy and eject nothing. 5.0 × 10¹⁴ is the threshold frequency in hertz, not a wavelength.

questions.s: In the Bohr model of hydrogen the orbit radii are r_n = n²r₁. When the electron moves from n = 1 to n = 3, by what factor does its orbit radius increase?
questions.e: r₃/r₁ = 3² = 9. Answering 3 times assumes the radius is proportional to n rather than n².

questions.s: Which list orders the radiations from least penetrating to most penetrating?
questions.e: α particles are stopped by paper, β particles by a few millimetres of aluminium, and γ rays need thick lead. So the order of increasing penetration is α, β, γ; ionising power runs the other way.

questions.s: A nucleus emits one α particle. How do its mass number A and proton number Z change?
o: A decreases by 4, Z decreases by 2
A decreases by 2, Z decreases by 4
A is unchanged, Z increases by 1
A decreases by 4, Z increases by 2
questions.e: An α particle is ⁴₂He, carrying away 4 nucleons and 2 protons, so A falls by 4 and Z by 2. 'A unchanged, Z up by 1' describes β⁻ decay.

questions.s: A thorium nucleus ²³²₉₀Th undergoes two α decays followed by one β⁻ decay. Which nucleus is produced?
questions.e: Two α decays: A = 232 − 8 = 224 and Z = 90 − 4 = 86. One β⁻ decay: A stays 224 and Z rises to 87, giving ²²⁴₈₇Fr. ²²⁴₈₆Rn forgets the β⁻ decay.

questions.s: When photons of energy 4.0 eV fall on a metal, the stopping voltage is 1.5 V. What is the work function of the metal, and would photons of energy 2.0 eV eject electrons from it?
questions.e: E_k,max = eU_c = 1.5 eV, so W = 4.0 − 1.5 = 2.5 eV. A 2.0 eV photon has less energy than the work function, so no electrons are emitted however bright the light. 5.5 eV adds instead of subtracting.
